The senses are our first and proper judges, and they perceive things only through external accidents; no wonder, then, that throughout the service of our society there is so constant and universal a mixture of ceremonies and surface appearances — to the point that the best and most effective part of our politics consists in just these. We are still dealing with man, whose condition is wonderfully bodily. Let those who, in recent years, have wanted to set up for us such a contemplative and immaterial exercise of religion not be surprised if there are some who think it would have vanished and melted through their fingers had it not held itself up among us more as a banner, title, and instrument of division and faction than by itself. As in conference, the gravity, robe, and fortune of the speaker often give weight to vain arguments and idle words, it is hard not to assume that a man so attended and feared has more than ordinary capacity, and that one to whom the king has given so many offices, commissions, and charges, so proud and supercilious, has a great deal more in him than another who greets him from a respectful distance and holds no office at all. Not only the words but the very grimaces of these people are considered and weighed, with everyone making it his business to give them some fine, solid interpretation. If they stoop to common conversation, and you offer anything but approval and reverence, they knock you down with the authority of their experience: they have heard, they have seen, they have done such-and-such; you are crushed under examples. I would gladly tell them that the fruit of a surgeon's experience is not the history of his practice and his remembering that he has cured four people of the plague and three of the gout, unless he knows how to extract from this something on which to form his judgment, and to make us feel that he has thereby become more skilled in his art. As in a concert of instruments, we don't hear a lute, a harpsichord, or a flute by itself, but one entire harmony, the result of all together. If travel and offices have improved them, it's the product of their understanding to make it show. It's not enough to count up experiences — they must be weighed, sorted, and distilled to extract the reasons and conclusions they carry within them. There were never so many historians; it is indeed good, and useful, to read them, for they everywhere furnish us with excellent and praiseworthy lessons from the magazine of their memory, which is doubtless of great help in living. But that's not what we are looking for now: we are asking whether these relaters and collectors of things are themselves worth anything.

I hate all sorts of tyranny, in word and in deed. I am very ready to set myself against those vain trappings that deceive our judgment through the senses; and keeping a close eye on those extraordinary greatnesses, I find that at best they are men just like the rest:
"Rarus enim ferme sensus communis in illa Fortuna."
["For in those high fortunes, common sense is generally rare." — Juvenal, viii. 73.]

Perhaps we esteem and look up to them at less than they really are, because they undertake more and expose themselves more; they don't measure up to the burden they have taken on. There has to be more vigour and strength in the carrier than in the load. A man who has not lifted as much as he can leaves you to guess that he still has strength in reserve, that he has not been tested to the limit of what he can do; a man who collapses under his load lays his best on display, along with the weakness of his shoulders. This is why we see so many silly souls among the learned — more of them than among those of better stock. They would have made good farmers, good merchants, and good artisans; their natural vigour was cut to that proportion. Knowledge is a thing of great weight, and they sink under it. Their understanding has neither the vigour nor the dexterity to display and distribute, to put to use, this rich and powerful matter. It has prevailing power only in a strong nature, and such natures are very rare — and the weak ones, says Socrates, corrupt the dignity of philosophy in the handling. It seems useless and vicious when lodged in an ill-formed mind. They spoil themselves and make fools of themselves:
"Humani qualis simulator simius oris, Quem puer arridens pretioso stamine serum Velavit, nudasque nates ac terga reliquit, Ludibrium mensis."

["Just like an ape, that mimic of the human face, whom a teasing boy has dressed up in rich silks above but left the lower parts bare, for a laughing-stock at the tables." — Claudian, in Eutrop., i. 303.]

Nor is it enough for those who govern and command us, and who hold the whole world in their hands, to have a common understanding, to be able to do what we can do; they fall far below us if they are not infinitely above us. As they promise more, so they have to deliver more.

And yet for them silence is not only a face of respect and gravity, but very often of great advantage too. For when Megabyzus went to see Apelles in his painting room, he stood a long while without speaking a word, and finally began to talk about the paintings — for which he was given this blunt rebuke: "While you were silent you seemed something great, because of your chains and rich dress; but now that we have heard you speak, there is not the meanest boy in my workshop who does not despise you." Those princely ornaments, that mighty state, did not permit him to be ignorant with a common ignorance, or to speak impertinently of painting; he ought to have kept that external, presumptive knowledge intact by remaining silent. To how many of the foolish fellows of my time has a sullen, silent demeanour brought the credit of prudence and capacity!

Dignities and offices are necessarily given out more by fortune than on account of merit, and we are often wrong to blame the kings when these are misplaced; on the contrary, it is a wonder that they have such good luck where there is so little skill involved:
"Principis est virtus maxima nosse suos;"
["It is the chief virtue of a prince to know his own people." — Martial, viii. 15.]

for nature has not given them a sight that can extend to so many people, to discern which of them excels the rest, nor to see into our hearts where the knowledge of our wills and our real worth lies. They have to choose us by conjecture and groping — by family, wealth, learning, and popular reputation, all of them very feeble grounds. Whoever could find a way for kings to judge by justice and to choose men by reason would by that single thing establish a perfect form of government.

"Ah, but he brought that great affair to a successful conclusion." That is to say something, but not enough; for the saying is justly received that "we are not to judge of counsels by their outcomes." The Carthaginians punished the bad counsel of their captains even when it was salvaged by a successful issue; and the Roman people often refused a triumph for great and very advantageous victories because the general's conduct didn't match his good fortune. We commonly see, in the actions of the world, that Fortune, to show us her power in all things, and taking pride in deflating our presumption, since she could not make fools wise, has made them fortunate in rivalry with virtue. She favours most those operations the web of which is most purely her own — which is why the simplest among us bring great affairs to pass, both public and private. As Seiramnes the Persian answered those who wondered that his affairs turned out so badly when his deliberations were so wise: "I am sole master of my designs, but success is wholly in the power of fortune." These men might answer the same, only with the opposite spin. Most worldly affairs perform themselves:
"Fata viam inveniunt;"
["The destinies find the way." — Aeneid, iii. 395.]

the outcome often justifies a very foolish course of action; our interference is little more than running on by rote, and more usually a matter of custom and example than of reason. Having been amazed at the greatness of some affair, I have been told by those who carried it out how it was done, and have found nothing but very ordinary calculations. The most common and ordinary ones are perhaps the surest and most convenient in practice, if not in display. What if the plainest reasons are the best founded? The meanest, lowest, and most beaten the best suited to affairs? To maintain the authority of the counsels of kings, it is not needed that profane persons should take part in them, or see further into them than the outer barrier; he who would husband its reputation must be reverenced on credit and taken altogether. My consultation roughs out the matter a little and considers it lightly by the first face it shows; the weight and main of the business I have made a habit of leaving to heaven:
"Permitte divis caetera."
["Leave the rest to the gods." — Horace, Od., i. 9, 9.]

Good and ill fortune are, in my opinion, two sovereign powers; it is folly to think that human prudence can play the part of Fortune; and vain is the man who imagines he can grasp both causes and consequences and conduct the progress of his design by the hand — most especially vain in the deliberations of war. There was never greater circumspection and military prudence than is sometimes seen among us; can it be that men are afraid of losing themselves on the way, that they save themselves up for the end of the game? Moreover, I affirm that our wisdom and counsel for the most part submit themselves to the conduct of chance. My will and my reason are sometimes moved by one breath and sometimes by another, and many of these movements are governed without me; my reason has uncertain and accidental impulses:
"Vertuntur species animorum, et pectora motus Nunc alios, alios, dum nubila ventus agebat, Concipiunt."
["The aspects of their minds change; and they conceive now one set of ideas, now another, just so long as the wind keeps stirring the clouds." — Virgil, Georg., i. 42.]

Just observe who carry the greatest authority in cities, and who best run their own affairs; you will find they are usually men of the lowest abilities. Women, children, and madmen have had the fortune to govern great kingdoms as well as the wisest princes, and Thucydides says that the stupid more often do it than men of better understanding. We attribute the effects of their good fortune to their prudence:
"Ut quisque Fortuna utitur, Ita praecellet; atque exinde sapere illum omnes dicimus;"
["He makes his way who knows how to use Fortune, and on that account we all call him wise." — Plautus, Pseudol., ii. 3, 13.]
and so I say without reservation: outcomes are a very poor testimony of our worth and parts.

Now, I was making this point — that you need only see a man promoted to high office; though three days before we held him in little regard, an image of grandeur and capacity insensibly creeps into our view, and we persuade ourselves that, since he is increased in reputation and retinue, he must be increased in merit too. We judge him not by his worth but, like counters, by the value of the place he occupies. If he happens to fall again and be mixed back into the common crowd, everyone asks in amazement how he ever came to be raised so high. "Is this him?" they say. "Did he know no more when he was up there? Do princes content themselves with so little? We were truly in good hands." This is something I have often seen in my time. Even the mere disguise of grandeur put on stage in our comedies in some sense moves and gulls us. What I myself adore in kings is the crowd of their adorers. All reverence and submission are due to them, except that of the understanding. My reason is not obliged to bow and bend; my knees are. Melanthius, asked what he thought of the tragedy of Dionysius, said, "I couldn't see it — it was so clouded over with language"; so most of those who judge the speeches of great men ought to say, "I didn't understand the words, they were so clouded with gravity, grandeur, and majesty." Antisthenes one day tried to persuade the Athenians to order their donkeys to be used in tilling the ground, just as horses were; he was told that that animal was not destined for such service. "That's all the same to me," he replied; "you have only to order it. For the most ignorant and incapable men whom you put in command of your wars promptly become worthy enough, simply because you employ them" — which is very close to the custom of so many peoples who canonise the king they have chosen from their own ranks, and are not content to honour him but must adore him. The Mexicans, after the ceremonies of their king's coronation are over, dare no longer look him in the face but, as if they had deified him by his royalty. Among the oaths they make him take to uphold their religion, their laws, and their liberties, to be valiant, just, and mild, he further swears to make the sun run its course in its accustomed light, to drain the clouds in due season, to make rivers run their course, and to make the earth bear everything necessary for his people.

I differ from this common fashion, and am more apt to suspect a man's capacity when I see it accompanied by that grandeur of fortune and public applause. We have to consider what an advantage it is to be able to speak when one pleases, to choose one's subject, to interrupt or change it with magisterial authority, to fend off others' opposition by a nod, a smile, or silence, in front of an assembly that trembles with reverence and respect. A man of prodigious fortune, when called on to give his judgment on some slight dispute foolishly started up at his table, began with these words: "It can only be a liar or a fool who says otherwise than so-and-so." Pursue that philosophical point with a dagger in your hand.

There is another observation I have made, from which I draw great benefit: in conferences and disputes, not every word that seems good is to be accepted on the spot. Most men are rich in borrowed sufficiency: someone can say a good thing, give a good answer, cite a good sentence, without at all seeing the force of either the answer or the sentence. That a man may not understand all he borrows can perhaps be verified in myself. One must not always give in straight off, however much truth or beauty seems to lie in the opposing argument; either we must firmly meet it, or back off under cover of not understanding it, so as to test on every side how it sits in the author. It may happen that we entangle ourselves and help to reinforce the point itself. I have sometimes, in the heat of combat, made answers that hit home far beyond my expectation or hope; I gave them only as filler, they were received as full weight. As, when I contend with a vigorous man, I please myself by anticipating his conclusions, easing him of the trouble of explaining himself, trying to forestall his imagination while it is still springing and incomplete — the order and pertinence of his understanding warn and threaten me from afar — I deal in quite the opposite way with the others: I must understand nothing and presuppose nothing except by them. If they pronounce in general terms, "this is good, that is bad," and happen to be right, see whether it isn't fortune that has hit it for them; let them limit and circumscribe their judgment a little, say why, or how it is so. These universal judgments which I see everywhere are meaningless; they are like men who salute a whole crowd at once; those who really know take notice of individuals and greet them by name. But it's a risky undertaking; more than every day I have seen weak understandings, eager to look clever by picking out, as they read a book, what is best and most to be admired, fix their admiration on something so ill chosen that, instead of making us see the excellence of the author, they make us see their own ignorance perfectly well. The exclamation "That's fine" is safe enough, after having heard a whole page of Virgil; that's how the cunning sort save themselves. But to undertake to follow him line by line, with a trained and tested judgment, to observe where a good author surpasses himself, weighing the words, the phrases, the inventions, his various excellences one after another — stay clear of that:
"Videndum est, non modo quid quisque loquatur, sed etiam quid quisque sentiat, atque etiam qua de causa quisque sentiat."
["A man must examine not only what each person says, but also what each one thinks, and from what reason each one thinks it." — Cicero, De Offic., i. 41.]

Every day I hear fools say things that aren't foolish. They say a good thing; let's see how far they understand it, where they got it from, and what they mean by it. We help them make use of this fine expression, this fine sentence which isn't theirs; they only have it on loan; they've blurted it out at random; we set it up for them in credit and esteem. You're lending them a hand. To what end? They don't feel they owe you anything for it, and they grow even more inept. Don't help them; let them alone. They will handle the matter like people afraid of burning their fingers; they dare neither change its position nor light, nor break into it; jolt it ever so slightly, and it slips through their fingers; they let it go, however strong or beautiful it may be. They are fine weapons, but poorly hafted. How many times have I seen this proved? Now, if you go and explain something to them and try to confirm them in it, they snatch at it and immediately rob you of the credit of your interpretation: "That's just what I was about to say; that was exactly my idea; if I didn't express it that way, it was for lack of the right words." Hot air! Even malice must be brought into play to correct this arrogant ignorance. The doctrine of Hegesias, "that we are neither to hate nor accuse, but to instruct," is right elsewhere; but here it is injustice and inhumanity to help and set right a man who needs no help and is the worse for it. I love to let them sink deeper into the mire — so deep, if possible, that they may at last see their own error.

Folly and absurdity are not to be cured by mere admonition; what Cyrus answered to the man who urged him to harangue his army on the point of battle — "that men do not become valiant and warlike on the sudden, by a fine speech, any more than a man becomes a good musician by hearing a fine song" — may properly be said of an admonition like this. These are apprenticeships to be served beforehand, by long and continued training. We owe this care, this assiduity of correction and instruction, to our own people; but to go and preach to the first passer-by, to become tutor to the ignorance and folly of the first man we meet — that is a thing I detest. I rarely do it, even in private conversation, and would rather give the whole thing up than launch into these elementary, schoolmasterly lessons. My temper is unfit either to speak or write for beginners; but as for things said in common conversation, or in passing, I never oppose them by word or sign, however false or absurd.

As for the rest, nothing vexes me so much in folly as that it is more satisfied with itself than any sane reason can reasonably be. It is unfortunate that prudence forbids us to satisfy and trust ourselves, and always sends us away timorous and discontented, while obstinacy and rashness fill those possessed by them with joy and assurance. It is the most ignorant who look at other men over their shoulder, always coming back from the combat full of joy and triumph. And what's more, this arrogance of speech and gaiety of countenance usually gives them the upper hand in the audience's opinion, which is commonly weak and incapable of judging and discerning the real advantage. Obstinacy of opinion and heat in argument are the surest proofs of folly; is there anything so assured, resolute, disdainful, contemplative, serious, and grave as the donkey?

May we not include under the heading of conference and communication the quick and sharp repartees which mirth and familiarity introduce among friends, pleasantly and wittily jesting and rallying with one another? It's an exercise for which my natural cheerfulness makes me fit enough, and which, if not as tense and serious as the other I mentioned, is, as Lycurgus thought, no less keen and ingenious, and no less useful. For my part, I contribute more freedom than wit to it, and have more luck in it than invention; but I am perfect at taking it, for I endure a comeback that is not only tart but indiscreet too, without being at all moved; and when anyone attacks me, if I don't have a brisk answer ready straight away, I don't bother to pursue the point with a tedious and impertinent contest verging on obstinacy — I let it pass, drop my ears cheerfully, and put off my revenge to another and better time. There's no merchant who always wins. Most men change their countenance and voice when their wits fail them, and through ill-timed anger, instead of taking revenge, betray at once their folly and their impatience. In this kind of jollity, we sometimes pinch the secret strings of our imperfections which, at a graver moment, we could not touch without offence — and so we usefully give one another a hint of our defects. There are other kinds of horseplay, rude and indiscreet, in the French manner, which I hate mortally; my skin is very tender and sensitive. In my time I have seen two princes of the blood put in their graves on that very account. It is unhandsome to fight in play. For the rest, when I have a mind to judge anyone, I ask him how far he is content with himself, how much his speech or his work pleases him. I will have none of those fine excuses: "I only did it in sport,
'Ablatum mediis opus est incudibus istud.'
["That work was taken from the anvil half finished." — Ovid, Trist., i. 6, 29.]

I wasn't an hour at it; I haven't looked at it since." Well then, I say, set those aside and give me a finished one, the sort you'd have yourself measured by. And then, what do you think is the best thing in your work? Is it this part, or that? Is it the grace, the matter, the invention, the judgment, or the learning? For I find that men are usually as wide of the mark in judging their own work as they are in judging other people's — not only because of the affection they have for it, but for want of the capacity to know and distinguish it. The work, by its own force and fortune, may second the workman and sometimes outstrip him, beyond his invention and knowledge. For my part, I judge the value of other men's work more obscurely than that of my own; and I rate the Essays, now high, now low, with great doubt and inconstancy. There are several books that are useful because of their subjects, from which the author gets no praise; and good books, like good works, that shame their workman. I may write about the manner of our feasts and the fashion of our clothes, and write them ill; I may publish the edicts of my time and the letters of princes that pass from hand to hand; I may make an abridgment of a good book (and every abridgment of a good book is a foolish abridgment), which book then gets lost; and so on — posterity will get singular use out of such compositions, but what honour will I have from them, except by great good luck? Most famous books are of this kind.

When I read Philippe de Commines, doubtless a very good author, several years ago, I noticed this as no commonplace saying: "That a man must take care not to do his master so great a service that at last he won't know how to give him his just reward." But I ought to commend the invention, not him, because I came across it in Tacitus not long ago:
"Beneficia eo usque laeta sunt, dum videntur exsolvi posse; ubi multum antevenere, pro gratia odium redditur;"
["Benefits are welcome only as long as they seem capable of being repaid; when they go much beyond that, hatred is returned instead of thanks." — Tacitus, Annal., iv. 18.]
and Seneca puts it vigorously:
"Nam qui putat esse turpe non reddere, non vult esse cui reddat:"
["For he who thinks it shameful not to repay does not wish the man to be alive to whom he owes the return." — Seneca, Ep., 81.]
Q. Cicero puts it less pointedly:
"Qui se non putat satisfacere, amicus esse nullo modo potest."
["He who does not think he has done enough can in no way be a friend." — Q. Cicero, De Petitione Consulatus, c. 9.]

The subject, depending on what it is, may make an author look learned and of good memory; but to judge in him the parts that are most truly his own and most worthy — the vigour and beauty of his soul — one must first know what is his own and what is not; and in what is not his own, how much we owe him for the choice, arrangement, ornament, and language in which he has presented it. What if he has borrowed the matter and spoiled the form, as often happens? We, who are little read in books, find ourselves in this fix: when we meet a high-flying fancy in some new poet, or a strong argument in a preacher, we still don't dare to praise it until we have first asked some learned man whether it is the writer's own wit or borrowed from someone else; until then I always stay on my guard.

I have lately been reading right through the history of Tacitus, without interrupting it with anything else (which rarely happens with me — it being twenty years since I have stayed with any one book for an hour together), and I did it at the urging of a gentleman whom France much esteems, both for his own worth and on account of the constant form of capacity and virtue that runs through many of his brothers. I don't know any author who, in a public narrative, mixes in so much consideration of manners and individual inclinations; and I am of quite the opposite opinion to him, holding that, since he had especially to follow the lives of the emperors of his time, so various and extreme in every sort of form, and so many notable acts as their cruelty in particular produced in their subjects, he had a stronger and more attractive matter to handle than if he had had to describe battles and general upheavals. So I often find him sterile, hurrying over those brave deaths as if he feared to weary us with their number and length. This form of history is by far the most useful; public movements depend mostly on the conduct of fortune, private ones on our own. It is rather a judgment than a narration of history; there are more precepts in it than stories; it is not a book to read, it is a book to study and learn from; it is full of sententious opinions, right or wrong; it is a nursery of ethical and political discourses for the use and ornament of those who have any place in the government of the world. He always argues by strong and solid reasons, after a pointed and subtle manner, according to the affected style of that age, which was so in love with an inflated manner that, where point and subtlety were lacking in the matter, it supplied them with lofty and swelling words. The style is not unlike Seneca's: I find Tacitus more sinewy, and Seneca more sharp. His pen seems most suited to a troubled and sickly state, such as ours at present is; you would often say he paints and pinches us.

Those who doubt his good faith accuse themselves sufficiently of being his enemy on some other account. His opinions are sound, and lean to the right side in Roman affairs. And yet I am angry with him for judging Pompey more severely than is consistent with the opinion of those worthy men who lived in the same age and had dealings with him — and for having reckoned him on a par with Marius and Sylla, except that Pompey was more guarded. Other writers have not cleared his intentions in the management of affairs of ambition and revenge; even his friends were afraid that victory would have carried him beyond the bounds of reason — but not to so immeasurable a degree as theirs. Nothing in his life threatened such open cruelty and tyranny. Nor should we set suspicion against evidence; and so I do not believe Plutarch on this point. That Tacitus's narrations were genuine and straightforward may perhaps be argued from this very thing: that they do not always square with the conclusions of his judgments, which he follows according to the bias he has taken, often beyond the matter he presents — which he has not deigned to alter in the slightest. He needs no excuse for having approved the religion of his time, as the laws enjoined, and for having been ignorant of the true one; that was his misfortune, not his fault.

I have chiefly considered his judgment, and am not entirely satisfied with it throughout — as with these words in the letter that Tiberius, old and sick, sent to the senate: "What shall I write to you, sirs, or how should I write to you, or what should I not write to you at this time? May the gods and goddesses lay a worse punishment upon me than I am daily tormented with, if I know!" I don't see why he should so positively apply them to a sharp remorse tormenting Tiberius's conscience; at any rate, when I was in the same condition, I felt no such thing.

And this also seemed to me a little mean of him: that, having to say he had held an honourable office in Rome, he excuses himself by saying he doesn't mention it out of ostentation. That seems mean, I say, for such a soul as his; for not to speak frankly of oneself implies some want of courage. A man of solid and lofty judgment, who judges soundly and surely, makes use of his own example on every occasion, just as he does of other people's, and gives evidence about himself as freely as about a third party. We are to set aside these common rules of civility in favour of truth and freedom. I dare not only to speak of myself, but to speak only of myself; when I write of anything else, I lose my way and wander from my subject. I am not so indiscreetly in love with myself, so wholly mixed up with and bound to myself, that I cannot distinguish and consider myself apart, as I do a neighbour or a tree. It is equally a fault not to see how far one's worth extends, and to say more than a man finds in himself. We owe more love to God than to ourselves, and yet know him less, and speak of him as much as we please.

If the writings of Tacitus reveal anything true about his qualities, he was a great personage, upright and bold, of a virtue not superstitious but philosophical and generous. One may think him bold in his reporting — as where he tells us that a soldier carrying a load of wood had his hands so frozen and so stuck to the load that they stayed clenched and dead on it, severed from his arms. In such things I always defer to the authority of so great a witness.

What he also says — that Vespasian, by the favour of the god Serapis, cured a blind woman at Alexandria by anointing her eyes with his spittle, and I don't know what other miracle — he says following the example and duty of all his good historians. They record every event of importance; and among public happenings are the popular rumours and opinions. It is their part to relate common beliefs, not to regulate them; that part belongs to divines and philosophers, the directors of consciences. And so this fellow historian of his, and a great man like himself, very wisely said:
"Equidem plura transcribo, quam credo: nam nec affirmare sustineo, de quibus dubito, nec subducere quae accepi;"
["Truly, I set down more things than I believe, for I can neither affirm what I doubt, nor suppress what I have heard." — Quintus Curtius, ix.]
and this other:
"Haec neque affirmare neque refellere operae pretium est; famae rerum standum est."
["It is not worth the trouble to affirm or refute these things; we must stand by report." — Livy, i., Praef., and viii. 6.]

And writing in an age when belief in prodigies was beginning to decline, he says he would not, even so, leave off including them in his Annals and giving an account of things received by so many worthy men, and with such reverence of antiquity. Very well said. Let them deliver history to us more as they have received it than as they themselves believe it. I, who am sovereign over the matter I treat, and accountable to no one, do not, even so, always believe myself. I often hazard sallies of my own wit, in which I have much doubt of myself, and certain verbal quibbles at which I shake my own ears; but I let them go at a venture. I see that others get a reputation by such things: it is not for me alone to judge. I present myself standing and lying, before and behind, on my right and on my left, in all my natural postures. Wits, though equal in force, are not always equal in taste and application.
This is what my memory presents to me roughly, and with uncertainty enough; all judgments in the rough are weak and imperfect.

title: Of vanity
paragraphs: There is, perhaps, no more obvious vanity than to write about it so vainly. What divinity has so divinely set down for us ought to be carefully and continually meditated by men of understanding. Who does not see that I have taken a road on which, ceaselessly and without effort, I shall keep going as long as there is ink and paper in the world? I cannot give an account of my life through my actions; fortune has placed them too low: I have to do it through my fancies. And yet I have known a gentleman who communicated his life only through the workings of his belly: in his quarters you might see a display of basins lined up, seven or eight days old; that was his study, his conversation; all other talk stank in his nostrils. Here, less nauseously, are the excretions of an old mind, sometimes thick, sometimes thin, and always undigested. And when will I be done representing the constant agitation and mutation of my thoughts as they fall into my head, seeing that Diomedes wrote six thousand books on the single subject of grammar?

[It was not Diomedes but Didymus the grammarian who, as Seneca tells us (Ep. 88), wrote four — not six — thousand books on questions of vain literature, which was the chief study of the ancient grammarians. — Coste. But the number is probably exaggerated, and for books we should doubtless read pamphlets or essays.]

What, then, ought talking to produce, since prattling and the first beginnings of speech have stuffed the world with such a horrible load of volumes? So many words for the sake of words alone. O Pythagoras, why didn't you put a stop to this tempest? They accused a man called Galba in the old days of living idly; his answer was, "Every man ought to give an account of his actions, but not of his time at home." He was mistaken — justice also takes notice of those who glean after the reaper.

But there should be some legal restraint against foolish and impertinent scribblers, as there is against vagabonds and idlers; if there were, both I and a hundred others would be banished from the reach of our people. I don't say this as a joke: scribbling seems to be a symptom of a disordered and licentious age. When did we ever write as much as since our troubles? When did the Romans, as much as on the brink of ruin? Besides, the refining of wits doesn't make people wiser in a government: this idle employment springs from the fact that everyone neglects the duty of his vocation and is easily distracted from it. The corruption of the age is made up of each individual man's particular contribution; some contribute treachery, others injustice, irreligion, tyranny, avarice, cruelty, according to their power; the weaker sort contribute folly, vanity, and idleness, and I am one of those. It seems as if it were the season for vain things when the harmful ones oppress us; in a time when doing ill is common, doing what merely signifies nothing is a kind of commendation. My comfort is that I will be one of the last to be called to account; while greater offenders are being brought to book, I shall have leisure to mend, since it seems unreasonable to punish small inconveniences while we are infested with great ones. As the physician Philotimus said to a man who held out his finger to be dressed when he saw, by complexion and breath, that the man had an ulcer in his lungs: "Friend, it's not now the time to fuss with your nails."

And yet I saw, a few years ago, a person whose name and memory I hold in very great esteem publish — at the very height of our great disorders, when there was neither law nor justice nor a magistrate who did his job, no more than there is now — I don't know what pitiful little reforms about clothing, cookery, and legal chicanery. Those are amusements with which to feed an ill-used people, to show that they are not entirely forgotten. Others do the same who insist on prohibiting particular ways of speaking, dances, and games to a people utterly given over to every kind of execrable vice. It is no time to bathe and cleanse oneself when one is gripped by a violent fever; only the Spartans could afford to fall to combing and curling their hair when they were on the very brink of running headlong into mortal danger.
For my part, I have the worse habit: if my slipper goes crooked, I let my shirt and my cloak go crooked too; I scorn to mend myself by halves.

When I am in a bad way, I clamp down on the trouble; I abandon myself in despair; I let myself slide towards the precipice and, as the saying goes, "throw the helve after the hatchet"; I am stubborn in growing worse, and decide I am no longer worth my own care; I am either well or ill all through. It is a favour to me that the desolation of this kingdom falls in the desolation of my old age: I would rather have my ill multiplied than my good disturbed. The words I speak in misfortune are words of anger: my courage bristles instead of lying down; and contrary to what others do, I am more devout in good fortune than in bad, after Xenophon's precept if not his reasoning; I am more ready to raise my eyes to heaven in thanks than to beg. I am more concerned to improve my health when I am well than to restore it when I am sick; prosperity teaches and disciplines me the way adversity and the rod teach others. As if good fortune were inconsistent with good conscience, men only grow good in evil fortune. Good fortune is for me a singular spur to modesty and moderation: an entreaty wins me, a threat checks me; favour makes me bend, fear stiffens me.
Among human conditions, this is common enough: to be better pleased with foreign things than with our own, and to love innovation and change:
"Ipsa dies ideo nos grato perluit haustu, Quod permutatis hora recurrit equis:"
["The light of day itself shines more pleasantly upon us because it changes its horses every hour." Said of a water-clock, Cotton adds.]

I have my share. Those who follow the opposite extreme — being entirely satisfied and pleased with themselves, valuing what they have above all else, and deciding that no beauty could be greater than the one they see — if they are not wiser than us, they are really happier; I do not envy their wisdom, but their good fortune.

This greedy appetite for new and unknown things helps to feed my desire to travel; but plenty of other circumstances contribute to it. I am very willing to be quit of the running of my house. There is, I admit, a kind of convenience in being in command, even if only over a barn, and in being obeyed by one's own people; but it's too uniform and languid a pleasure, and it is necessarily mixed with a thousand vexing thoughts: one moment the poverty and oppression of your tenants, the next quarrels among neighbours, the next the trespasses they make upon your land afflict you;
"Aut verberatae grandine vineae, Fundusque mendax, arbore nunc aquas Culpante, nunc torrentia agros Sidera, nunc hyemes iniquas."
["Or hail-smitten vines and the deceptive farm; now trees damaged by the rains, or years of dearth, now summer's heat burning up the petals, now destructive winters." — Horace, Odes, iii. 1, 29.]
and God scarcely sends a season in six months in which your bailiff can do his work properly; if it suits the vines, it spoils the meadows:
"Aut nimiis torret fervoribus aetherius sol, Aut subiti perimunt imbres, gelidoeque pruinae, Flabraque ventorum violento turbine vexant;"
["Either the scorching sun burns up your fields, or sudden rains or frosts destroy your harvests, or a violent wind carries away all before it." — Lucretius, V. 216.]
To which add the new, neatly made shoe of the man in the old story, which hurts your foot,

[Leclerc maliciously suggests that this is a sly dig at Montaigne's wife — the man of old being the figure mentioned in Plutarch's Life of Paulus Aemilius (c. 3), who, when his friends reproached him for repudiating his wife and extolled her various merits, pointed to his shoe and said, "That looks a nice well-made shoe to you, but I alone know where it pinches."]
and that a stranger has no idea how much it costs you, what you contribute to keep up that look of order seen in your household, and perhaps how dearly you pay for it.

I came late to the running of a household: those whom nature sent into the world before me long spared me that trouble, so I had already taken another path more suited to my temper. Still, from what I have seen, running a house is more troublesome than hard; anyone capable of anything else will easily do this. If I had wanted to be rich, that route would have seemed too slow; I should have served my kings — a more profitable trade than any other. Since I aspire to nothing but the reputation of having neither gained nor squandered anything, in keeping with the rest of my life, and being fit neither for doing significant good nor significant evil, and since I only wish to go on quietly, I can manage it, thanks be to God, without much effort. At worst, you can always head off poverty by trimming your expenses; that's what I make my main concern, and I have no doubt I'll manage it before I'm forced to. As for the rest, I have settled my mind well enough to live on less than I have, and live contentedly:
"Non aestimatione census, verum victu atque cultu, terminantur pecunix modus."
["Our wealth is properly measured not by the value of our possessions, but by our daily living and tillage." — Cicero, Paradoxa, vi. 3.]

My real needs do not so wholly consume all I have that Fortune can find no edge to sink her teeth into without biting to the quick. My presence, careless and ignorant as it is, does me great service in my domestic affairs; I do involve myself in them, but it goes against the grain — finding that, even in my own house, I burn my candle at one end alone while the other is not spared either.

Journeys harm me only by their expense, which is heavy, more than I can well bear, since I am used to travelling not just adequately but with handsome equipage; I must make them shorter and rarer; I spend on them only the froth, what I have reserved for the purpose, delaying and putting off my departure until that fund is ready. I do not want the pleasure of going abroad to spoil the pleasure of being at home; on the contrary, I want them to nourish and favour each other. Fortune has helped me here: since my main profession in this life was to live at ease, idly rather than busily, she has spared me the necessity of growing rich to provide for a horde of heirs. If what I had in such ample sufficiency is not enough for one, that's his problem: his imprudence won't deserve that I should wish him more. And everyone, after Phocion's example, provides sufficiently for his children when he provides for them so as to leave them as much as was left to him. I would by no means follow Crates' method. He left his money with a banker on this condition: that if his children were fools, the banker should give it to them; if wise, he should distribute it to the most foolish of the people — as if fools, being less capable of living without riches, were more capable of using them.
At any rate, the damage caused by my absence does not seem, so long as I am able to bear it, to justify forgoing chances to amuse myself for that troublesome assistance.

There is always something going wrong. The affairs of one house, then of another, tear you to pieces; you pry into everything too closely; your perspicacity hurts you here, as it does elsewhere. I sneak away from occasions of annoyance, and turn away from knowing what is going wrong; and yet I can't manage so well that every hour I don't jostle against something that displeases me; and the tricks most carefully hidden from me are the ones I come to know soonest; some of them, just not to make things worse, a man must himself help to conceal. Vain vexations; sometimes vain, but always vexing. The smallest and slightest impediments pierce deepest; just as small letters most tire the eyes, so small affairs most disturb us. A swarm of little ills offends more than a single great one. The more numerous and slight the domestic thorns, the deeper and more unexpectedly they prick, easily catching us by surprise.

[Now Homer shows us clearly enough how surprise gives the advantage: he depicts Ulysses weeping at the death of his dog, but not weeping at his mother's tears; the first incident, trivial as it was, got the better of him by coming on him quite unexpectedly; he bore the second, though more powerful, because he was prepared for it. It is light occasions that humble our lives.]

I am no philosopher; evils oppress me according to their weight, and they weigh as much by their form as by their matter, often more. If I have more perceptiveness than the common run, I also have more patience; in short, they weigh on me even if they do not hurt me. Life is a tender thing, and easily troubled. Since age has made me more pensive and morose,
"Nemo enim resistit sibi, cum caeperit impelli,"
["For no man resists himself once he has begun to be driven forward." — Seneca, Ep., 13.]
for the most trivial cause imaginable, I irritate that mood, which afterwards feeds and exasperates itself, drawing in and piling up matter on matter to feed on:
"Stillicidi casus lapidem cavat:"
["The ever-falling drop hollows out a stone." — Lucretius, i. 314.]

these continual drippings consume and ulcerate me. Ordinary inconveniences are never light; they are continual and inseparable, especially when they spring from members of one's family. When I consider my affairs from a distance and in the lump, I find — perhaps because my memory is poor — that they have so far gone on improving beyond my reckoning or expectation; my income seems greater than it is; its prosperity tricks me. But when I look more closely at the business and see how everything actually goes:
"Tum vero in curas animum diducimus omnes;"
["Indeed we lead the mind into all sorts of cares." — Aeneid, v. 720.]

I have a thousand things to want and to fear. To give them up entirely is very easy for me; to attend to them without trouble is very hard. It is a miserable thing to be in a place where everything you see involves and concerns you; and I fancy I more cheerfully enjoy the pleasures of another man's house, with a greater and purer taste, than those of my own. Diogenes' answer suited my own temper when someone asked him what wine he liked best: "Someone else's," he said.

My father took delight in building at Montaigne, where he was born; and in the running of domestic affairs, I love to follow his example and rules, and I shall press those who come after me, as far as I can, to do the same. If I could do better for him, I would; and I am proud that his will is still being performed and acted through me. God forbid that, in my hands, I should ever let any feature of the life I am able to render to so good a father fail. And wherever I have taken in hand to strengthen some old foundations of walls and to repair some ruinous buildings, I have honestly done it more out of respect for his design than for my own satisfaction; and I am angry with myself for not having gone further to finish the beginnings he left in his house — the more so because I am very likely the last possessor of my line, and shall be the last to lay a hand on it. For as far as I personally am concerned, neither the pleasure of building, which they say is so bewitching, nor hunting, nor gardens, nor the other pleasures of a retired life can hold me much. And it's what I'm angry with myself about, as for all other opinions of mine that are inconvenient to me. I would rather have my opinions easy and convenient for life than vigorous and learned; they are true and sound enough if they are useful and agreeable. Those who hear me confess my ignorance of farming whisper in my ear that this is disdain, that I refuse to know its instruments, seasons, order, how they dress my vines and graft, the names and shapes of herbs and fruits, the cooking of the food I eat, the names and prices of the cloth I wear, because, they say, I have set my heart on some higher knowledge; that kills me. It is not disdain; it is folly, and stupidity rather than glory; I would rather be a good horseman than a good logician:
"Quin to aliquid saltem potius, quorum indiget usus, Viminibus mollique paras detexere junco."
["Why not rather do something useful — make osier and rush baskets." — Virgil, Eclog., ii. 71.]

We occupy our thoughts with the general, with universal causes and conducts, which will very well carry themselves on without our care; and leave our own business to chance, and Michael much more our concern than Man. Now, I am indeed mostly at home; but I would like to be better pleased there than anywhere else:
"Sit meae sedes utinam senectae, Sit modus lasso maris, et viarum, Militiaeque."
["Let my old age have a fixed seat; let there be a limit to fatigues from the sea, journeys, warfare." — Horace, Od., ii. 6, 6.]

I don't know whether I will manage it. I could wish that, instead of some other piece of his inheritance, my father had passed on to me the passionate affection he had in his old age for household affairs; he was happy in being able to fit his desires to his fortune and to satisfy himself with what he had. Political philosophy may condemn at length the meanness and sterility of my occupation if only I can come to relish it as he did. I hold that the most honourable calling is to serve the public and be useful to many,
"Fructus enim ingenii et virtutis, omnisque praestantiae, tum maximus capitur, quum in proximum quemque confertur:"
["For the greatest fruit of talent and virtue, and of every excellence, is gathered when it is conferred on those nearest us." — Cicero, De Amicitia, c.]

but for myself, I decline it; partly out of conscience (for where I see the weight that lies on such employments, I also see how little I have to meet it; and Plato, himself a master in all political government, nevertheless took care to abstain from it), and partly out of cowardice. I content myself with enjoying the world without fuss; only to live an excusable life, one that is neither a burden to myself nor to anyone else.

No man ever more fully and feebly suffered himself to be governed by a third person than I would, if I had anyone to whom I might entrust myself. One of my wishes at this point would be to have a son-in-law who knew how to cherish my old age handsomely and rock it to sleep — into whose hands I might place, in full sovereignty, the management and use of all my goods, that he might dispose of them as I do and earn from them what I earn, provided that, for his part, he was truly grateful and a friend. But we live in a world where the loyalty even of one's own children is unknown.

Whoever has charge of my purse on my travels has it purely and without check; he could thoroughly cheat me, if it ever came to a reckoning; and if he isn't a devil, I oblige him to deal honestly with me by such complete trust:
"Multi fallere do cuerunt, dum timent falli; et aliis jus peccandi suspicando fecerunt."
["Many have taught others to deceive while fearing to be deceived, and by their suspicions have given them a licence to do wrong." — Seneca, Ep., 3.]

The most common security I take of my people is ignorance; I never assume anyone to be vicious until I have first found him so; and I place most confidence in the younger sort, whom I judge least spoiled by bad example. I would rather be told at the end of two months that I have spent four hundred crowns than have my ears battered every night with three, five, seven; and I have, this way, been robbed as little as anyone. It is true I am quite willing not to see; up to a point I deliberately keep a vague and uncertain awareness of my money; up to a point, I am content to doubt. One must leave a little room for a servant's infidelity or indiscretion; if you have left enough overall to handle your business, let the overflow of Fortune's generosity run a little more freely at her mercy; that's the gleaner's portion. After all, I do not so much value the fidelity of my people as I despise their injury. What a low and ridiculous thing it is for a man to study his money, to delight in handling and counting it over and over! That is how avarice creeps in.

In the eighteen years I have had my estate in my own hands, I have never been able to bring myself either to read over my deeds or to examine my principal affairs, things that should of necessity pass under my knowledge and inspection. It is not a philosophical disdain for worldly and transitory things; my taste is not refined to that degree, and I value them at as great a rate, at least, as they are worth; in truth, it is an inexcusable and childish laziness and negligence. What would I not rather do than read a contract — or, like a slave to my own business, plough through those dusty papers? Or, worse still, those of another man, as so many do nowadays for money? I grudge nothing but care and trouble, and aim at nothing so much as being careless and at ease. I would have been much better suited, I believe — had it been possible without obligation and servitude — to live off another man's fortune than my own. Indeed, when I look more closely, I'm not sure whether, given my temper, what I have to suffer from my affairs and servants doesn't have something more abject, troublesome, and tormenting about it than serving a man better born than myself who would govern me with a gentle rein and a little at my own ease:
"Servitus obedientia est fracti animi et abjecti, arbitrio carentis suo."
["Servitude is the obedience of a subdued and abject mind, lacking its own free will." — Cicero, Paradoxa, V. 1.]

Crates did worse: he threw himself into the freedom of poverty just to rid himself of the inconveniences and cares of his house. That I would not do; I hate poverty as much as I hate pain; but I could be content to exchange my present way of life for one humbler and less costly.

When I am away from home, I shed all these thoughts, and would be less concerned by the ruin of a tower than I am, when present, by the fall of a tile. My mind is easily composed at a distance, but it suffers as much as that of the meanest peasant when I am at home: the reins of my bridle wrongly put on, or a strap flapping against my leg, will keep me out of humour for a whole day. I can summon my courage well enough against inconveniences; lift up my eyes I cannot:
"Sensus, o superi, sensus."
The senses, O ye gods, the senses.

At home, I am responsible for whatever goes wrong. Few masters (I speak of those of medium condition, like mine) — and if there are any, they are happier — can rely so much on another that the greater part of the burden does not lie on their own shoulders. This takes much from my grace in entertaining visitors, so that I have, perhaps, retained some more by the expectation of a good dinner than by my own manner; and I lose much of the pleasure I ought to take, in my own house, from the visits and gatherings of my friends. The most ridiculous bearing in a gentleman in his own house is to see him bustling about the business of the place, whispering to one servant, throwing an angry look at another: it ought to slide along imperceptibly, presenting an ordinary current; and I think it ugly to talk much to one's guests about the food they are getting, whether by way of bragging or apology. I love order and cleanliness —
"Et cantharus et lanx Ostendunt mihi me" —
["The dishes and the glasses show me my own reflection." — Horace, Ep., i. 5, 23.]

more than I love abundance; and at home I attend strictly to necessity, little to outward show. If a footman falls to blows at someone else's house, or stumbles and drops a dish before him as he is carrying it up, you only laugh and make a joke of it; you sleep peacefully while the master of the house is arranging tomorrow's menu with his steward. I'm speaking by my own measure; I quite appreciate, all the same, good household management in general, and how pleasant a quiet and prosperous house, carried on regularly, is to some natures; and I don't wish to fasten my own errors and inconveniences onto the thing, nor to give Plato the lie when he calls it the most pleasant employment for each man to attend to his own affairs without wronging another.

When I travel I have nothing to worry about but myself and the spending of my money, which is settled by a single rule; gathering it together takes many things, and of those I understand nothing; spending I understand a little, and how to make some show of the expense, which is indeed its principal use; but I rely on that too ambitiously, which makes my spending uneven and ill-shaped, and immoderate both ways; if it makes a show, if it serves the purpose, I let it run carelessly; and just as carelessly tie up my purse-strings, if it does not shine and does not please me. Whatever it be, whether art or nature, that imprints in us this condition of living by reference to others, it does us much more harm than good; we deprive ourselves of our own benefits in order to fit appearances to common opinion; we don't care so much what our being is, to ourselves and in reality, as what it is to public observation. Even the qualities of mind, and wisdom itself, seem fruitless to us if enjoyed only by ourselves, and not displayed for others to see and approve. There is a sort of man whose gold runs in streams underground imperceptibly; others display it all in plates and branches, so that to the one a small coin is worth a crown, to the other the reverse — the world rating its use and value by the show. All over-finical concern about riches smells of avarice; even the disposing of it, with too systematic and artificial a liberality, is not worth a painful supervision and worry: he who tries to set his spending at just so much makes it too cramped and narrow. Saving or spending are in themselves indifferent things, and take on the colour of good or ill only according to the way the will applies them.
The other thing that tempts me out onto these journeys is my unfitness for the present manners of our state. As far as the public interest goes, I could easily console myself for this corruption:
"Pejoraque saecula ferri Temporibus, quorum sceleri non invenit ipsa Nomen, et a nullo posuit natura metallo;"
["And worse than the iron ages, for whose crimes there is no parallel in any of Nature's metals." — Juvenal, xiii. 28.]

but not as far as my own concerns. I am, in particular, too much oppressed by them: for in my neighbourhood we have, of late, by the long licence of our civil wars, grown old in so riotous a form of state,
"Quippe ubi fas versum atque nefas,"
["Where right and wrong have changed places." — Virgil, Georg., i. 504.]
that, in earnest, it is a wonder how it can survive:
"Armati terram exercent, semperque recentes Convectare juvat praedas; et vivere rapto."
["Men plough armed, always delighting in fresh plunder, and living by robbery." — Aeneid, vii. 748.]

In short, I see by our own example that human society is maintained and held together at whatever cost; whatever condition men are placed in, they still close ranks and stick together, both moving and at rest; like ill-fitted bodies that, shuffled together at random, find a way of their own to unite and settle, often better than they could have been arranged by art. King Philip mustered up a rabble of the most wicked and incorrigible rascals he could find, and put them all together into a city he had built for the purpose, which took their name; I believe they formed, even out of their vices, a government among them, and a commodious and just society. I see, not one act, or three, or a hundred, but customs in common and accepted use, so ferocious — especially in inhumanity and treachery, which are to me the worst of all vices — that I cannot bear to think of them without horror; and I admire them almost as much as I detest them: the practice of these signal villainies carries with it as great signs of vigour and force of soul as of error and disorder. Necessity reconciles and brings men together; and this accidental connection later forms itself into laws. For there have been some, as savage as any human opinion could conceive, who nevertheless have maintained themselves as a body in as much health and length of life as any Plato or Aristotle could invent. And certainly all these political systems contrived by art turn out to be ridiculous and unfit for use.

Those great, tedious debates about the best form of society and the most convenient rules to bind us are debates fit only to exercise our wits; like certain arts whose whole being lies in agitation and controversy, and have no life except there. Such an ideal government might be of some value in a new world; but we take a world already made and shaped to certain customs; we do not beget it as Pyrrha or Cadmus did. By whatever means we may have the privilege to redress and reform it afresh, we can hardly wrench it from its accustomed bent without breaking everything. Solon, asked whether he had given the Athenians the best laws he could, replied, "Yes — of the ones they would accept." Varro excuses himself in the same way: if he were starting to write on religion, he would say what he believed; but seeing that it was already received, he would write according to custom rather than nature.

Not in opinion, but in truth and reality, the best and most excellent government for every nation is the one under which it has held together; its form and essential fitness depend on custom. We tend to be displeased with the present condition; but I maintain, even so, that to wish for rule by a few in a republic, or for some other sort of government than the established one in a monarchy, is both vice and folly:
"Ayme l'estat, tel que to le veois estre S'il est royal ayme la royaute; S'il est de peu, ou biers communaute, Ayme l'aussi; car Dieu t'y a faict naistre."
Love the government such as you see it to be. If it is royal, love royalty; if it is a republic of any kind, still love it; for God himself made you to be born under it.

So wrote the good Monsieur de Pibrac, whom we lately lost, a man of such excellent wit, such sound opinions, and such gentle manners. This loss, and that of Monsieur de Foix at the same time, are of such importance to the crown that I don't know whether there is another pair in France worthy to fill the places of these two Gascons in honesty and wisdom in the council of our kings. They were both, in their different ways, great men, and certainly, for the age, rare and great each in his own kind: but what destiny set them in these times — men so remote from, so disproportionate to, our corruption and internal tumults?

Nothing presses so hard on a state as innovation: change is the only thing that gives shape to injustice and tyranny. When a piece is loosened, it may be proper to prop it; one may take care that the natural alteration and corruption of things does not carry us too far from our beginnings and principles; but to undertake to lay so great a mass anew and to change the foundations of so vast a building is the work of those who, to clean, efface; who reform particular defects by a universal confusion, and cure diseases by death:
"Non tam commutandarum quam evertendarum rerum cupidi."
["Not so much desirous of changing things as of overthrowing them." — Cicero, De Officiis, ii. 1.]

The world is hard to cure; and so impatient of anything that presses on it that it thinks of nothing but shaking itself loose at any price. We see by a thousand examples that it ordinarily cures itself to its own cost. The discharge of a present evil is no cure unless there is a general mending of condition. The surgeon's aim isn't simply to cut away the dead flesh; that is only a stage of his cure: beyond that, he means to fill up the wound with better and more natural flesh, and to restore the limb to its proper state. Whoever proposes only to remove what offends him falls short, for good does not necessarily succeed evil; another evil may succeed, and a worse — as it did with Caesar's murderers, who brought the republic to such a pass that they had reason to regret meddling with it. The same has happened since to many others, even in our own day; the French, my contemporaries, know it well enough. All great mutations shake and disorder a state.

Anyone who would look squarely at a cure and weigh it well before he began would be very willing to keep his hands out of it. Pacuvius Calavius corrected the vice of this proceeding by a striking example. His fellow citizens were in mutiny against their magistrates; being a man of great authority in Capua, he found a way one day to shut up the senators in the palace; then, calling the people together in the marketplace, he told them that the day had now come when they could, at full liberty, revenge themselves on the tyrants who had so long oppressed them — whom he had now, alone and unarmed, at their mercy. He then advised that they should call these out, one by one, by lot, deciding individually about each, and have whatever was decreed immediately executed; with this proviso, that they should at the same time appoint some honest man in place of the one condemned, so that there would be no vacancy in the Senate. They had no sooner heard the name of one senator than a great cry of general dislike went up against him. "I see," says Pacuvius, "we must throw him out; he is a bad fellow; let us look out for a good one in his place." Immediately there was profound silence, every man at a loss whom to choose. But one, bolder than the rest, having named his man, an even greater chorus of opposition arose, with a hundred imperfections laid to his charge and as many good reasons why he should not stand. As these conflicting moods grew hot, things went worse with the second senator, and worse with the third, with as much disagreement in electing new ones as agreement in throwing out the old. In the end, growing tired of this fruitless commotion, they began, one way and another, to steal out of the assembly, every man carrying back this resolution in his mind: that the oldest and best-known evil is more bearable than one that is new and untried.
Seeing how miserably we are agitated (for what have we not done!) —
"Eheu! cicatricum, et sceleris pudet, Fratrumque: quid nos dura refugimus AEtas? quid intactum nefasti Liquimus? Unde manus inventus Metu Deorum continuit? quibus Pepercit aris."

["Alas! our scars, our crimes, our fratricides are a shame to us! What crime does this hard age shrink from? What wickedness have we left untouched? What youth has been held back from evil by the fear of the gods? What altar is spared?" — Horace, Od., i. 33, 35.]
I do not at once conclude,
"Ipsa si velit Salus, Servare prorsus non potest hanc familiam;"
["If the goddess Salus herself wished to save this family, she absolutely cannot." — Terence, Adelph., iv. 7, 43.]

we are perhaps not at our last gasp. The preservation of states is, in all likelihood, a thing beyond our understanding; a civil government is, as Plato says, a mighty and powerful thing, hard to dissolve; it often holds out against mortal and internal diseases, against the injury of unjust laws, against tyranny, against the corruption and ignorance of magistrates, against the licence and sedition of the people. In all our fortunes, we compare ourselves to what is above us, and always look towards those better off; but let us measure ourselves against what is below us: there is no condition so wretched in which a man may not find a thousand examples that will give him consolation. It is our vice that we more unwillingly look at what is above than willingly at what is below; and Solon used to say that if anyone made one heap of all the ills together, there is no one who would not rather take away the ills he has than come to an equal division with every other man from that heap and take his share. Our government is, indeed, very sick; but there have been others sicker and not died. The gods play ball with us and bandy us about every way:
"Enimvero Dii nos homines quasi pilas habent."

The stars fatally destined the state of Rome to be an example of what they could do in this line: in it are gathered all the forms and adventures that can befall a state — all that order or disorder, good or ill fortune, can do. Who, then, can despair of his own condition, seeing the shocks and convulsions that toppled and tossed Rome, and yet she withstood them all? If extent of dominion is the health of a state (which I in no way think it is, and I am pleased when Isocrates instructs Nicocles not to envy princes who have large dominions but those who know how to preserve what has fallen to them), Rome was never sounder than when it was sickest. Her worst form was her most fortunate; one can hardly discern any image of government under the first emperors — it is the most horrible and tumultuous confusion imaginable; she endured it nevertheless, and lasted through it, preserving not a monarchy confined within its own bounds but so many nations so different, so remote, so disaffected, so confusedly commanded, and so unjustly conquered:
"Nec gentibus ullis Commodat in populum, terra pelagique potentem, Invidiam fortuna suam."
["Fortune never gave it to any nation to indulge its hatred against the people who were masters of sea and land." — Lucan, i. 32.]

Everything that totters does not fall. The fabric of so great a body holds by more nails than one; it holds even by its antiquity, like old buildings whose foundations are worn away by time, without rough-cast or mortar, and which yet live and support themselves by their own weight:
"Nec jam validis radicibus haerens, Pondere tuta suo est."

Besides, it is not the right way to go about it, to examine only the flank and the ditch when judging the security of a fortress; we must observe by what approach an assault may be made on it, and what condition the assailant is in. Few vessels sink under their own weight, without some outside violence. Now let us cast our eyes everywhere: everything around us totters. In all the great states known to us, both in Christendom and elsewhere, if you only look, you will see clear signs of alteration and ruin:
"Et sua sunt illis incommoda; parque per omnes Tempestas."
["They all have their share of misfortunes; the storm rages everywhere." — Aeneid, ii.]

Astrologers may very well, as they do, warn us of great revolutions and looming upheavals: their prophecies are present and palpable; they don't need to go to heaven to foretell this. There is consolation to be drawn from this universal combination of ills and threats, and even some hope of our state's continuation, since, naturally, nothing falls where everything falls: universal sickness is particular health; conformity is antagonistic to dissolution. For my part, I do not despair, and I imagine I can see ways to save us:
"Deus haec fortasse benigna Reducet in sedem vice."
["The deity will perhaps, by a favourable turn, restore us to our former position." — Horace, Epodes, xiii. 7.]

Who knows if God will make it happen as with human bodies, which purge and restore themselves to a better state by long and grievous maladies, and which then enjoy a fuller and more perfect health than they had before? What weighs most with me is that, in counting up the symptoms of our ill, I see as many natural ones, sent by Heaven and properly its own, as those that our disorder and human imprudence contribute. The very stars seem to declare that we have already lasted long enough, and beyond the ordinary term. This too distresses me: that the danger most pressing on us is not an alteration in the whole solid mass but its dissolution and tearing apart — which is the most extreme of our fears.

Moreover, in these fancies of mine, I fear the treachery of my memory, lest by inadvertence it should make me write the same thing twice. I hate to examine myself, and never review what has once escaped my pen, except very unwillingly. I set down nothing new here. These are common thoughts; having perhaps conceived them a hundred times, I am afraid I have set them down somewhere already. Repetition is troublesome everywhere, even in Homer; but it is ruinous in things that have only a superficial and transitory show. I dislike over-insistence even in the most profitable matters, as in Seneca; and the practice of his Stoic school displeases me — of repeating on every subject, at full length and breadth, the principles and presuppositions that serve in general, and of always rehearsing the same common and universal reasons.
My memory grows cruelly worse every day:
"Pocula Lethaeos ut si ducentia somnos, Arente fauce traxerim;"
["As if my dry throat had drunk seducing cups of Lethean oblivion." — Horace, Epodes, xiv. 3.]

I shall be forced from now on (for so far, thank God, nothing has gone much amiss) — where others seek time and opportunity to think over what they have to say — to avoid all preparation, for fear of tying myself to some obligation I must then keep up. To be bound and tied to a thing puts me quite out, and so does depending on so weak an instrument as my memory. I never read the following story without a personal and natural resentment: Lyncestes, accused of conspiracy against Alexander, was brought out before the army on the day appointed (according to custom) to be heard in his defence. He had learned a studied speech, of which, hesitating and stammering, he got out some words. Growing more and more confused, struggling with his memory, trying to recollect what he had to say, the soldiers nearest him charged their pikes against him and killed him, treating him as already convicted; his confusion and silence served them as a confession; having had so much leisure to prepare himself in prison, they concluded that it wasn't his memory that failed him, but his conscience that tied his tongue and stopped his mouth. And, truly, well said: the place, the crowd, the expectation, knock a man flat, even when his only ambition is to speak well; what can a man do when it is a speech on which his life depends?

For my part, just being tied to what I am to say is enough to undo me. When I wholly commit and entrust myself to my memory, I lean so hard on it that it buckles under me; it grows dismayed at the burden. The more I trust it, the more I put myself out of my own power, even to the point of finding it hard to keep my countenance; I have sometimes been very hard put to it to hide the slavery I was in, when my whole design in speaking is to show a perfect calm of face and voice, with casual unpremeditated movements, as if rising from the occasion itself — choosing rather to say nothing to the point than to show I had come prepared to speak well, a thing especially unbecoming in a man of my profession, and laying too great a burden on one who can hold little in his head. The preparation begets a great deal more expectation than it will satisfy. A man often strips down to his doublet to leap no further than he would in his gown:
"Nihil est his, qui placere volunt, turn adversarium, quam expectatio."
["Nothing is so adverse to those whose business it is to please as expectation." — Cicero, Acad., ii. 4.]

It is recorded of the orator Curio that when he proposed to divide his oration into three or four parts, or three or four arguments or reasons, it often happened that he either forgot one or added one or two more. I have always avoided falling into this difficulty, having ever hated such promises and prescriptions, not only from distrust of my memory but also because the method smells too much of the rhetorician:
"Simpliciora militares decent."
["Simplicity becomes warriors." — Quintilian, Instit. Orat., xi. 1.]

It is enough that I have promised myself never again to take it upon me to speak in a place of distinction; for as for speaking from a written text, besides being very absurd, it is a great disadvantage to those who could naturally give it grace by action; and relying on the mercy of my off-the-cuff invention I would do still less; mine is heavy and tangled, and would never serve me in sudden and important emergencies.

Permit, reader, this essay also its own course, and let this third sitting finish the rest of my picture: I add, but I do not correct. First, because I hold that a man, having once parted with his labours to the world, has no further right to them; let him do better, if he can, in some new undertaking, but not adulterate what he has already sold. Of such dealers, nothing should be bought until they are dead. Let them think well about what they do before bringing it into the light: who hurries them? My book is always the same, except that on every new edition (so that the buyer may not go away empty-handed) I take the liberty to add (it being but ill-jointed marquetry) some supernumerary ornament; this is just overweight, which does not disfigure the original form of the essays, but, by a little artful subtlety, gives a kind of particular value to each of the ones that follow. From this, however, will easily arise some transposition of chronology, my stories taking their place by aptness, not always by age.

Secondly, because, where I myself am concerned, I am afraid of losing by change: my understanding does not always march forward, it marches backward too. I do not much less mistrust my fancies for being the second or the third than for being the first, the present, or the past; we often correct ourselves as foolishly as we do others. I am many years older than I was at my first publications, which were in 1580; but I doubt very much whether I have grown an inch wiser. I now, and I a moment ago, are two different persons; but whether I am better, I cannot say. It would be a fine thing to be old if we only travelled towards improvement; but it is a drunken, stumbling, reeling, infirm motion, like that of reeds which the air casually waves to and fro at its pleasure. Antiochus, in his youth, had written strongly in favour of the Academy; in his old age he wrote as much against it. Whichever of these two I followed, would I not still be following Antiochus? Having first established the uncertainty, to go about establishing the certainty of human opinions, was it not to establish doubt, not certainty, and to promise that, if he had yet another lifetime, he would always be on the verge of altering his judgment — not so much for the better as for something else?

The public favour has given me a little more confidence than I expected; but what I most fear is that I should glut the world with my writings; I would rather, of the two, sting my reader than tire him, as a certain learned man of my time has done.
