Praise is always pleasing, no matter from whom or on what account; yet a man ought to understand why he is being commended, that he may know how to keep up the same reputation: imperfections themselves can earn commendation. The vulgar and common estimation rarely hits the mark; and I am much mistaken if, among the writings of my time, the worst are not those that have won most popular applause. For my part, I return my thanks to those good-natured men who are pleased to take my weak endeavours kindly; the faults of workmanship are nowhere so apparent as in a matter that has nothing in itself to recommend it. Don't blame me, reader, for those that slip in by the fancy or inadvertence of others; every hand, every artisan, contributes its own materials; I am not bothered with orthography (and only care to have it after the old fashion), nor with pointing, being very inept at both. Where they wholly break the sense, I am little concerned, since at least they let me off; but where they substitute a false one, as they so often do, and twist me to their own conception, they ruin me. When a sentence is not strong enough for my proportion, a civil person ought to reject it as spurious and not mine. Whoever knows how lazy I am, and how indulgent to my own humour, will easily believe that I had rather write as many essays again than be tied to revise these over for so childish a correction.

I said elsewhere that, planted in the very heart of this new religion, I am not only deprived of much familiarity with men of different manners and opinions from my own (men who hold together by such a tie as supersedes all other obligations), but moreover I do not live without danger among men to whom all things are equally lawful, most of whom cannot offend the laws more than they have already done — from which the extremest degree of licence proceeds. Adding it all up, I do not find one man in my own country who pays so dearly, both in loss and damages (as the lawyers say), for the defence of our laws as I do; and some there are who blow and brag about their zeal and constancy who, if things were justly weighed, do much less than I. My house, which has always been open and free to all comers, and civil to all (for I could never bring myself to make it a garrison of war, war being a thing I prefer to keep as remote as possible), has sufficiently deserved popular goodwill, so that it would be hard to insult me justly on my own dunghill; and I count it a wonderful, exemplary thing that it has so far remained virgin of blood and plunder through so long a storm, and so many revolutions and tumults all around. To tell the truth, it would have been possible enough for a man of my temper to have made peace with any one constant and continued state of things; but the contrary invasions and incursions, the alternations and vicissitudes of fortune round about me, have hitherto more exasperated than calmed and softened the temper of the country, and have repeatedly entangled me in invincible difficulties and dangers.

I escape, true; but I am troubled that it is more by chance, and by something of my own prudence, than by justice; and I am not satisfied to be outside the protection of the laws and under any other safeguard than theirs. As matters stand, I live, more than half, by the favour of others, which is an awkward obligation. I don't like to owe my safety either to the generosity or affection of great persons, who allow me my legality and my liberty, or to the good manners of my predecessors, or my own — for what if I were another sort of man? If my conduct and the frankness of my conversation or kinship oblige my neighbours, that is what should make them feel they have discharged the debt by merely permitting me to live, and they may say, "We allow him the free privilege of having divine service held in his own private chapel, when it is forbidden in all the churches around about, and we allow him the use of his goods and his life, as one who protects our wives and cattle in time of need." For my house has, for many generations, shared in the reputation of Lycurgus the Athenian, who was the general depositary and guardian of his fellow-citizens' purses. Now, I am clearly of opinion that a man should live by right and by authority, and not by recompense or favour. How many gallant men have rather chosen to lose their lives than to be in debt for them? I hate to subject myself to any sort of obligation, but above all to the kind that binds me by the duty of honour. I think nothing so costly as what has been given me, because my will lies in pawn under the title of gratitude; and I more willingly accept services I have to pay for: for the last I give only money, but for the other I give myself.

The knot that binds me by the laws of courtesy binds me more than that of civil constraint; I am much more at ease when bound by a notary than by myself. Is it not reasonable that my conscience should be much more engaged when men simply rely on it? In a bond, my honesty owes nothing, because nothing has been lent to it; let them trust to the security they have taken without me. I would much rather break the wall of a prison and the laws themselves than my own word. I am nice, even to superstition, in keeping my promises, and so on every occasion am careful to make them uncertain and conditional. To those of no great moment, I add the strictness of my own rule, to give them weight; it racks and oppresses me with its own interest. Even in actions wholly my own and free, if I once say a thing, I conceive that I have bound myself, and that, by delivering it to the knowledge of another, I have positively enjoined its performance on myself. It seems to me I promise it if I merely say it; and therefore I am not apt to say much of that kind. The sentence I pass on myself is more severe than that of a judge, who only considers the common obligation; my conscience looks on it with a more severe and penetrating eye. I lag in those duties to which I should be compelled if I did not go:
"Hoc ipsum ita justum est, quod recte fit, si est voluntarium."
["This very thing is just only insofar as it is rightly done, if it is voluntary." — Cicero, De Officiis, i. 9.]
If the action lacks some splendour of liberty, it has neither grace nor honour:
"Quod vos jus cogit, vix voluntate impetrent:"
["What the law compels us to do, we scarcely do with a will." — Terence, Adelph., iii. 3, 44.]
Where necessity drags me, I like to let my will take its own course:
"Quia quicquid imperio cogitur, exigenti magis, quam praestanti, acceptum refertur."
["For whatever is compelled by power is more credited to the one exacting it than to the one performing it." — Valerius Maximus, ii. 2, 6.]

I know some who carry this rule to the point of injustice; they will sooner give than restore, sooner lend than pay, and will do the least good to those to whom they are most obliged. I don't go that far, but I'm not far off.

I so love to disengage and disobligate myself that I have sometimes looked on ingratitudes, affronts, and indignities received from those to whom either nature or accident bound me in some kind of friendship as an advantage to me; taking this occasion of their ill-usage as an acknowledgment and discharge of so much of my debt. And though I continue to pay them all the external offices of common civility, I find, nevertheless, a great saving in doing on the account of justice what I had been doing on the score of affection, and am a little eased of the attention and solicitude of my inner will:
"Est prudentis sustinere, ut currum, sic impetum benevolentia;"
["It is the part of a wise man to keep a curbing hand on the impulse of friendship, as on that of a horse." — Cicero, De Amicitia, c. 17.]

this impulse, in me, is too urgent and pressing where I take to anyone, at least for a man who hates being strained at all. And this husbanding of my friendship serves me as a sort of consolation for the imperfections of those I am concerned with. I am very sorry they are not such as I could wish, but then I am also spared some of the application and engagement towards them. I approve of a man who is less fond of his child for having a scald-head, or for being crooked, and not only when the child is ill-natured but also when of unhappy disposition and imperfect in his limbs (God himself has lowered so much from his value and natural estimation), provided he conducts himself in this coldness of affection with moderation and exact justice: with me, proximity does not lessen defects, but rather aggravates them.

After all, by what I understand of the science of benefit and acknowledgment — which is a subtle science and of great use — I know no man more free and less indebted than I am at this hour. What I do owe is owed to foreign obligations and benefits; otherwise, no man is more absolutely clear:
"Nec sunt mihi nota potentum Munera."
["The gifts of great men are unknown to me." — Aeneid, xii. 529.]

Princes give me a great deal if they take nothing from me, and do me good enough if they do me no harm; that is all I ask of them. Oh, how I am obliged to God for being pleased that I should receive directly from his bounty all I have, and that he has reserved all my obligation specially to himself. How earnestly I beg of his holy compassion that I may never owe any essential thanks to anyone. Oh happy liberty in which I have so far lived! May it continue with me to the last. I do my best to have no express need of anyone:
"In me omnis spec est mihi."
["All my hope is in myself." — Terence, Adelph., iii. 5, 9.]

It is what every man can do in himself, but more easily those whom God has placed in a condition exempt from natural and pressing necessities. It is a wretched and dangerous thing to depend on others; we ourselves, in whom is always the justest and safest dependence, are not sufficiently sure.

I have nothing of my own but myself, and even that possession is partly defective and borrowed. I fortify myself in courage, which is the strongest support, and also in fortune, that I may have something to satisfy myself with even if everything else should fail. Hippias of Elis didn't only furnish himself with knowledge so that, at need, he could cheerfully retire from all other company to enjoy the Muses; not only with knowledge of philosophy, to teach his soul to be content with itself and bravely to subsist without outward comforts when fate would have it so; he was, moreover, careful enough to learn to cook, to shave himself, to make his own clothes, his own shoes and drawers, to provide for all his needs out of himself, and to wean himself from any reliance on others. A man more freely and cheerfully enjoys borrowed conveniences when the enjoyment isn't forced and constrained by need, and when he has, in his own will and fortune, the means to live without them. I know myself very well; but it's hard for me to imagine any liberality so pure towards me, any hospitality so frank and free, that would not appear discreditable, tyrannical, and stained with reproach if necessity had reduced me to it. Just as giving is an ambitious and authoritative quality, so accepting is a quality of submission; witness the insulting and quarrelsome refusal Bajazet gave to the presents Tamerlane sent him; and those that were offered on the part of the Emperor Solyman to the Emperor of Calicut so angered the latter that he not only rudely rejected them, saying that neither he nor any of his predecessors had ever been in the habit of taking and that it was their office to give, but, what is more, had the ambassadors who came with the gifts thrown into a dungeon. When Thetis, says Aristotle, flatters Jupiter, when the Lacedaemonians flatter the Athenians, they do not remind them of the good they have done them — which is always odious — but of the benefits they have received from them. Such as I see so often employing every one in their affairs, and thrusting themselves into so much obligation, would never do it if they relished, as I do, the sweetness of a pure liberty, and if they weighed, as wise men should, the burden of obligation: it is sometimes, perhaps, fully paid, but it is never dissolved. It is a miserable slavery to a man who loves to be at full liberty in everything. Those who know me, both above and below me in station, can say whether they have ever known a man less importunate, less given to soliciting, entreating, or pressing on others. If I am so, even to a degree beyond all modern example, no wonder, with so many parts of my character contributing to it: a touch of natural pride, an impatience at being refused, the moderation of my desires and designs, my incapacity for business, and my best-loved qualities, idleness and freedom — together they have bred in me a mortal hatred of being indebted to anyone, or by anyone, but myself. I leave no stone unturned to do without it, rather than employ the bounty of another in any light or weighty occasion or need whatever. My friends strangely trouble me when they ask me to ask a third person; it costs me little less, I think, to disengage someone who is in my debt by making use of him than to engage myself to someone who owes me nothing. Provided these conditions are removed, and they ask of me nothing requiring any great trouble or care (for I have declared mortal war on all care), I am very ready to do everyone the best service I can. I have been very willing to seek occasions of doing people a good turn, and to attach them to me; and to me there is no more agreeable employment for our means. But I have yet more avoided receiving than sought occasions of giving, and besides, according to Aristotle, it is easier. My fortune has allowed me little to do good to others with, and the little it can afford is held in a pretty tight hand. Had I been born to a great station, I would have been ambitious to make myself loved, not to make myself feared or admired: shall I express it more plainly? I would have tried more to please than to profit others. Cyrus very wisely, and through the mouth of a great captain and still greater philosopher, prefers his kindness and benefits much before his valour and warlike conquests; and the elder Scipio, whenever he would raise himself in esteem, sets a higher value on his affability and humanity than on his prowess and victories, and has always this glorious saying in his mouth: "That he has given his enemies as much reason to love him as his friends." I will say, then, that if a man must, of necessity, owe something, it should be by a more legitimate title than the one I am speaking of, to which the necessity of this miserable war compels me; and not as great a debt as that of my total preservation, of both life and fortune: it overwhelms me.

I have gone to bed in my own house a thousand times fearing I would be betrayed and murdered that very night; bargaining with fortune that it might be without terror and quickly over; and, after my Paternoster, I have cried out,
"Impius haec tam culta novalia miles habebit!"
["Shall impious soldiers have these new-ploughed grounds?" — Virgil, Eclog., i. 71.]

What's the remedy? It is the place of my birth, and of most of my ancestors; they have fixed here their affection and their name. We grow used to whatever we are accustomed to; and in a condition as miserable as ours, custom is a great gift of nature, which numbs our senses to the bearing of many evils. A civil war has this worse than other wars: it makes us stand sentinels in our own houses.
"Quam miserum, porta vitam muroque tueri, Vixque suae tutum viribus esse domus!"
["It is miserable to have to protect one's life by doors and walls, and to be scarcely safe by the strength of one's own house." — Ovid, Trist., iv. 1, 69.]

It is a grievous extremity to be jostled even in one's own house and domestic repose. The country I live in is always the first to take up arms and the last to lay them down, and where there is never an absolute peace:
"Tunc quoque, cum pax est, trepidant formidine belli.... Quoties Romam fortuna lacessit; Hac iter est bellis.... Melius, Fortuna, dedisses Orbe sub Eco sedem, gelidaque sub Arcto, Errantesque domos."
["Even when there is peace, here we still tremble with fear of war: whenever Fortune troubles peace, this is the road war takes." — Ovid, Trist., iii. 10, 67.]
["We might have lived happier in the remote East, or in the icy North, or among the wandering tribes." — Lucan, i. 255.]

I sometimes draw the means to fortify myself against these considerations from indifference and indolence, which, in their own way, bring us round to resolution. It often happens that I imagine and look for mortal dangers with a kind of pleasure: I stupidly plunge myself headlong into death, without weighing it or taking a look at it, as into a deep and dark abyss that swallows me at one leap and instantly engulfs me in profound sleep, without any sense of pain. And in these short violent deaths, the consequence I foresee gives me more consolation than the effect gives fear. They say that as life is not made better by being long, so death is made better by not being long. I am not so much avoiding being dead as I am entering into confidence with dying. I wrap and shroud myself in the storm that is to blind me and carry me off with the fury of a sudden, unfelt assault. Moreover, if it should turn out that, as some gardeners say, roses and violets grow more fragrant near garlic and onions because the latter suck up all the bad smell from the earth, then if these depraved natures around me should also draw off all the malignity of my air and climate, and render mine that much better and purer by their proximity, I shouldn't lose entirely. That can't be, perhaps; but this much may be true: goodness is more beautiful and attractive when it is rare, and contrariety and diversity fortify and consolidate well-doing in itself, kindling it by the jealousy of opposition and by glory. Thieves and robbers have, of their special favour, no particular spite against me; nor I against them: I'd have my hands too full. The same kinds of conscience are lodged under various sorts of robes; the same cruelty, disloyalty, rapine; and so much the worse, and more falsely, when more secure and concealed under colour of the laws. I less hate an open declared injury than a treacherous one; an enemy in arms than an enemy in a gown. Our fever has gripped a body not much the worse for it: there was fire before, and now it has burst into flame; the noise is greater, not the evil. I commonly answer those who ask me the reason for my journeys, "That I know very well what I am running from, but not what I am seeking." If they tell me there may be just as little soundness among foreigners, and that their manners are no better than ours, I reply, first, that it is hard to believe;
"Tam multa: scelerum facies!"
["There are so many forms of crime." — Virgil, Georg., i. 506.]
and second, that it is always a gain to change an ill condition for an uncertain one; and that other people's ills should not afflict us as much as our own.

I won't omit here that I never mutiny so much against France that I am not perfectly friends with Paris; that city has had my heart from my infancy, and as happens with all truly excellent things, the more beautiful cities I have seen since, the more the beauty of this one wins on my affection. I love her for herself, and more in her native being than in all the pomp of acquired and foreign embellishments. I love her tenderly, even to her warts and blemishes. I am a Frenchman only through this great city — great in people, great in the felicity of her site, but above all great and incomparable in variety and diversity of commodities: the glory of France, and one of the noblest ornaments of the world. May God drive our divisions far from her. Whole and united, I think her sufficiently defended from any other violence. I warn her that, of all sorts of people, the worst will be those who set her at discord with herself; I have no fear for her except from herself, and certainly I fear as much for her as for any other part of the kingdom. While she stands, I shall never lack a retreat to fall back on, sufficient to make up for the loss of any other.

Not because Socrates said so, but because it is in truth my own temper — and perhaps not without some excess — I look on all men as my compatriots, and embrace a Pole as a Frenchman, preferring the universal and common bond to all national ones. I am not much taken with the sweetness of a native air: acquaintances wholly new and wholly my own seem to me quite as good as the other common and accidental ones with our neighbours; friendships purely of our own making ordinarily outrank those that the bond of climate or blood imposes on us. Nature has placed us in the world free and unbound; we imprison ourselves in certain corners, like the kings of Persia, who bound themselves to drink no water but that of the river Choaspes, and so foolishly relinquished their claim to all other streams, and, as far as concerned themselves, dried up all the other rivers of the world. What Socrates did at the end of his life — looking on a sentence of banishment as worse than a sentence of death — I think I shall never be either so decrepit or so strictly habituated to my own country as to be of that opinion. These celestial lives have plenty of features I embrace more by esteem than affection; and some so elevated and extraordinary that I cannot embrace them even by esteem, since I cannot conceive of them. That fancy was singular in a man who thought the whole world his city; it is true he disdained travel, and had hardly ever set his foot outside the Attic territory. What of his complaint about the money his friends offered to save his life, and his refusal to come out of prison by the intervention of others, so as not to disobey the laws at a time when they were otherwise so corrupt? Such examples are of the first kind for me; of the second sort, there are others I could find in the same person. Many of these rare examples surpass the force of my action, but some of them, moreover, surpass the force of my judgment.

Besides these reasons, travel is in my opinion a very profitable exercise; the soul is there continually employed in observing new and unknown things, and, as I have often said, I know no better school for modelling life than constantly to expose it to the diversity of so many other lives, fancies, and customs, and to make it taste a perpetual variety of forms of human nature. The body is, in such an exercise, neither idle nor overworked; and that moderate motion puts it in breath. I can stay on horseback, tormented as I am with the stone, eight or ten hours together without dismounting or being weary:
"Vires ultra sorternque senectae."
["Beyond the strength and lot of age." — Aeneid, vi. 114.]

No season is my enemy except the parching heat of a scorching sun, for the umbrellas used in Italy ever since the time of the ancient Romans burden a man's arm more than they relieve his head. I would like to know how the Persians, so long ago and at the dawn of luxury, made fans where they needed them and planted shade-trees, as Xenophon reports they did. I love the rain, and to dabble in the mud, as much as ducks do. The change of air and climate never affects me; every sky is the same to me; I am only troubled by inward alterations of my own breeding, and those are less frequent in travel. I am hard to get going, but once on the road, I hold out as well as the best. I take as much pains over a small expedition as a great one, and am as careful in equipping myself for a short journey, if only to visit a neighbour, as for the longest voyage. I have learned to travel after the Spanish fashion, making one stage of many miles; and in excessive heats I always travel by night, from sunset to sunrise. The other method, of stopping along the way in haste and hurry to bolt a midday meal, is, especially on short days, very inconvenient. My horses do the better for it; no horse ever broke down under me that was able to make the first day's journey. I water them at every brook I meet, only taking care that there is enough way still to go before I reach my inn for them to digest the water in their bellies. My unwillingness to rise early in the morning gives my servants leisure to dine at their ease before we set out; for myself, I never eat too late; my appetite comes to me in eating, and not before; I am never hungry except at table.

Some of my friends blame me for keeping up this travelling humour, being married and old. But they are mistaken; it is the best time to leave a man's house, when he has set it on a course of running on without him, and arranged matters in keeping with their former government. It is much greater imprudence to abandon it to a less faithful housekeeper, who will be less concerned to look after your affairs.

The most useful and honourable knowledge and employment for the mother of a family is the science of good housewifery. I see some women who are covetous indeed, but very few who are good managers. It is the supreme quality of a woman, the one a man ought to seek before any other, as the only dowry that must ruin or preserve our houses. Whatever men may say, in my experience I require in married women, above all other virtues, the household virtue; I put my wife to it as a concern of her own, leaving her, by my absence, the whole government of my affairs. I am vexed to see in several families I know Monsieur come home about noon, jaded and harassed by his affairs, while Madame is still dressing her hair and titivating in her closet: that's for queens to do — and even that's a question; it is ridiculous and unjust that the laziness of our wives should be kept up by our sweat and labour. No man, so far as in me lies, shall have a clearer, quieter, freer enjoyment of his estate than I. If the husband brings matter, nature herself wills that the wife find the form.

As to the duties of conjugal friendship, that some think are impaired by these absences, I am quite of the opposite opinion. On the contrary, it is an intelligence that easily cools by too frequent and assiduous companionship. Every strange woman appears charming, and we all find by experience that being continually together is not as pleasing as parting for a time and meeting again. These interruptions fill me with fresh affection for my family and make my house more pleasant to me. Change warms my appetite first to the one and then to the other. I know that the arms of friendship are long enough to reach from one end of the world to the other, and especially this friendship, where there is continual communication of offices that rouse the obligation and the remembrance. The Stoics say there is so great a connection and relation among the sages that he who dines in France nourishes his companion in Egypt; and that whoever does but stretch out his finger, in whatever part of the world, all the sages on the habitable earth feel themselves aided by it. Enjoyment and possession belong principally to the imagination; it embraces what it is in quest of more fervently and constantly than what we hold in our arms. Reckon up your daily amusements; you will find that you are most absent from your friend when he is present with you; his presence relaxes your attention, and gives you liberty to absent yourself at every turn and on every pretext. When I am away in Rome, I keep and govern my house and the conveniences I left there; I see my walls rising, my trees shooting, and my revenue rising or falling much as well as if I were there:
"Ante oculos errat domus, errat forma locorum."
["My house and the forms of places float before my eyes." — Ovid, Trist., iii. 4, 57.]

If we enjoy nothing but what we touch, we may say farewell to the money in our chests and to our sons when they have gone out hunting. We will have them nearer to us: is the garden, or half a day's journey from home, far? What is ten leagues — far or near? If near, what about eleven, twelve, or thirteen, and so on by degrees? In earnest, if there is a woman who can tell her husband what step ends "near" and what step begins "far," I would advise her to stop halfway:
"Excludat jurgia finis . . . . Utor permisso; caudaeque pilos ut equinae Paulatim vello, et demo unum, demo etiam unum Dum cadat elusus ratione ruentis acervi:"
["Let the end shut out all disputes . . . . I use what is permitted; I pluck out the hairs of the horse's tail one by one; while I thus outwit my opponent." — Horace, Ep., ii. 1, 38, 45.]

and let them boldly call philosophy to their aid; though it may be thrown in its teeth that, since it discerns neither end of the joint — between too much and too little, the long and the short, the light and the heavy, the near and the far — and since it does not discover either the beginning or the end, it must necessarily judge very uncertainly of the middle:
"Rerum natura nullam nobis dedit cognitionem finium."
["Nature has given us no knowledge of the end of things." — Cicero, Acad., ii. 29.]

Are they not still wives and friends to the dead, who are not at the end of this life but in the other world? We embrace not only the absent, but those who have been and those who are not yet. We do not promise in marriage to be continually twisted and linked together, like certain little animals one sees, or like the bewitched folks of Karenty, tied together like dogs; and a wife ought not to be so greedily enamoured of her husband's front parts that she cannot bear to see him turn his back, if there is need. But may not this saying of that excellent painter of women's tempers be brought in here to show the reason for their complaints?
"Uxor, si cesses, aut to amare cogitat, Aut tete amari, aut potare, aut animo obsequi; Et tibi bene esse soli, cum sibi sit male;"

["Your wife, if you loiter, thinks that you love or are beloved; or that you are drinking or following your inclination; and that things are well with you when they are ill with her (all the pleasure is yours, all the trouble hers)." — Terence, Adelph., Act i., sc. 1, v. 7.]
or may it not be that opposition and contradiction of themselves entertain and nourish them, and that they accommodate themselves well enough provided they inconvenience you?

In true friendship, in which I am expert, I more give myself to my friend than try to draw him to me. I am not only better pleased to do him service than if he conferred a benefit on me, but moreover I would rather he should do himself good than me, and he most obliges me when he does so; and if absence is more pleasant or convenient for him, it is also more acceptable to me than his presence; neither is it properly absence when we can write to one another. I have sometimes made good use of our separation: we filled up and extended our possession of life more completely by being apart. He lived, enjoyed, and saw for me, and I for him, as fully as if he had himself been there; one part of us remained idle, and we were too much blended in one another when together: distance of place made the conjunction of our wills richer. This insatiable desire for personal presence implies a certain weakness in the enjoyment of souls.

As for age, which is brought up against me, it is quite the contrary; it is for youth to subject itself to common opinions and curb itself to please others; it has the means to please both others and itself; we have but too much ado to please ourselves alone. As natural conveniences fail, let us supply them with artificial ones. It is unjust to excuse youth for pursuing its pleasures and to forbid old men to seek them. When young, I concealed my wanton passions with prudence; now I am old, I chase away melancholy with diversion. And so the Platonic laws forbid men to travel until forty or fifty, that travel may be more useful and instructive at such a mature age. I would sooner subscribe to the second article of those same laws, which forbids it after sixty.

"But, at your age, you will never come back from so long a journey." What do I care? I undertake it neither to come back, nor to finish it; my business is only to keep myself in motion while motion pleases me; I only walk for the walk's sake. They who chase after a benefit, or a hare, do not really run; only they run who run at base, and to exercise their running. My design is divisible throughout: it is not founded on any great hopes; every day concludes my expectation: and the journey of my life is carried on the same way. And yet I have seen places far enough off where I would gladly have stayed. And why not, if Chrysippus, Cleanthes, Diogenes, Zeno, Antipater — so many sages of the sourest sect — readily abandoned their country, without any cause for complaint, and only for the enjoyment of another air. In earnest, what most displeases me in all my travels is that I cannot resolve to settle where I would most like to, but must always look ahead to coming back, to fitting in with the common humour.

If I were afraid to die anywhere but the place of my birth, if I thought I should die more uneasily far from my own household, I should hardly go out of France; I should not, without fear, step out of my parish; I feel death always pinching me by the throat or by the back. But I am made otherwise; it is all alike to me in all places. Still, if I could choose, I think I should rather die on horseback than in bed, away from my own house and far from my own people. There is more heartbreak than consolation in taking leave of one's friends; I am willing to skip that civility, for, of all the offices of friendship, it is the only one that is unpleasant; and I could very willingly do without that great and eternal farewell. If there is any convenience in so many bystanders, it brings a hundred inconveniences with it. I have seen many dying miserably surrounded by all this train: it is a crowd that chokes them. It is against duty, and is evidence of little kindness and little care, to keep you from dying in peace; one torments your eyes, another your ears, another your tongue; you have neither sense nor limb that is not worried by them. Your heart is wounded with compassion at hearing the mourning of friends, and perhaps with anger at the counterfeit condolings of pretenders. Whoever has been delicate and sensitive when well is much more so when ill. In such a need, a gentle hand is required, attuned to his feeling, to scratch him just where it itches; otherwise don't scratch him at all. If we need a wise woman to bring us into the world, we need a still wiser man to help us out of it. Such a one, and a friend to boot, a man should buy at any cost for such an occasion. I have not yet reached that pitch of disdainful vigour that is fortified within itself, that nothing can help or disturb; I am of a lower form; I try to hide myself and slip out of this passage, not by fear, but by art. I don't intend, in this act of dying, to give a demonstration of my constancy. For whom should I do it? all the right and interest I have in reputation will then cease. I content myself with a death folded in on itself, quiet, solitary, and all my own, suited to my retired and private life — quite contrary to the Roman superstition, which held a man unfortunate who died without speaking, and without his nearest relations to close his eyes. I have enough to do to comfort myself, without having to console others; thoughts enough in my head, without needing circumstance to give me new ones; and matter enough to occupy me without borrowing. This business is no part of society; it is the act of one single person. Let us live and be merry among our friends; let us go fret and die among strangers; one may find people, for money, who will plump up his pillow and rub his feet, and trouble him no more than he wants; who will show him an indifferent face, and let him govern himself and complain in his own way.

I wean myself daily, by reason, from this childish and inhuman humour of wanting our sufferings to move our friends to compassion and grief: we stretch our own troubles beyond their just extent when we draw tears from others; and the constancy we praise in everyone for supporting his adverse fortune, we accuse and reproach in our friends when the misfortune is our own; we are not satisfied that they should merely be sensible of our condition, unless they are also afflicted by it. A man should diffuse joy, but, as much as he can, smother grief. He who makes himself lamented without cause is a man not to be lamented when there is real cause; constantly complaining is the way never to be commiserated; by always making a pitiful show of himself, he ends commiserated by none. He who plays dead while alive is liable to be thought living when dying. I have seen some who took it ill when told they looked well and that their pulse was good; restrained their smiles, because the smile betrayed a recovery; got angry at their own health because it was not to be lamented — and, what is more, these were not women. I describe my infirmities as they really are, at most, and avoid all expressions of ill omen and composed exclamations. If not mirth, then at least a temperate countenance in the bystanders is proper in the presence of a wise sick man; he doesn't quarrel with health, for seeing himself in the opposite condition, he is pleased to contemplate it sound and entire in others, at least to enjoy it for company. He doesn't, because he feels himself melting away, abandon all living thoughts, nor avoid ordinary discourse. I would study sickness while I am well; when it has seized me, it will make its impression real enough without any help from my imagination. We prepare beforehand for the journeys we are to undertake, and resolve on them; we leave the choice of the hour for taking horse to the company, and put it off out of consideration for them.

I find this unexpected advantage in publishing my manners: it serves me, in some sort, as a rule. I now and then think about not betraying the history of my life: this public declaration obliges me to keep on track, and not give the lie to the picture I have drawn of my qualities — commonly less deformed and contradictory than is consistent with the malignity and infirmity of the judgments of this age. The uniformity and simplicity of my manners produce a face of easy interpretation; but because the fashion is a little new and not in use, it gives too great an opening to slander. Yet, as it is, whoever wishes to attack me fairly, I think I sufficiently assist his purpose by my known and avowed imperfections, so that he may, that way, satisfy his ill-nature without fighting with the wind. If I myself, to anticipate accusation and discovery, confess enough to frustrate his malice, as he conceives it, it is only fair that he make use of his right of amplification and stretch my vices as far as he can; attack has its rights beyond justice; let him make the roots of those errors I have laid open to him shoot up into trees; let him make use not only of those I am really affected by, but also of those that only threaten me; injurious vices, both in quality and number; let him cudgel me that way. I should willingly follow the example of the philosopher Bion: when Antigonus was about to reproach him with the meanness of his birth, he cut him short at once with this declaration: "I am," he said, "the son of a slave, a butcher, and branded, and of a strumpet whom my father married in his lowest fortunes; both of them were whipped for offences they had committed. An orator bought me as a child, and finding me a pretty and hopeful boy, brought me up; when he died, he left me all his estate, which I have brought to this city of Athens, and here settled to the study of philosophy. Let the historians spare themselves the trouble of inquiring about me: I will tell them about it myself." A free and generous confession blunts reproach and disarms slander. So that, one thing with another, I find men commend me as often as they undervalue me beyond reason; as it seems to me, also, from my childhood, that in rank and degree of honour they have given me a place rather above than below my right. I would find myself more at ease in a country where these degrees were either regulated or unobserved. Among men, when an altercation about precedence in walking or sitting exceeds three replies, it is reckoned uncivil. I never stick at giving or taking place out of rule, to avoid the trouble of such ceremony; and no man ever had a mind to go before me but I let him do it.

Besides this benefit I get from writing of myself, I have also hoped for this other advantage: that if it should happen that my humour pleased, or coincided with, that of some honest man before I die, he would then desire and seek to be acquainted with me. I have given him a great deal of head-start; all he could have acquired by close familiarity in many years, he has seen in three days in this memoir, and more surely and exactly. A pleasant fancy: many things that I would not confess to any one in particular, I deliver to the public, and send my best friends to a bookseller's shop to inform themselves of my most secret thoughts;
"Excutienda damus praecordia."
["We give our hearts to be examined." — Persius, V. 22.]

If I knew, by good direction, where to find someone fit for my conversation, I should certainly go a long way to find him; for the sweetness of suitable and agreeable company cannot, in my opinion, be bought too dearly. Oh, what a thing is a true friend! How true is that old saying: that the use of a friend is more pleasing and necessary than the elements of water and fire!

To return to my subject: there is, then, no great harm in dying privately and far from home; we conceive ourselves obliged to retire for natural acts less unseemly and less terrible than this. Moreover, those who are reduced to spinning out a long languishing life ought, perhaps, not to wish to trouble a great household with their continual miseries; therefore the Indians, in a certain province, thought it just to knock a man on the head when reduced to such a need; and in another of their provinces, they all abandoned him to shift for himself as best he could. To whom do they not, at last, become tedious and insupportable? the ordinary offices of life do not stretch that far. You teach your best friends to be cruel by main force; you harden wife and children by long use, so that they neither regard nor lament your sufferings. The groans of the stone are so familiar to my people that nobody takes any notice of them. And though we should extract some pleasure from their company (which doesn't always happen, given the disparity of conditions, which easily breeds contempt or envy toward anyone), is it not too much to make this kind of abuse of half a lifetime? The more I should see them constrain themselves out of affection to be of service to me, the sorrier I should be for their pains. We have liberty to lean, but not to lay our whole weight on others, so as to prop ourselves up by their ruin — like the man who had little children's throats cut to use their blood as a cure for a disease he had, or the other who kept being supplied with tender young girls to keep his old limbs warm at night, and to mix the sweetness of their breath with his, sour and stinking. I should readily recommend Venice as a retreat in this decline of life. Decrepitude is a solitary quality. I am sociable, even to excess, yet I think it reasonable that I should now withdraw my troubles from the sight of the world and keep them to myself. Let me shrink and draw myself up into my own shell, like a tortoise, and learn to look at men without leaning on them. I should endanger them in so slippery a passage: it is time to turn my back on company.

"But, on these travels, you will fall ill in some wretched place, where nothing can be had to relieve you." I always carry most necessary things with me; and besides, we cannot escape Fortune if she once resolves to attack us. I need nothing extraordinary when I am sick. I won't be beholden to a bolus to do for me what nature cannot. At the very beginning of fevers and sicknesses that lay me low, while I am still whole and only slightly disordered in health, I reconcile myself to Almighty God by the last Christian offices, and find myself the less oppressed and the easier for it, and have, methinks, so much the better of my disease. And I have even less need of a notary or counsellor than of a physician. What I have not settled of my affairs when in health, let no one expect me to settle when sick. What I will do for the service of death is always done; I dare not so much as one day defer it; and if nothing is done, it is as much as to say either that doubt hindered my choice (and sometimes it is well chosen not to choose), or that I was positively resolved to do nothing at all.

I write my book for few men and for few years. Had it been a matter of duration, I would have put it into firmer language. Given the continual variation our language has been subject to up to this day, who can expect its present form to be in use fifty years from now? It slips through our fingers every day; since I was born, it is altered more than half. We say that it is now perfect, and every age says the same of its own. I shall hardly trust to that, so long as it varies and changes as it does. It is for good and useful writings to rivet language to themselves, and its reputation will go according to the fortune of our state. For that reason, I am not afraid to insert several private articles, which will spend their use among the men now living, and which concern the particular knowledge of some who will see further into them than every ordinary reader. After all, I do not want, as I often hear of dead men, that people should say of me: "He judged so, he lived so and so; he would have done this or that; could he have spoken when he was dying, he would have said so or so, and given this thing or the other; I knew him better than anybody." Now, as far as decency permits, I here disclose my inclinations and affections; but I do this more willingly and freely by word of mouth to anyone who wishes to be informed. So that in these memoirs, if anyone observes, he will find that I have either told everything, or set out to. What I cannot express, I point out with my finger:
"Verum animo satis haec vestigia parva sagaci Sunt, per quae possis cognoscere caetera tute"
["By these footsteps a sagacious mind may easily find all other matters (these are enough to enable one to learn the rest well)." — Lucretius, i. 403.]

I leave nothing to be desired or guessed at concerning me. If people must talk about me, I would have it be justly and truly; I would gladly come back from the other world to give the lie to anyone who reported me other than I was, even if he did it to honour me. I notice that people represent even living men as quite different from what they really are; and had I not stoutly defended a friend I have lost, they would have torn him into a thousand contradictory pieces.

To finish accounting for my poor humours, I confess that in my travels I seldom reach my inn without it crossing my mind to consider whether I could there be sick and dying at my ease. I want to be lodged in some private part of the house, away from all noise, bad smells, and smoke. I try to flatter death by these trivial circumstances — or, to put it better, to discharge myself of every other encumbrance, so that I may have nothing to do, nor be troubled with anything but that which will weigh heavily enough on me without any other load. I would have my death share in the ease and conveniences of my life; it is a great part of life, and of great importance, and I hope it will not in future contradict the past. Death has some forms that are easier than others, and takes on different qualities according to every man's fancy. Among the natural deaths, the one that comes from weakness and stupor I think most favourable; among the violent ones, I can less easily think of a precipice than of the fall of a house that will crush me in a moment, and of a wound by a sword than of an arquebus shot; I should rather poison myself with Socrates than stab myself with Cato. And though it amounts to the same thing, my imagination makes as great a difference as that between death and life, between throwing myself into a burning furnace and plunging into the channel of a river — so emptily does our fear concern itself more with the means than the effect. It is but an instant, true; but an instant of such weight that I would willingly give many days of my life to pass it over after my own fashion. Since every man's imagination renders it more or less terrible, and since every man has some choice among the various forms of dying, let us try a little further to find one that is wholly clear of any offence. Might one not render it even voluptuous, like the Commorientes of Antony and Cleopatra? I set aside the brave and exemplary efforts produced by philosophy and religion; but among men of little mark there have been some, like Petronius and Tigellinus at Rome, condemned to despatch themselves, who have, so to speak, rocked death to sleep with the delicacy of their preparations; they made it slip and steal away in the midst of their accustomed diversions, among girls and good fellows; not a word of consolation, no mention of making a will, no ambitious affectation of constancy, no talk of their future condition; amid sport, feasting, wit and mirth, common and indifferent conversation, music, and amorous verses. Could we not imitate this resolution after a more decent fashion? Since there are deaths good for fools and deaths good for the wise, let us find ones fit for those between the two. My imagination suggests one that is easy, and, since we must die, to be desired. The Roman tyrants thought they granted a criminal his life when they gave him the choice of his death. But was not Theophrastus, that so delicate, modest, and wise philosopher, compelled by reason when he dared utter this verse, translated by Cicero:
"Vitam regit fortuna, non sapientia?"
["Fortune, not wisdom, sways human life." — Cicero, Tusc. Quaes., V. 31.]

Fortune assists the bargain of my life by placing it in such a condition that, from now on, it can be neither an advantage nor a hindrance to those who have a stake in me; it is a condition I would have accepted at any time of life, but on this occasion of trussing up my baggage, I am particularly pleased that in dying I shall do them neither good nor harm. She has so arranged it, by a cunning compensation, that those who may pretend to any considerable advantage from my death will, at the same time, sustain a material inconvenience. Death is sometimes more painful to us because it is painful to others, and engages us in their interest as much as our own, and sometimes more.

In this convenience of lodging that I look for, I mix nothing of pomp and amplitude — I rather hate it; but a certain plain neatness, oftenest found in places where there is less of art and where Nature has added some grace of her own:
"Non ampliter, sea munditer convivium."
["A feast not lavish, but clean." — Nepos, Life of Atticus, c. 13.]
"Plus salis quam sumptus."
["More wit than cost." — Nonius, xi. 19.]

And besides, it is for those whose business compels them to travel in the depth of winter through the Grisons country to be caught on the road with great inconveniences. I, who for the most part travel for pleasure, do not order my affairs so badly. If the road is foul on my right, I turn to my left; if I find myself unfit to ride, I stay where I am; and, doing so, I see, in earnest, nothing that is not as pleasant and convenient as my own house. It is true I always find superfluity superfluous, and observe a sort of trouble even in abundance itself. Have I left anything behind unseen? I go back to see it; it is still on my way; I trace no fixed line, straight or crooked. Do I not find at the place I am going to what was reported to me — as it often falls out that other people's judgments do not match mine, and that I have found their reports for the most part false? I never complain of losing my pains; I have at least learned that what I was told was not true.

I have as free a constitution and as indifferent a palate as any man alive; the diversity of the manners of different nations affects me only in the pleasure of variety: every usage has its reason. Let the plates and dishes be pewter, wood, or earthenware; let my meat be boiled or roasted; let them give me butter or oil, from nuts or olives, hot or cold — it is all one to me; and so indifferent that, growing old, I find fault with this generous capacity, and would wish that delicacy and choice should correct the indiscretion of my appetite, and sometimes soothe my stomach. When I have been abroad out of France, and people, out of courtesy, have asked me whether I would be served in the French fashion, I have laughed at the question and always frequented the tables most filled with foreigners. I am ashamed to see our countrymen besotted with the foolish humour of quarrelling with forms unlike their own; they seem to be out of their element when out of their own village; wherever they go, they cling to their own fashions and abominate those of strangers. Do they meet a compatriot in Hungary? Oh, what a happy chance! They are inseparable from then on; they cling together, and their whole conversation is condemning the barbarous manners they see about them. Why barbarous, because they are not French? And those have made the best use of their travels who have observed most to speak against. Most of them go for no other end but to come back; they proceed on their travel with vast gravity and circumspection, with a silent and incommunicable prudence, preserving themselves from the contagion of an unknown air. What I am saying of them puts me in mind of something similar I have at times observed in some of our young courtiers; they won't mix with any but men of their own sort, and look on us as men from another world, with disdain or pity. Put them on any topic but the intrigues of the court, and they are utterly at a loss; as much owls and novices to us as we are to them. It is truly said that a well-bred man is a compound man. I, on the contrary, travel very much surfeited with our own ways; I do not look for Gascons in Sicily; I have left enough of them at home; I rather seek out Greeks and Persians; those are the men I try to get acquainted with and the men I study; that is where I lay out and employ myself. And, what is more, I find I have met few customs that aren't as good as our own; I have not, I confess, travelled very far — scarcely out of sight of the weathervanes of my own house.

As for the rest, most of the accidental company a man falls in with on the road brings him more trouble than pleasure; I avoid them as much as I civilly can, especially now that age seems somehow to privilege and sequester me from the common forms. Either you suffer for others or others suffer for you; both are inconveniences of importance enough, but the latter seems to me the greater. It is a rare fortune, but of inestimable solace, to have a worthy man, one of sound judgment and of manners conformable to your own, who delights to keep you company. I have felt the lack of such men infinitely on my travels. But such a companion should be chosen and acquired from your first setting out. There can be no pleasure for me without communication: not so much as a lively thought enters my mind without my regretting that I have produced it alone and have no one to communicate it to:
"Si cum hac exceptione detur sapientia, ut illam inclusam teneam, nec enuntiem, rejiciam."
["If wisdom were granted me with this proviso, that I keep it locked up and not communicate it to others, I would have none of it." — Seneca, Ep., 6.]
Another has taken this a note higher:

"Si contigerit ea vita sapienti, ut ommum rerum afliuentibus copiis, quamvis omnia, quae cognitione digna sunt, summo otio secum ipse consideret et contempletur, tamen, si solitudo tanta sit, ut hominem videre non possit, excedat a vita."

["If such a life should fall to a wise man, that in the greatest plenty of every comfort he might, at the most undisturbed leisure, consider and contemplate everything worth knowing — yet if his solitude were so great that he could not see another human being, let him depart from life." — Cicero, De Officiis, i. 43.]

Architas pleases me when he says that even in heaven itself it would be unpleasant to wander among those great and divine celestial bodies without a companion. But yet it is much better to be alone than in foolish and troublesome company. Aristippus loved to live as a stranger in all places:
"Me si fata meis paterentur ducere vitam Auspiciis,"
["If the fates would let me live in my own way." — Aeneid, iv. 340.]
I should choose to spend the greatest part of my life on horseback:
"Visere gestiens, Qua pane debacchentur ignes, Qua nebula, pluviique rores."
["Visit the regions where the sun rages, where are the thick rain-clouds and the frosts." — Horace, Od., iii. 3, 54.]

"Don't you have easier diversions at home? What do you lack there? Isn't your house set in a sweet and healthful air, sufficiently furnished, and more than sufficiently large? Has not royal majesty been more than once entertained there with all its train? Are there not more below your family in modest comfort than there are above it in eminence? Is there any local, extraordinary, indigestible thought afflicting you?"
"Qua to nunc coquat, et vexet sub pectore fixa."
["That may now worry you, and vex, fixed in your breast." — Cicero, De Senect., c. 1, Ex Ennio.]
"Where do you think to live without disturbance?"
"Nunquam simpliciter Fortuna indulget."
["Fortune is never simply complaisant (unmixed)." — Quintus Curtius, iv. 14.]

You see, then, it is only you that troubles yourself; you will follow yourself everywhere and everywhere complain; for there is no satisfaction here below, except either for brutish or for divine souls. He who, with so just an occasion, has no contentment — where will he think to find it? How many thousands of men have their wishes terminate in such a condition as yours? Only reform yourself; for that lies wholly in your own power, whereas towards fortune you have no right but patience:
"Nulla placida quies est, nisi quam ratio composuit."
["There is no tranquillity but that which reason has conferred." — Seneca, Ep., 56.]

I see the sense of this advice, and see it perfectly well; but he might have done sooner, and more to the point, by telling me in a word, "Be wise." That resolution is beyond wisdom; it is her precise work and product. So the physician keeps preaching to a poor languishing patient to "be cheerful"; but he would advise him a little more discreetly by telling him "be well." For my part, I am only a man of the common sort. It is a wholesome precept, certain and easy to understand: "Be content with what you have," that is, with reason; and yet to follow this advice is no more in the power of the world's wise men than it is in mine. It is a common saying, but of a terrible reach: what does it not include? All things fall under discretion and qualification. I know very well that, taking it by the letter, this pleasure of travelling testifies to a certain uneasiness and irresolution; and, in truth, these are our governing and predominant qualities. Yes, I confess, I see nothing — not so much as in a dream or a wish — on which I could settle; only variety, only the enjoyment of diversity, can satisfy me — that is, if anything can. In travelling, it pleases me that I can stay where I like without inconvenience, and that I have a place where I can comfortably divert myself. I love a private life because it is my own choice to love it, not from any dissent or dislike of public life, which is perhaps just as suitable to my temper. I serve my prince more cheerfully because it is by the free election of my own judgment and reason, with no particular obligation, and that I am not reduced and constrained to do so for being rejected or disliked by the other party; and so of all the rest. I hate the morsels that necessity carves for me; any benefit on which I had to depend alone would have me by the throat;
"Alter remus aquas, alter mihi radat arenas;"
["Let me have one oar in the water, and with the other rake the shore." — Propertius, iii. 3, 23.]
one cord will never hold me fast enough. You will say there is vanity in this way of living. But where is there not? All these fine precepts are vanity, and all wisdom is vanity:
"Dominus novit cogitationes sapientum, quoniam vanae sunt."
["The Lord knoweth the thoughts of the wise, that they are vain." — Ps. xciii. 11; or 1 Cor. iii. 20.]

These exquisite subtleties are only fit for sermons; they are discourses that would send us all packing into the other world. Life is a material and corporal motion, an action imperfect and irregular of its very essence; I make it my business to serve it according to itself:
"Quisque suos patimur manes."
["We each suffer our own particular demon." — Aeneid, vi. 743.]
"Sic est faciendum, ut contra naturam universam nihil contendamus; ea tamen conservata propriam sequamur."
["We should so order things as in no way to contend against universal nature; but, that rule being observed, to follow our own." — Cicero, De Officiis, i. 31.]
To what end are these lofty points of philosophy, on which no human being can rely? and those rules that exceed both our use and force?

I often see theories of life set before us which neither the proposer nor those who hear him have any hope, nor even any inclination, to follow. From the very same sheet of paper on which the judge has just written a sentence against an adulterer, he steals a piece on which to write a love-letter to a colleague's wife. The woman whom you have just now illicitly embraced will presently, even in your hearing, inveigh more loudly against the same fault in her companion than any Portia would; and there are men who will condemn others to death for crimes they themselves do not consider so much as faults. I have, in my youth, seen a man of good rank present to the public with one hand verses that excelled both in wit and debauchery, and with the other, at the same time, the most ripe and pugnacious theological reformation that the world has been treated to in many years. And so men proceed: we let the laws and precepts go their own way; we ourselves keep another course, not only by debauchery of manners, but often by judgment and contrary opinion. Just listen to a philosophical lecture: the invention, eloquence, and pertinency strike the mind at once and move you; there is nothing that touches or stings your conscience; it is not that they are addressing. Is it not true? It made Ariston say that neither a bath nor a lecture is any good unless it scours and makes men clean. One may stop at the skin; but it is after the marrow has been picked out — as, after we have swallowed good wine out of a fine cup, we examine the designs and the workmanship. In all the schools of ancient philosophy, this is to be found: that the same teacher publishes rules of temperance and at the same time lessons of love and wantonness; Xenophon, in the very lap of Clinias, wrote against the Aristippic virtue. It isn't that there is any miraculous conversion making them so wavering; it is that Solon represents himself sometimes in his own person, sometimes in that of a legislator; one moment he speaks for the crowd, another for himself; taking the free and natural rules for his own share, feeling assured of firm and entire health:
"Curentur dubii medicis majoribus aegri."
["Desperate maladies require the best doctors." — Juvenal, xiii. 124.]

Antisthenes allows a sage to love, and to do whatever he thinks fit, without regard to the laws, since he is better advised than they and has a greater knowledge of virtue. His disciple Diogenes said that "to perturbations men should oppose reason; to fortune, courage; to the laws, nature." For tender stomachs, constrained and artificial recipes must be prescribed: good and strong stomachs serve themselves simply with the prescriptions of their own natural appetite. So our physicians proceed, who eat melons and drink iced wines while they confine their patients to syrups and sops. "I don't know," said the courtesan Lais, "what they may say about books, wisdom, and philosophy; but these men knock at my door as often as any others." At the same rate that our licence carries us beyond what is lawful and allowed, men have, often beyond universal reason, stretched the precepts and rules of our life:
"Nemo satis credit tantum delinquere, quantum Permittas."
["No one thinks he has done ill to the full extent of what he is permitted." — Juvenal, xiv. 233.]

It is to be wished there were more proportion between the command and the obedience; and the mark seems unjust that one cannot reach. There is no man so good that, if he squared all his thoughts and actions to the laws, he would not be faulty enough to deserve hanging ten times in his life; and he might well be such a man that it would be great injustice and great harm to punish and ruin him:
"Ole, quid ad te De cute quid faciat ille vel ille sua?"
["Olus, what is it to thee what he or she does with their skin?" — Martial, vii. 9, 1.]

and there may be such a man who has in no way offended the laws, who nevertheless does not deserve the character of a virtuous man, and whom philosophy would justly condemn to be whipped; so unequal and tangled is this relationship. We are so far from being good men, by the laws of God, that we cannot be so by our own; human wisdom never yet attained the duties it had itself prescribed; and if it could attain them, it would still prescribe to itself others beyond, to which it would ever aspire and pretend — our human condition being so great an enemy to consistency. Man condemns himself necessarily to be in fault: he is not very discreet to cut out his own duty by the measure of a being other than his own. To whom does he prescribe what he does not expect anyone to perform? Is he unjust not to do what is impossible for him to do? The laws that condemn us for not being able, condemn us for not being able.

At worst, this misshapen licence of presenting ourselves in two different ways — the actions one way and the reasoning another — may be allowed those who only speak of things; but it cannot be allowed those who speak of themselves, as I do: I must march my pen as I do my feet. Common life ought to bear some relation to the other lives: the virtue of Cato was vigorous beyond the reason of the age he lived in; and for a man who made it his business to govern others, a man dedicated to the public service, it might be called a justice, if not unjust, at least vain and out of season. Even my own manners, which differ no more than an inch from the manners current among us, render me, nevertheless, a little rough and unsociable in my age. I don't know whether it's without reason that I am disgusted with the world I move in; but I know very well that it would be without reason if I complained of its being disgusted with me, since I am with it. The virtue assigned to the affairs of the world is a virtue of many windings, corners, and elbows, used to join and adapt itself to human frailty — mixed and artificial, not straight, clean, constant, nor purely innocent. Our annals to this very day reproach one of our kings for letting himself be carried away too simply by the conscientious counsels of his confessor: affairs of state have bolder precepts;
"Exeat aula, Qui vult esse pius."
["Let him who would be pious withdraw from court." — Lucan, viii. 493.]

I once tried to employ in the service of public affairs opinions and rules of living as rough, new, and unpolished as they were either born with me, or brought away from my education, and that I use to serve my own turn — if not so commodiously, at least securely, in my own particular concerns: a scholastic and novice virtue; but I have found them unsuitable and dangerous. He who goes into a crowd must now go one way, then another, keep his elbows close, retire or advance, and quit the straight way according to what he encounters; and must live not so much according to his own method as according to that of others; not according to what he proposes to himself, but according to what is proposed to him — according to the time, according to the men, according to the occasions. Plato says that whoever escapes from the world's handling with clean breeches escapes by miracle; and he says also that when he appoints his philosopher head of a government, he doesn't mean a corrupt one like that of Athens, much less such a one as ours, where wisdom itself would be at a loss. A good herb, transplanted into a soil contrary to its own nature, much sooner conforms itself to the soil than it reforms the soil to itself. I found that if I had to apply myself wholly to such employments, it would require a great deal of change and remodelling in me before I could be in any way fit for it; and even if I could so far prevail upon myself (and why might I not, with time and diligence, work such a feat), I would not do it. The little experience I have had of public employment has been so much disgust to me; I feel at times temptations to ambition rising in my soul, but I stubbornly oppose them:
"At tu, Catulle, obstinatus obdura."
["But thou, Catullus, be obstinately firm." — Catullus, viii. 19.]

I am seldom called to it, and as seldom offer myself uncalled; liberty and laziness, the qualities most predominant in me, are diametrically contrary to that trade. We cannot well distinguish the faculties of men; they have divisions and limits hard and delicate to choose; to conclude from the discreet conduct of a private life a capacity for the management of public affairs is to conclude wrongly; a man may govern himself well who cannot govern others so, and compose Essays who could not work effects; there may be men who can order a siege well but would marshal a battle ill; who can speak well in private, but would harangue a people or a prince ill; indeed, it is perhaps rather a sign in him who can do the one that he cannot do the other, than otherwise. I find that elevated souls are no more fit for mean things than mean souls are for high ones. Could it be imagined that Socrates would have given the Athenians occasion to laugh at his expense, for never having been able to sum up the votes of his tribe and deliver them to the council? Truly, the veneration I have for the perfections of this great man deserves that his fortune should furnish, for the excuse of my principal imperfections, so magnificent an example. Our capacity is cut out into small parcels; mine has no scope, and is also very contemptible in number. Saturninus, to those who had conferred on him the supreme command: "Companions," he said, "you have lost a good captain to make of him a bad general."

Whoever boasts, in so sick a time as this, of employing a true and sincere virtue in the world's service, either does not know what it is — opinions growing corrupt with manners (and, in truth, to hear them describe it, to hear most of them glorify themselves in their conduct and lay down their rules; instead of painting virtue, they paint pure vice and injustice, and so represent it falsely in the education of princes) — or, if he does know it, he boasts unjustly, and whatever he says, does a thousand things of which his own conscience must necessarily accuse him. I would willingly take Seneca's word on the experience he made on a like occasion, provided he would deal sincerely with me. The most honourable mark of goodness in such a necessity is freely to confess both one's own faults and those of others; by the power of one's virtue to stay one's inclination towards evil; unwillingly to follow this propensity; to hope better, to desire better. I see that in these divisions in which we are involved in France, every one labours to defend his cause; but even the very best of them with dissimulation and disguise. He who would write straightforwardly about the true state of the quarrel would write rashly and wrongly. The most just party is, at best, only a member of a decayed and worm-eaten body; but of such a body, the member that is least affected calls itself sound, and rightly, since our qualities have no title but by comparison; civil innocence is measured according to times and places. Imagine this in Xenophon, related as a fine commendation of Agesilaus: that, being entreated by a neighbouring prince with whom he had formerly been at war to permit him to pass through his country, he granted his request, giving him free passage through Peloponnesus; and not only did not imprison or poison him, having him at his mercy, but courteously received him according to the obligation of his promise, without doing him the least injury or offence. To minds like theirs, this would be no especially noteworthy act; elsewhere, and in another age, the frankness and openness of such an action would be thought wonderful; our monkeyish capets
[Capets, so called from their short capes, were the students of Montaigne College in Paris, and were held in great contempt.]

would have laughed at it — so little does the Spartan innocence resemble that of France. We are not without virtuous men, but it is by our standards of virtue. Whoever has his manners established in regularity above the standard of the age he lives in, let him either wrest or blunt his rules, or — what I would rather advise him — let him retire, and not meddle with us at all. What will he gain by it?
"Egregium sanctumque virum si cerno, bimembri Hoc monstrum puero, et miranti jam sub aratro Piscibus inventis, et foetae comparo mulae."
["If I see an exemplary and saintly man, I liken it to a two-headed boy, or a fish turned up by the plough, or a teeming mule." — Juvenal, xiii. 64.]

One may regret better times, but cannot flee the present; we may wish for other magistrates, but we must, nevertheless, obey those we have; and perhaps it is more laudable to obey the bad than the good. So long as the image of the ancient and received laws of this monarchy shall shine in any corner of the kingdom, there will I be. If they unhappily come to thwart and contradict one another, so as to produce two factions of doubtful and difficult choice, I would willingly choose to withdraw and escape the storm; in the meantime, nature or the hazards of war may lend me a helping hand. Between Caesar and Pompey, I should have declared myself frankly; but among the three robbers who came after, a man must have either hidden himself or gone along with the current of the time — which I think one may fairly do when reason no longer guides:
"Quo diversus abis?"
["Whither dost thou wander?" — Aeneid, v. 166.]

This medley is a little off my theme; I am going out of my way; but it is more by licence than oversight; my fancies follow one another, but sometimes at a great distance, and look towards each other, but with a sideways glance. I have read a dialogue of Plato of similarly motley and fantastic composition, beginning about love and ending about rhetoric; they don't fear these variations, and have a marvellous grace in letting themselves be carried away at the wind's pleasure — or at least to seem as though they were. The titles of my chapters don't always cover the whole matter; often they signal it by some mark only, like those others, Andria, Eunuchus; or these, Sulla, Cicero, Torquatus. I love a poetic progress, by leaps and skips; it is an art, as Plato says, light, nimble, daemonic. There are pieces in Plutarch where he forgets his theme; where the proposition of his argument is only found in passing, stuffed and half stifled in foreign matter. Observe his footsteps in the Daemon of Socrates. O God! how beautiful are those playful digressions, those variations and sideways excursions, all the more so when they seem most accidental and casual. It is the careless reader who loses my subject, not I; somewhere in a corner there will always be found some word or other to the purpose, even if it lies very close. I ramble indiscriminately and tumultuously; my style and my wit wander at the same rate. He must play the fool a little who would not be deemed wholly a fool, say both the precepts and, still more, the examples of our masters. A thousand poets flag and languish after a prosaic manner; but the best old prose (and I sprinkle it here up and down indifferently for verse) shines throughout with the lustre, vigour, and boldness of poetry, and not without some air of its fury. And certainly prose ought to have the pre-eminence in speech. The poet, says Plato, seated on the muses' tripod, pours out in a fury whatever comes into his mouth, like the pipe of a fountain, without considering or weighing it; and things escape him of various colours, of contrary substance, in an irregular torrent. Plato himself is throughout poetic; and the old theology, as the learned tell us, is all poetry; and the first philosophy is the original language of the gods. I would have my matter distinguish itself; it sufficiently shows where it changes, where it concludes, where it begins, and where it picks up again, without interlacing it with words of connection brought in to help weak or careless ears, and without explaining myself. Who would not rather not be read at all than read in a drowsy or perfunctory manner?
"Nihil est tam utile, quod intransitu prosit."
["Nothing is so useful as that which is cursorily so." — Seneca, Ep., 2.]

If taking books in hand were the same as learning them, looking at them as considering them, and running over them slightly as grasping them, then I would be wrong to make myself out so ignorant as I say I am. Since I cannot fix my reader's attention by the weight of what I write, manco male if I should manage it by my intricacies. "Well, but he will afterwards repent that ever he troubled himself about it." Quite so; but he will still have been troubled. Besides, there are some humours in which comprehension breeds disdain; who will think the better of me for not understanding what I say, and will conclude the depth of my sense by its obscurity; which, to speak in good earnest, I mortally hate, and would avoid if I could. Aristotle boasts somewhere in his writings that he aimed at it: a vicious affectation. The frequent breaks into short chapters that I used at the beginning of my book, having since seemed to me to scatter the attention before it was raised, since it made them disdain to settle on so little, I have on that account made them longer, of the kind that require deliberate proposition and assigned leisure. In such an occupation, if you won't give a man an hour, you give him nothing; and you do nothing for him for whom you only do something while you are doing something else. To this may be added that I have, perhaps, some particular obligation to speak only by halves, to speak confusedly and discordantly. I am therefore angry with this killjoy reason and its extravagant projects that worry one's life — and its opinions, however fine and subtle and however true they may be, I think too dear bought and too inconvenient.
