It belongs perhaps only to that one all-powerful testimony to tell us, "This is, and that is, and not the other." God should be believed; and certainly with very good reason; but not one of us is for that reason to be astonished at his own narration — and he must necessarily be astonished if he is not out of his wits — whether he is using it about other men's affairs or against himself.
I am plain and heavy, and I stick to the solid and the probable, avoiding those ancient reproaches:
"Majorem fidem homines adhibent iis, quae non intelligunt; --Cupidine humani ingenii libentius obscura creduntur."
["Men give most credence to things they do not understand; and from the appetite of the human mind, obscure things are more readily believed." The second sentence is from Tacitus, Hist. 1. 22.]

I see very well that people get angry, and that I am forbidden to doubt on pain of monstrous insults; a novel way of persuading! Thank God, I am not to be slapped into belief. Let them be angry with those who accuse their opinion of being false; I only accuse it of difficulty and rashness, and I condemn the opposite affirmation just as much, though not so imperiously, as they do. He who tries to establish a proposition by authority and bluster shows that his reasoning is very weak. In a verbal and scholastic argument, let them have as much appearance of being right as their opponents;
"Videantur sane, non affirmentur modo;"
["Let them indeed appear to be so; let them not merely be asserted (Let them state the probabilities, but not affirm.)" --Cicero, Acad., ii. 27.]

but in the real consequences they draw from it, these have a great advantage. To kill men, a clear and strong light is required, and our life is too real and essential to vouch for these supernatural and fantastic accidents.

As for drugs and poisons, I leave them out of my reckoning, since they are the worst kind of homicides; yet even there it is said men cannot always rely on the personal confessions of these people, since they have sometimes been known to confess to the murder of persons later found alive and well. In these other outlandish accusations, I would say that it is enough that a man, with whatever credentials he may have, should be believed about human matters; but in what is beyond his understanding, and of supernatural effect, he ought to be believed only when authorised by a supernatural sanction. The privilege which it has pleased Almighty God to give to some of His witnesses ought not to be cheaply and lightly extended. My ears are battered with a thousand tales like these: "Three persons saw him on such a day in the east, three the next day in the west, at such an hour, in such a place, and in such clothes"; I would not believe it myself. How much more natural and likely I find it that two men should lie than that one man in twelve hours' time should fly with the wind from east to west? How much more natural that our understanding should be carried out of its place by the volatility of our disordered minds, than that one of us, flesh and bones as we are, should be carried by a strange spirit on a broomstick up a chimney? Let us not seek illusions from outside and from the unknown — we who are perpetually unsettled by illusions of our own. It seems to me a man may be excused for disbelieving a miracle, at least wherever one can sidestep its claim to be a miracle by non-miraculous means; and I am of St. Augustine's opinion, that "it is better to lean toward doubt than toward certainty in things hard to prove and dangerous to believe."

It is now some years ago that I travelled through the territories of a sovereign prince who, as a favour to me and to reduce my unbelief, did me the honour to let me see, in his own presence and in a private place, ten or twelve prisoners of this sort — and among them, an old woman, a real witch in foulness and deformity, who had long been famous in that profession. I saw the proofs and free confessions, and I do not know what insensible mark on the wretched creature; I examined and talked with her and the rest as much and as long as I wanted, and gave the best and soundest attention I could, and I am not a man to let my judgment be made captive by preconception. In the end, in all conscience, I would sooner have prescribed them hellebore than hemlock;
"Captisque res magis mentibus, quam consceleratis similis visa;"
["The thing was more to be ascribed to madness than to malice." ("The thing seemed to resemble minds possessed rather than guilty.") --Livy, viii. 18.]

justice has its proper corrections for such illnesses. As for the objections and arguments worthy men have made to me, both there and often in other places, I have met none that have convinced me, and none that have not admitted a more likely solution than their conclusions. It is true that the proofs and reasons founded on experience and fact I do not try to untie, since they have no end; I often cut them, as Alexander did the Gordian knot. After all, it is paying a very high price for one's conjectures to have a man roasted alive on the strength of them.

We are told by several examples — Praestantius's father, for one — that, being more deeply asleep than men usually are, he fancied himself to be a mare and that he served the soldiers as a packhorse; and what he fancied himself to be, he actually became. If sorcerers really dream so materially, if dreams can sometimes so embody themselves in effects, still I cannot believe that our will should on that account answer to justice. I say this as one who is neither judge nor privy councillor, and who thinks himself, by many degrees, unworthy to be either — but as one of the common sort, born and pledged to obey public reason in both its words and its acts. Anyone who recorded my idle talk as something prejudicial to the smallest law, opinion, or custom of his parish would do himself a great deal of harm, and me much more; for in what I say, I guarantee no other certainty than that this is what I had in my mind at the time — a tumultuous and wavering thought. All I say is by way of discussion, and nothing by way of advice:
"Nec me pudet, ut istos fateri nescire, quod nesciam;"
["Nor am I ashamed, as they are, to confess that I do not know what I do not know."--Cicero, Tusc. Quaes., i. 25.]

I would not speak so boldly if it were my right to be believed; and so I told a great man who complained of the sharpness and contentiousness of my exhortations. Seeing you ready and prepared on one side, I propose the other to you, with all the diligence and care I can, to clarify your judgment, not to compel it. God has your hearts in His hand and will furnish you with the means of choice. I am not so presumptuous as even to wish that my opinions should sway you in a thing of such importance; my fortune has not trained them up to such powerful and lofty conclusions. Truly, I have not only a great many quirks but also a great many opinions that I would try to make my son dislike, if I had one. What if the truest are not always the most convenient for man, given how wild a composition we are?

Whether it fits or not, it doesn't much matter — there is a common proverb in Italy that he does not know Venus in her perfect sweetness who has never lain with a lame mistress. Fortune, or some particular incident, long ago put this saying into people's mouths; and the same is said of men as well as of women — for the Queen of the Amazons answered the Scythian who courted her: "Lame men perform best." In this feminine republic, to evade the dominion of the males, they crippled them in infancy — arms, legs, and the other limbs that gave them the advantage — and only made use of them for the one thing that we in these parts of the world also use them for. I would have been inclined to think that the shuffling gait of a lame mistress added some new pleasure to the work and some extra titillation for those at the sport; but I have lately learned that ancient philosophy itself has decided the question, saying that, because the legs and thighs of lame women do not receive their proper nourishment (owing to their defect), it follows that the genital parts above are fuller and better supplied and much more vigorous; or else that this defect, hindering exercise, leaves those who suffer it less worn down by activity, so that they come more intact to the sports of Venus — which is also why the Greeks decried women weavers as being hotter than other women, because of their sedentary trade, carried on without much exercise of the body. What is there we cannot reason about at this rate? I might also say of these weavers that the rocking back and forth at their work rouses and provokes their desire, as the swaying and jolting of carriages does that of our ladies.

Don't these examples bear out what I said at the start: that our reasoning often runs ahead of the effect, and has so endless a range of jurisdiction that it judges and exercises itself even on emptiness and non-existence? Besides our talent for fabricating reasons for all sorts of dreams, our imagination is equally ready to take impressions of falsity from the most trivial appearances; for, on the sole authority of this ancient and common proverb, I formerly made myself believe that I had taken more pleasure in a woman because she was not straight, and put that deformity down as one of her graces.

Torquato Tasso, in his comparison between France and Italy, says he has observed that our legs are generally smaller than those of Italian gentlemen, and attributes the cause to our being continually on horseback; which is the very same cause from which Suetonius draws the opposite conclusion, for he says on the contrary that Germanicus enlarged his legs by the continuation of the same exercise.

Nothing is so pliable and erratic as our understanding; it is the shoe of Theramenes, which fits any foot. It is double and various, and the matters it deals with are double and various too. "Give me a drachma of silver," said a Cynic philosopher to Antigonus. "That is not a present befitting a king," he replied. "Give me then a talent," said the other. "That is not a present befitting a Cynic."

"Seu plures calor ille vias et caeca relaxat Spiramenta, novas veniat qua succus in herbas; Seu durat magis, et venas astringit hiantes; Ne tenues pluviae, rapidive potentia solis Acrior, aut Boreae penetrabile frigus adurat."

["Whether the heat opens up more passages and hidden pores through which the sap can pass into the new-growing herbs; or whether instead it hardens and binds the gaping veins, so that the thin rains and the keener force of the violent sun, or the penetrating cold of Boreas, may not damage them."--Virg., Georg., i. 89.]
"Ogni medaglia ha il suo rovescio."
["Every medal has its reverse."--Italian Proverb.]

This is why Clitomachus said long ago that Carneades had outdone the labours of Hercules in having eradicated consent from men — that is to say, opinion and the courage to judge. This so vigorous fancy of Carneades sprang, in my opinion, originally from the impudence of those who claimed to know everything and their boundless self-conceit. Aesop was put up for sale with two other slaves; the buyer asked the first what he could do, and he, to raise his price, promised mountains and marvels — saying he could do this and that and I don't know what; the second said as much of himself or more; when it came to Aesop's turn and he too was asked what he could do, he said, "Nothing, for these two have taken up everything before me; they know it all." The same has happened in the schools of philosophy: the arrogance of those who claimed the capacity of all things for the human mind created in others, out of spite and rivalry, the opposite opinion that it is capable of nothing; the one party holding the same extreme in ignorance that the others hold in knowledge — to make it manifestly undeniable that man is immoderate throughout, and can never stop except of necessity and from being unable to go any further.

title: Of physiognomy
paragraphs: Almost all the opinions we hold are taken on authority and trust — and that's not entirely a bad thing; in so weak an age, we could hardly choose worse than by relying on ourselves. The image of Socrates' conversations that his friends have handed down to us, we approve of only out of reverence for public sanction; we don't approve it from our own knowledge. His discourses are not in our style; if anything of the kind sprang up today, few people would value it. We can't recognise any grace that isn't sharpened, puffed out, and inflated by art; whatever glides past in its own purity and simplicity easily escapes a sight as coarse as ours. Such grace has a delicate, hidden beauty that requires a clear and purified vision to discover its secret light. Isn't simplicity, the way we use the word, close kin to foolishness, a quality fit for reproach? Socrates makes his soul move in a natural, ordinary motion. A peasant said this; a woman said that; he has nobody in his mouth but carters, joiners, cobblers, and masons. His arguments and analogies are drawn from the most common, familiar human activities; everyone understands him. We would never have recognised the nobility and splendour of his admirable thoughts under so plain a form — we, who think everything low and flat that isn't lifted up by learned doctrine, and who see no riches except in pomp and display. This world of ours is built only for show: men are puffed up with wind and batted back and forth like tennis balls. He set himself no vain, idle fancies; his aim was to give us precepts and things that genuinely and fitly serve the use of life;
"Servare modum, finemque tenere, Naturamque sequi."
["To keep a just mean, to observe a just limit, and to follow Nature." — Lucan, ii. 381.]

He was also always one and the same, and raised himself, not in bursts but by temperament, to the highest pitch of vigour — or better put, he didn't climb up at all but rather brought down, reduced, and subjected all hardships and difficulties to his original, natural state. In Cato, by contrast, it's perfectly obvious that the procedure goes far beyond the ordinary way of men: in the brave exploits of his life, and in his death, we always find him mounted on the great horse. Socrates, meanwhile, walks always on the ground, and with a gentle, ordinary pace handles the most useful matters; both at his death and in the harshest difficulties that could arise, he carries himself in the common manner of human life.

It has worked out well that the man most worthy to be known and held up as an example for the world should be the one we know most certainly about. He has been examined by the most clear-sighted men who ever lived; the testimonies we have of him are admirable both in their accuracy and their fullness. It's a great thing that he was able to order the pure imaginations of a child so that, without altering or twisting them, he produced from them the most beautiful effects of our soul. He shows the soul as neither elevated nor rich; he simply represents it as sound — but certainly with a brisk, robust health. By these common, natural springs, by these ordinary, popular thoughts, without being shaken or thrown off, he set up not only the most disciplined but the most lofty and vigorous beliefs, actions, and manners that ever existed. He's the one who brought human wisdom back down from heaven, where she was wasting her time, to restore her to man — with whom her most fitting and important business lies. Watch him plead before his judges; observe by what reasoning he rouses his courage to face the hazards of war; with what arguments he fortifies his patience against slander, tyranny, death, and his wife's bad temper. You'll find nothing in all this borrowed from arts and sciences; the simplest person can find his own means and strength in it. It's not possible to be more unassuming or to walk more low. He did human nature a great kindness by showing it how much it can do of itself.

We're all richer than we think we are, but we're taught to borrow and to beg, and brought up to make more use of what belongs to others than of what's our own. In nothing can man fix himself to his actual need: of pleasure, wealth, and power he grabs at more than he can hold; his greed is incapable of moderation. And I find that he's the same in his appetite for knowledge: he cuts out more work for himself than he can do, and more than he needs to do, stretching the usefulness of knowledge to the limits of its subject matter:
"Ut omnium rerum, sic litterarum quoque, intemperantia laboramus."
["We carry intemperance into the study of literature, as we do into everything else." — Seneca, Ep., 106.]
And Tacitus was right to praise Agricola's mother for having restrained her son in his too-violent appetite for learning.

It's a good, if you think about it properly, that has in it — like our other goods — a great deal of vanity and weakness proper and natural to itself, and that costs a lot. Acquiring it is far more hazardous than acquiring any other food or drink. With other things, what we've bought we carry home in some container, and there we have full leisure to examine our purchase — how much we'll eat or drink of it, and when. But sciences we can stow only in the soul from the very first; we swallow them in buying, and come back from the market already either infected or improved. Some only burden and overload the stomach instead of nourishing it; and some, under the pretext of curing, actually poison us. I've been pleased, in places I've travelled, to see men in their devotion take a vow of ignorance alongside vows of chastity, poverty, and penitence. It's also a kind of gelding of our unruly appetites to blunt this craving that drives us to study books, and to deprive the soul of that voluptuous self-satisfaction that tickles us with the opinion of knowledge; and it fully completes the vow of poverty to add to it that of the mind. We need little doctrine to live at ease. Socrates teaches us that this is already in us — and the way to find it, and the manner of using it. All our capacity that goes beyond the natural is pretty much superfluous and vain; it's a lot if it doesn't burden and clutter us rather than help us:
"Paucis opus est literis ad mentem bonam:"
["Little learning is needed to form a sound mind." — Seneca, Ep., 106.]

It's a feverish excess of the mind, a stormy and restless instrument. Just collect yourself, and you'll find within yourself natural arguments against death — true ones, the fittest to serve you when you need them. They're the arguments that make a peasant, and whole nations, die with as much firmness as a philosopher. Would I have died less cheerfully before I'd read Cicero's Tusculan Disputations? I don't believe so; and even when I find myself at my best, I notice that my tongue is enriched but my courage hardly elevated by them. My courage is just what nature framed at the outset, and it defends itself against the struggle only in a natural, ordinary way. Books have served me less for instruction than for exercise. What if knowledge, in trying to arm us with new defences against natural troubles, has only impressed their weight and greatness more deeply on our imagination, rather than securing us with her reasons and subtleties? They're subtleties, indeed, with which she often alarms us to little purpose. Just notice how many slight, frivolous, and — when examined closely — incorporeal arguments the closest, wisest authors scatter around one good one. They're verbal tricks and fallacies to amuse and fool us; but since they may have some profit, I won't sift them further. Many of that sort are scattered up and down this book, either borrowed or by imitation. So one ought to be a little careful not to call something forceful when it's only a clever turn of writing, not to call something solid when it's only sharp, not to call something good when it's only fine:
"Quae magis gustata quam potata, delectant,"
["Which more delight in the tasting than in being drunk." — Cicero, Tusc. Quaes., v. 5.]
everything that pleases doesn't nourish:
"Ubi non ingenii, sed animi negotium agitur."
["Where the question is not about the wit, but about the soul." — Seneca, Ep., 75.]

To see the trouble Seneca takes to brace himself against death — to see him sweat and pant so to harden and encourage himself, and bustle so long on this perch — would have lessened his reputation in my eyes, if he hadn't held himself very bravely at the end. His so ardent and frequent agitations show that he was, in himself, impetuous and passionate.
"Magnus animus remissius loquitur, et securius . . . non est alius ingenio, alius animo color;"
["A great courage speaks more calmly and more securely. There is not one complexion for the wit and another for the mind." — Seneca, Ep. 114, 115.]

He has to convince himself at his own expense, and he reveals in a way that he was hard pressed by his enemy. Plutarch's manner, in being more disdainful and more sustained, is in my opinion that much more manly and persuasive; and I'm inclined to believe his soul had more assured and more regular motions. The one — Seneca — is sharper, pricks us and makes us flinch, and touches the soul more; the other is more steadily solid, forms, establishes, and supports us, and touches the understanding more. Seneca carries away the judgment, Plutarch wins it. I've likewise seen other writings, more revered still than these, that in describing the struggle they maintain against the temptations of the flesh paint those temptations so sharp, so powerful, so invincible, that we who are of the common herd are as much astonished at the strangeness and unknown force of their temptation as at their resisting it.

To what end do we so arm ourselves with this harness of science? Let's look down at the poor people we see scattered across the face of the earth, head down and intent on their work, who know neither Aristotle nor Cato, neither example nor precept. From these, nature every day extracts effects of constancy and patience purer and more manly than the ones we so inquisitively study in the schools. How many do I see, regularly, who shrug off poverty? How many who long to die, or who die without alarm or regret? The man who is now digging in my garden has this morning buried his father or his son. The very names by which they call their diseases sweeten and soften the harshness of them: tuberculosis is just a cough to them, dysentery just a looseness, pleurisy just a stitch. And as gently as they name them, so patiently do they endure them; the diseases are really great and grievous only when they interrupt their ordinary work. They never take to their beds except to die:
"Simplex illa et aperta virtus in obscuram et solertem scientiam versa est."
["That overt and simple virtue is converted into an obscure and subtle science." — Seneca, Ep., 95.]

I was writing this around the time when a great burden of our domestic troubles lay with all its weight on me for several months. I had the enemy at my door on one side, and the freebooters — worse enemies — on the other,
"Non armis, sed vitiis, certatur;"
["The fight is not with arms, but with vices." — Seneca, Ep., 95.]
and I was suffering every kind of military injury at once:
"Hostis adest dextra laevaque a parte timendus. Vicinoque malo terret utrumque latus."
["Right and left a formidable enemy is to be feared, and threatens me on both sides with impending danger." — Ovid, De Ponto, i. 3, 57.]

A monstrous war! Other wars are aimed at strangers; this one is aimed at itself, destroying itself with its own poison. It's of such a malignant and ruinous nature that it ruins itself along with everything else, and in its own rage mangles and tears itself to pieces. We more often see it dissolve of itself than collapse from scarcity of supplies or the force of the enemy. All discipline evades it. It comes to put down sedition and is itself full of sedition; it would chastise disobedience and is itself the example; employed to defend the laws, it rebels against its own. What a condition we're in! Our medicine makes us sick!
"Nostre mal s'empoisonne Du secours qu'on luy donne."
"Exuperat magis, aegrescitque medendo."
["Our disease is poisoned with its very remedies." — Aeneid, xii. 46.]
"Omnia fanda, nefanda, malo permista furore, Justificam nobis mentem avertere deorum."
["Right and wrong, all shuffled together in this wicked fury, have deprived us of the gods' protection." — Catullus, De Nuptiis Pelei et Thetidos, V. 405.]

At the beginning of these popular sicknesses, you can still distinguish the healthy from the sick; but when they go on, as ours have done, the whole body is infected from head to foot. No part is free from corruption — for there's no air men so greedily breathe in, none that diffuses itself so quickly and penetrates so deep, as the air of licence. Our armies subsist and hold together only by the cement of foreigners; we can no longer raise a steady, regular army out of Frenchmen. What a shame! There's no discipline left except what we see in the mercenary soldiers. As for us, our conduct is left to anyone's discretion — and not to that of the chief, but to each man's own. The general has a harder game to play within his own army than against the enemy outside. He's the one who has to follow, to court his soldiers, to give way to them; he alone has to obey: all the rest is dissolution and unbridled licence. It pleases me to notice how much cowardice and timidity there is in ambition, by what abject, servile paths it has to reach its end; but it displeases me to see good and generous natures, capable of justice, being daily corrupted in the management and command of this chaos. Long toleration breeds habit; habit, consent and imitation. We had enough ill-formed souls already, without spoiling those that were generous and good — so that if we go on like this, there'll be scarcely anyone left we could entrust with the health of this State of ours, in case fortune should happen to restore it:
"Hunc saltem everso juvenem succurrere seclo, Ne prohibete."
["Forbid not, at least, that this young man repair this ruined age." — Virgil, Georg., i. 500. Montaigne probably refers to Henry, king of Navarre, afterwards Henry IV.]

What has become of the old precept, "That soldiers should fear their chief more than the enemy"? And of that wonderful example where an orchard enclosed within the perimeter of a Roman camp was seen the day after they broke camp in the same condition — not an apple, however ripe and delicious, pulled off, but every one left to its owner? I could wish our young men, instead of spending their time on less fruitful travels and less honourable pursuits, would devote half of it to being eyewitnesses of naval exploits under some good captain of Rhodes, and the other half to observing the discipline of the Turkish armies; for theirs has many differences from, and advantages over, ours. One difference is that our soldiers grow more dissolute on expeditions, theirs more temperate and circumspect. Thefts and insolences against the common people — which are only punished with a cudgel in peacetime — are capital offences in war. For an egg taken by a Turkish soldier without payment, the fixed rate is fifty blows with a stick; for anything else, of whatever kind, no matter how trivial, that isn't necessary for nourishment, they're immediately impaled or beheaded without mercy. I'm astonished, in the history of Selim — the most cruel conqueror who ever lived — to see that when he subdued Egypt, the beautiful gardens around Damascus, all open and in a conquered land, with his army encamped on the very spot, were left untouched by the soldiers' hands, because they hadn't received the signal to pillage.

But is there any disease in a government worth treating with such a deadly drug? No, said Favonius — not even the tyrannical usurpation of a commonwealth. Plato, likewise, will not allow that a man should violate the peace of his country in order to cure it, and by no means approves of a reformation that disturbs and endangers everything, and is to be purchased at the price of the citizens' blood and ruin. He holds that in such a case it's the duty of a good patriot to leave things alone and only pray to God for his extraordinary help; and he seems to be angry with his great friend Dion for having proceeded somewhat otherwise. I was a Platonist on this point before I knew there had ever been such a man as Plato. And if this person should be absolutely rejected from our society — he who by the sincerity of his conscience deserved divine favour so far that he penetrated deep into Christian light, through the universal darkness in which the world was enveloped in his time — then I don't think it becomes us to be instructed by a heathen on how great an impiety it is not to expect from God any relief that is simply his own, without our co-operation. I often wonder whether, among so many men who meddle in such affairs, there isn't some one of so weak an understanding that he's actually been persuaded he was moving toward reformation by the worst of deformations, and toward salvation by the very causes that most certainly damn us — namely, by overthrowing the government, the magistracy, and the laws, in whose protection God has placed him; by dismembering his good mother and giving her limbs to be mangled by her old enemies; by filling fraternal hearts with parricidal hatreds, calling up devils and furies to his aid; and by all this hoping to support the most holy sweetness and justice of the divine law. Ambition, avarice, cruelty, and revenge don't have natural impetuosity enough of their own; let's bait them with the glorious titles of justice and devotion. No worse state of things can be imagined than where wickedness comes to be legitimate and takes on, with the magistrates' permission, the cloak of virtue:
"Nihil in speciem fallacius, quam prava religio, ubi deorum numen praetenditur sceleribus."
["Nothing has a more deceiving face than false religion, where the divinity of the gods is obscured by crimes." — Livy, xxxix. 16.]
The extremest form of injustice, according to Plato, is when what is unjust is reputed to be just.
The common people then suffered very much — and not only present damage:
"Undique totis Usque adeo turbatur agris,"
["Such great disorders overtake our fields on every side." — Virgil, Eclog., i. 11.]

but future damage too. The living were to suffer, and so were those not yet born; they stripped them — and consequently myself — even of hope, taking from them everything they'd laid up to live on for many years:
"Quae nequeunt secum ferre aut abducere, perdunt; Et cremat insontes turba scelesta casas . . . Muris nulla fides, squalent populatibus agri."

["What they cannot bear away, they spoil; and the wicked mob burn harmless houses; walls cannot secure their masters, and the fields are squalid with devastation." — Ovid, Trist., iii. 10, 35; Claudianus, In Eutyop., i. 244.]

Besides this shock, I suffered others — the inconveniences that come with moderation in such a disease. I was robbed on every side: to the Ghibelline I was a Guelph, and to the Guelph a Ghibelline. One of my poets expresses this very well, but I forget where:
["So Tories called me Whig, and Whigs a Tory." — Pope, after Horace.]

The position of my house, and my friendliness with my neighbours, showed one face; my life and my actions showed another. They didn't bring formal accusations against me — they had no grounds. I never hide from the laws, and anyone who'd questioned me would have done himself more damage than me. It was only mute suspicions, whispered about, which never lack for appearance in so confused a mixture, any more than envious or idle minds do. I commonly lend a hand myself to the injurious presumptions that fortune scatters against me, through a habit I've always had of avoiding to justify, excuse, or explain myself — feeling it would compromise my conscience to plead in its own behalf:
"Perspicuitas enim argumentatione elevatur;"
["For perspicuity is lessened by argument." ("The clearness of a cause is clouded by argumentation.") — Cicero, De Nat. Deor., iii. 4.]

and, as if everyone saw into me as clearly as I do myself, instead of retreating from an accusation I step up to meet it, and rather give it some colour by an ironic and mocking confession — if I don't sit completely silent, as though the thing weren't worth answering. But those who take this manner of mine for too haughty a confidence have just as little affection for me as those who interpret it as the weakness of an indefensible case — namely, the great folks, toward whom lack of submission is the great fault, harsh toward any justice that knows and feels itself, and isn't submissive, humble, and suppliant. I've knocked my head against this pillar many times. As it is, an ambitious man, faced with what then happened to me, would have hanged himself; a greedy man would have done the same. I have no care at all for acquiring:
"Si mihi, quod nunc est, etiam minus; et mihi vivam Quod superest aevi, si quid superesse volent dii:"
["If I may have what I now own, or even less, and may live for myself what of life remains, if the gods grant me remaining years." — Horace, Ep., i. 18, 107.]

but the losses that come to me through other people's wrongdoing — whether by theft or violence — go almost as near my heart as they would to that of the most avaricious man. The offence troubles me, beyond comparison, more than the loss itself. A thousand different kinds of mischief fell on me one after another; I could have borne them all at once more cheerfully.

I was already wondering to whom, among my friends, I might commit a needy and discredited old age — and having turned my eyes all the way around, I found myself with no one. To let oneself drop straight down from such a height, you need to fall into the arms of a solid, vigorous, and fortunate friendship: these are very rare, if they exist at all. In the end, I saw it was safest to trust to myself in my own need; and if I should fall on cold terms with Fortune's favour, I should commit myself all the more urgently to my own resources and attach myself, look to myself, all the more closely. People on every occasion throw themselves on foreign help to spare their own — which is the only certain and sufficient help to the man who knows how to arm himself with it. Everyone runs elsewhere, and to the future, because no one has arrived at himself. And I was convinced these were profitable inconveniences: first, because bad pupils have to be corrected with the rod when reason won't do, the way a crooked piece of wood is straightened by fire and pressure. I'd been preaching to myself for a long time to stick to my own concerns and separate myself from other people's affairs — and yet I still turn my eyes aside. A bow, a kind word, a friendly look from some great person tempts me; and God knows how scarce those are in these days, and what they amount to. Without even wrinkling my forehead, I listen to the persuasions offered me to draw me into the marketplace, and refuse so gently that I seem half willing to be overcome. For such an unteachable spirit, blows are needed: this vessel which thus chips and cracks, and is ready to fall apart, must have its hoops hammered back into place with good sound blows of a mallet. Second, this accident served me as exercise to prepare me for worse — if I, who by Fortune's favour and by the cast of my character had hoped to be among the last, should happen to be one of the first hit by this storm; teaching me in time to constrain my life and fit it for a new state. True liberty is to be able to do as one pleases with oneself:
"Potentissimus est, qui se habet in potestate."
["He is most potent who is master of himself." — Seneca, Ep., 94.]

In an ordinary, quiet time, a man prepares himself for moderate, common accidents. But in the confusion we've been in for these thirty years, every Frenchman, whether as an individual or in general, sees himself every hour on the brink of the total ruin and overthrow of his fortune. So much the more should he keep his courage stocked with the strongest and most vigorous provisions. Let's thank fortune that hasn't made us live in an effeminate, idle, and languishing age; some who could never otherwise have been famous will be made so by their misfortunes. Just as I seldom read in histories about the confusions of other states without regretting that I wasn't present, the better to consider them, so does my curiosity make me, in some sort, take pleasure in seeing with my own eyes this notable spectacle of our public death — its form and symptoms. And since I can't prevent it, I'm content to have been destined to be present at it, and so to instruct myself. Just so do we eagerly seek to see — though only in shadow and in the fables of the theatre — the pomp of tragic representations of human fortune. It's not without compassion at what we hear; but we please ourselves by rousing our own displeasure with the rarity of these pitiable events. Nothing tickles that doesn't pinch. And good historians skip over the calm narrations as stagnant water and dead sea, to come back to seditions and wars, which they know we invite them to.

I wonder whether I can decently confess how small a sacrifice of repose and tranquillity it has cost me to have passed more than half my life amid the ruin of my country. I lend myself my patience somewhat too cheap in incidents that don't strike me personally; and I look not so much at what they take from me as at what remains safe, within and without. There's comfort in evading sometimes this, sometimes that, of the evils aimed at us in turn — which, at this moment, hurt only those around us. There's comfort, too, in the fact that in matters of public interest, the more universally my affection is spread, the weaker it is; and we may add that the saying is half true:
"Tantum ex publicis malis sentimus, quantum ad privatas res pertinet;"
["We are only so far sensible of public evils as they respect our private affairs." — Livy, xxx. 44.]

and that the health we fell from was so poor that it itself relieves the regret we ought to feel for it. It was health, but only by comparison with the sickness that has followed. We haven't fallen from any great height. The corruption and brigandage in dignity and office seem to me the least tolerable: we're less injuriously robbed in a wood than in a place of supposed safety. It was a general patchwork of particular members, each one corrupted by emulation of the others, and most of them with old ulcers that neither received nor required any cure. So this convulsion really animated rather than oppressed me — helped by my conscience, which was not only at peace within itself but actually elevated; and I had no reason to complain of myself. Also, as God never sends evils to men any more than goods absolutely pure, my health continued at that time more than usually good; and as I can do nothing without it, there are few things I can't do with it. It afforded me the means to rouse all my faculties and to lay my hand before the wound that might otherwise have gone deeper; and I learned, in my patience, that I had some defence against fortune — that it would take a great shock to throw me out of the saddle. I don't say this to provoke her into giving me a more vigorous charge: I'm her humble servant and submit to her pleasure; let her be content, in God's name. Do I feel her assaults? Yes, I do. But just as those who are possessed and oppressed with grief still sometimes, by intervals, allow themselves a taste of pleasure and are sometimes surprised by a smile, so I have enough power over myself to make my ordinary condition quiet and free from troubling thoughts — yet I still let myself, in fits, be surprised by the stings of those unpleasant imaginings that assault me while I'm arming myself to drive them off, or at least to wrestle with them.

But here was another aggravation of the evil that came on top of the rest: both outside the house and within it, I was assailed by a most violent plague — violent by comparison with all others. For just as sound bodies are subject to more grievous illnesses, since they can only be overcome by such, so my very healthy air, where no contagion in living memory had ever taken hold, became corrupted and produced strange effects:
"Mista senum et juvenum densentur funera; nullum Saeva caput Proserpina fugit;"
["Old and young die in mixed heaps. Cruel Proserpine forbears none." — Horace, Od., i. 28, 19.]

I had to put up with this pleasant condition: that the sight of my own house was frightful to me; whatever I had there was without guard, left to the mercy of anyone who wished to take it. I myself, so hospitable, was in great distress to find a refuge for my family — a distracted family, frightful to its friends and to itself, filling every place with horror where it tried to settle, having to shift its lodging the moment anyone's finger began to ache. Every disease is then concluded to be the plague; people don't stop to examine whether it is or isn't. And the mischief of it is that, according to the rules of art, in every danger you come near you have to undergo a quarantine in fear of the evil, with your imagination tormenting you at pleasure all the while, and turning even your health itself into a fever. Yet all this would have affected me much less if I hadn't been compelled, on top of it, to feel the sufferings of others, and to serve miserably for six months as guide to this caravan; for I carry my own antidotes within myself, which are resolution and patience. Apprehension, which is particularly feared in this disease, doesn't much trouble me; and if, being alone, I'd been taken, it would have been a less dreary and more remote departure. It's a kind of death that I don't think of as the worst sort: it's commonly short, stupid, painless, and consoled by the public condition — without ceremony, without mourning, without a crowd. But as for the people around us, not a hundredth part of them could be saved:
"Videas desertaque regna Pastorum, et longe saltus lateque vacantes."
["You would see shepherds' haunts deserted, and far and wide empty pastures." — Virgil, Georg., iii. 476.]
In this region, my largest income is from manual labour: what a hundred men had ploughed for me lay fallow for a long time.

But then, what an example of resolution we saw in the simplicity of all these people! Generally, every one of them gave up all care of life. The grapes, the country's chief wealth, remained untouched on the vines; every man indifferently prepared for and expected death, either tonight or tomorrow, with a face and voice so far from fear that they seemed to have come to terms with this necessity, taking it for a universal and inevitable sentence. It's always such; but how slight a hold the resolution to die has on us! The distance and difference of a few hours, the mere consideration of company, varies its apprehension. Look at these people: because they die in the same month — children, young people, and old — they're no longer astonished at it; they no longer grieve. I saw some who were afraid of being left behind, as in a dreadful solitude; and the only solicitude I commonly observed among them was for burial — they were troubled to see the dead bodies scattered about the fields, at the mercy of the wild beasts that immediately flocked to them. How different are men's fancies! The Neorites, a nation subdued by Alexander, threw the bodies of their dead into the deepest and least-frequented part of their woods, on purpose to have them eaten there: this was the only burial they reckoned happy. Some men who were still in health dug their own graves; others laid themselves down in them while still alive. And a labourer of mine, in dying, pulled the earth on top of himself with his hands and feet. Wasn't this to nestle and settle himself for an easier sleep? A bravery somewhat like that of the Roman soldiers after the battle of Cannae, who were found with their heads thrust into holes in the earth which they themselves had dug, and, suffocating themselves with their own hands, had pulled the earth in over their ears. In short, a whole province, by common usage, was at once brought to a course of conduct nothing inferior in courage to the most studied and premeditated resolution.

Most of the lessons of science meant to encourage us in such things have more show than force, more ornament than effect. We've abandoned Nature, and now we'll teach her what to do — teach her who so happily and so safely conducted us. And meanwhile, from the traces of her teaching, and from the little of her image that survives, by the benefit of ignorance, in the life of this rustic rabble of unpolished men, science is forced every day to borrow models for her own disciples of constancy, tranquillity, and innocence. It's pretty to see these people, full of so much fine knowledge, having to imitate this foolish simplicity — and to imitate it in the primary actions of virtue; to see that our wisdom must learn even from beasts the most profitable instructions in the greatest and most necessary concerns of life: how to live and die, how to manage our property, love and bring up our children, maintain justice. A singular testimony of human infirmity — and proof that this reason we handle as we please, finding always some diversity and novelty in it, leaves no apparent trace of nature in us. Men have done with nature as perfumers do with oils: they've sophisticated her with so many arguments and far-fetched discourses that she's become variable and individual to each, and has lost her proper, constant, and universal face. So we have to seek testimony from beasts, which aren't subject to favour, corruption, or diversity of opinion. It's true that even beasts themselves don't always go exactly in the path of nature; but where they swerve, it's so slightly that you can always see the track. Like horses that are led, which make many leaps and curvets but always at the length of the halter and still following their leader; or like a young hawk that takes flight but still within the restraint of its tether:
"Exsilia, tormenta, bella, morbos, naufragia meditare . . . ut nullo sis malo tiro."
["To meditate upon banishments, tortures, wars, diseases, and shipwrecks, that thou mayest not be a novice in any disaster." — Seneca, Ep., 91, 107.]
What good does this curiosity do us — to anticipate all the troubles of human nature, and to prepare ourselves with so much effort against things that, perhaps, will never come our way?
"Parem passis tristitiam facit, pati posse;"
["It troubles men as much that they may possibly suffer, as if they really did suffer." — Idem, ibid., 74.]

Not only the blow but the wind of the blow strikes us. Or — like people in a frenzy, for it certainly is a frenzy — to whip yourself right now because Fortune may someday make you undergo it; to put on your furred gown at Midsummer because you'll need it at Christmas! Throw yourselves, they say, into the experience of all evils, the most extreme evils that could possibly befall you, and so be ready for them. On the contrary, the easiest and most natural way would be to banish even the thought of them. They won't come soon enough; their actual being won't last with us long enough. Our mind has to lengthen and extend them; we have to incorporate them in us beforehand and entertain them there, as if otherwise they wouldn't sufficiently press on our senses. "We'll find them heavy enough when they come," says one of our masters — not from the tender sects, but from the most severe; "in the meantime, favour yourself; believe what pleases you best. What good will it do you to anticipate your bad fortune, to lose the present for fear of the future, and to make yourself miserable now because you'll have to be so in time?" Those are his words. Science indeed does us one good office: it instructs us exactly as to the dimensions of evils,
"Curis acuens mortalia corda!"
["Probing mortal hearts with cares." — Virgil, Georg., i. 23.]
A pity if any part of their greatness should escape our sense and knowledge.
It's certain that for the most part the preparation for death has caused more torment than the thing itself. It was rightly said long ago, by a very judicious author:
"Minus afficit sensus fatigatio, quam cogitatio."
["Suffering itself less afflicts the senses than the apprehension of suffering." — Quintilian, Inst. Orat., i. 12.]

The feeling of present death sometimes, on its own, fires us with a prompt resolution not to avoid a thing utterly inevitable. Many gladiators in the old days have been seen who, after fighting timidly and badly, have courageously welcomed death, offering their throats to the enemies' swords and bidding them dispatch. The sight of future death calls for a courage that's slow, and consequently hard to come by. If you don't know how to die, don't worry; nature will, at the time, fully and sufficiently instruct you. She'll do the job for you exactly; don't trouble yourself:
"Incertam frustra, mortales, funeris horam, Quaeritis et qua sit mors aditura via.... Poena minor certam subito perferre ruinam; Quod timeas, gravius sustinuisse diu."

["Mortals, in vain you seek to know the uncertain hour of death, and by what channel it will come upon you." — Propertius, ii. 27, 1. "It is less painful to undergo sudden destruction; it is hard to bear that which you long fear." — Incert. Auct.]

We trouble life with the care of death, and death with the care of life: one torments us, the other frightens us. It's not against death that we prepare — death is too momentary a thing; a quarter of an hour's suffering, without consequences and without lasting damage, doesn't deserve special precepts. To tell the truth, we prepare ourselves against the preparations for death. Philosophy orders us always to have death before our eyes, to see and consider it ahead of time, and then it gives us rules and precautions to ensure that this foresight and thought do us no harm — just like physicians, who throw us into diseases so they may have something on which to use their drugs and their art. If we haven't known how to live, it's unjust to teach us how to die, and to make the end out of keeping with all the rest. If we've known how to live firmly and quietly, we'll know how to die so too. They may boast as much as they please:
"Tota philosophorum vita commentatio mortis est;"
["The whole life of philosophers is the meditation of death." — Cicero, Tusc. Quaes., ii. 30.]

but I fancy that, though it's the end, it's not the aim of life: it's its end, its extremity, but not its object. Life ought to be its own aim, its own design; its true study is to order, govern, and endure itself. Among the various other duties that the general and principal chapter of Knowing How to Live includes, is this article of Knowing How to Die — and if our fears didn't give it weight, one of the lightest of them.

If we judge them by usefulness and by naked truth, the lessons of simplicity aren't much inferior to those that learning teaches us; quite the contrary. Men differ in sentiment and in force; they have to be led to their own good according to their capacities and by various paths:
"Quo me cumque rapit tempestas, deferor hospes."
["Wherever the season takes me (where the tempest drives me), there I am carried as a guest." — Horace, Ep., i. 1, 15.]

I never saw any peasant among my neighbours think over the bearing and assurance with which he should pass over his last hour. Nature teaches him not to think of death until he's actually dying; and then he does it with better grace than Aristotle, on whom death presses with a double weight — both its own and that of so long a premeditation. And that's why Caesar held that the least premeditated death was the easiest and the happiest:
"Plus dolet quam necesse est, qui ante dolet, quam necesse est."
["He grieves more than is necessary, who grieves before it is necessary." — Seneca, Ep., 98.]

The sharpness of this imagination springs from our curiosity: this is how we always trip ourselves up, by trying to anticipate and regulate nature's prescriptions. It's only the doctors who, in the best of health, eat their dinners less well for it and frown at the image of death; the common sort needs no remedy or consolation but just at the moment of the shock, when the blow comes, and they think no more about it than just what they actually endure. Isn't it then, as we say, that the dullness and lack of apprehension in ordinary people give them that patience in present evils, and that profound carelessness about future misfortunes? That their souls, being coarser and duller, are less penetrable and not so easily moved? If so, then let's from now on, in God's name, teach nothing but ignorance; it's the utmost fruit the sciences promise us, and this dullness leads its disciples there so gently.
We have plenty of good masters who interpret natural simplicity. Socrates shall be one; for as I remember, he says something to this effect to the judges who sat in judgment on his life and death.
[What follows is taken from the Apology of Socrates in Plato, chap. 17, etc.]

"I'm afraid, gentlemen, that if I beg you not to put me to death, I'll only confirm the charge of my accusers — which is that I pretend to be wiser than others, as though I had some secret knowledge of things above us and below us. I've neither sought out death nor known it, nor have I ever seen anyone who has tried out its qualities and could inform me of them. Those who fear it presuppose they know it; for my part, I neither know what it is nor what people do in the other world. Death is, perhaps, an indifferent thing; perhaps a thing to be desired. Still, it's to be believed that if it's a passage from one place to another, it's a bettering of one's condition to go and live with so many great persons now deceased, and to be exempt from having anything more to do with unjust and corrupt judges. If it's an annihilation of our being, it's still a bettering of one's condition to enter into a long and peaceable night; we find nothing more sweet in life than quiet repose and a profound sleep without dreams. The things I know to be evil — like injuring my neighbour or disobeying my superior, whether God or man — I carefully avoid; those I don't know to be either good or evil, I cannot fear. If I'm to die and leave you alive, the gods alone know whether things will go better with you or with me. Therefore, as far as I'm concerned, you may do as you think fit. But following my method of advising just and useful things, I say you'll do your consciences more right to set me free, unless you see further into my case than I do; and judging by my past actions, both public and private, by my intentions, and by the profit that so many of our citizens, both young and old, daily get from my conversation, and by the fruit you all reap from me, you can't more properly acquit yourselves toward my merit than by ordering that, given my poverty, I should be maintained at the Prytaneum at public expense — something I have often known you, with less reason, grant to others. Don't take it as obstinacy or disdain that I don't, according to custom, beg and try to move you to pity. I have friends and relatives — for I wasn't, as Homer says, begotten of wood or of stone, any more than other men — who could readily present themselves before you with tears and mourning, and I have three desolate children to move you to compassion. But it would shame our city, at the age I am, and in the reputation for wisdom that's now charged against me, to appear in such a base form. What would men say of the other Athenians? I've always warned those who attended my lectures not to redeem their lives by an unbecoming action; and in the wars of my country — at Amphipolis, Potidaea, Delium, and other expeditions where I served — I effectively showed how far I was from securing my safety by my shame. I'd also compromise your duty, and invite you to unbecoming things; for it's not for my prayers to persuade you, but for the pure and solid reasons of justice. You've sworn to the gods to keep yourselves upright, and it would look as if I suspected you or accused you, as though I didn't believe you would; and I'd testify against myself by not believing in them as I should, by mistrusting their handling of the matter, instead of purely committing my case into their hands. I rely on them completely, and hold myself assured they'll do in this what's fit both for you and for me. Good men, whether living or dead, have no reason to fear the gods."

Isn't this an innocent child's pleading, of an unimaginable loftiness — true, frank, and just, unexampled? And in what a necessity employed! He had every reason to prefer it over the one the great orator Lysias had written for him — admirably composed, indeed, in the judicial style, but unworthy of so noble a defendant. Had a suppliant voice been heard from Socrates' mouth, that lofty virtue would have struck sail at the height of its glory. Ought his rich and powerful nature to have entrusted her defence to art, and, at her highest test, to have renounced truth and simplicity, the ornaments of his speaking, to deck herself out with the embellishments of rhetorical figures and the flourishes of a premeditated speech? He did very wisely, and like himself, not to corrupt the texture of an uncorrupt life, and so sacred an image of human form, in order to spin out his decrepitude another year, and to betray the immortal memory of that glorious end. He owed his life not to himself but to the example of the world; wouldn't it have been a public loss for him to have ended it in a lazy and obscure way? Assuredly, that careless and indifferent way of considering his death deserved that posterity should consider it so much the more — and indeed they did. There's nothing more just in justice than what fortune ordained for his commendation; for the Athenians abhorred those who had caused his death to such a degree that they avoided them like excommunicated persons, and looked on everything they had touched as polluted. No one would wash with them in the public baths, no one would salute them or acknowledge their acquaintance; so that at last, unable to bear this public hatred any longer, they hanged themselves.

If anyone should think that, among so many other examples I had to choose from in Socrates' sayings for my present purpose, I've picked badly with this one — and shall judge this discourse of his to be elevated above common conceptions — I have to tell them I've chosen it precisely because I'm of the opposite opinion: I hold it to be, in rank and simplicity, much below and behind common conceptions. He represents, in an unartful boldness and infantine security, the pure first impression and ignorance of nature. For it's to be believed that we have naturally a fear of pain, but not of death in itself; death is part of our being, no less essential than living.

To what end should nature have begotten in us a hatred of it and a horror of it, considering that it's of such great use to her in maintaining the succession and rotation of her works — and that in this universal republic, it contributes more to birth and increase than to loss and ruin?
"Sic rerum summa novatur."
"Mille animas una necata dedit."
"The failing of one life is the passage to a thousand others."

Nature has imprinted in beasts the care of themselves and of their own preservation: they go so far in avoiding being hit or hurt as to be timorous of being made worse, of being haltered and beaten by us — accidents within their sense and experience; but that we should kill them, they can't fear, and they don't have the faculty to imagine and grasp such a thing as death. It's said that not only do we see them undergo it cheerfully (horses for the most part neighing, and swans singing as they die), but they actually seek it out at need — of which elephants have given many examples.

Besides, isn't the way of arguing that Socrates uses here equally admirable in simplicity and in force? Truly it's much easier to speak like Aristotle and live like Caesar than to speak and live as Socrates did. That's where the extreme degree of perfection and difficulty lies; art can't reach it. Now, our faculties aren't trained for it; we don't try them, we don't know them. We dress ourselves in other people's, and let our own lie idle — as one might say of me, that I've only made a posy here of foreign flowers, having furnished nothing of my own but the thread to tie them together.

Certainly I've yielded so far to public opinion that those borrowed ornaments accompany me; but I don't mean for them to cover me and hide me — that's quite contrary to my design, which is to make a show of nothing but what's my own, what's my own by nature. And had I taken my own advice, I would at all hazards have spoken purely on my own; I more and more load myself every day,

beyond my purpose and original method, out of idleness and the humour of the age. If it doesn't suit me, as I believe it doesn't, it doesn't matter; it may be useful to some others. There are people who quote Plato and Homer who have never seen either of them; and I, too, have taken things from places far enough from their source. Without effort and without learning, having a thousand volumes about me in the place where I write, I can readily borrow, if I please, from a dozen such scrap-gatherers — people I don't bother much about — enough to dress up this essay on Physiognomy. All it takes is a German's preliminary epistle to stuff me with quotations. And so we go in search of a tickling story to cheat a foolish world. These lumber-pies of commonplaces, with which so many people furnish their studies, are of little use except for common subjects, and serve only to show us off rather than to direct us — a ridiculous fruit of learning, that Socrates so pleasantly takes apart against Euthydemus. I've seen books made out of things that were never studied or understood, the author having committed the examination of this or that matter to several of his learned friends to compile it, contenting himself, for his share, with having projected the design, and having tied together by his industry this faggot of unfamiliar provisions; the ink and paper, at least, are his. This is to buy or borrow a book, not to make one; it's to show men, not that he can make a book, but — about which they might be in doubt — that he cannot. A president, where I was, boasted that he had piled together two hundred and odd commonplaces in one of his judgments; in telling which, he deprived himself of the glory he'd gained by it: in my opinion, a paltry and absurd vanity for such a subject and such a person. I do the opposite, and among so many borrowed things am glad if I can steal one, disguising and altering it for some new service — at the risk of having it said that this is because I don't understand its natural use; I give it some particular touch of my own hand, so that it won't be entirely foreign. These people show off their thefts and value themselves on them, and so have more credit with the laws than I do. We naturalists think there's a great and incomparable preference for the honour of invention over that of citation.

If I'd wanted to speak from learning, I'd have spoken sooner; I'd have written nearer to my studies, when I had more wit and a better memory, and would sooner have trusted to the vigour of that age than this one — if I'd meant to make a business of writing. And what if this gracious favour that Fortune has recently offered me on account of this work had come to me at that time of my life, instead of now, when it's equally desirable to possess and soon to lose! Two of my acquaintances, great men in this field, have, in my opinion, lost half by refusing to publish at forty so they could wait until sixty. Maturity has its defects as well as green years — worse ones; and old age is as unfit for this kind of work as for any other. Anyone who commits his decrepitude to the press plays the fool if he thinks to squeeze anything out of it that doesn't taste of dreaming, dotage, and drivelling; the mind grows constipated and thick as one grows old. I deliver my ignorance in pomp and state, and my learning meagrely and poorly — the second accidentally and incidentally, the first principally and expressly. And I write specifically of nothing but nothing, of no science but of that not-science. I've chosen a time when my life, of which I'm to give an account, lies wholly before me; what remains has more to do with death; and of my own death itself, should I find it a talkative death, as others do, I would willingly give an account at my departure.

Socrates was a perfect model in all great qualities, and I'm vexed that he had so deformed a face and body as people say, and so unsuited to the beauty of his soul — he being himself so amorous and such an admirer of beauty. Nature did him wrong. Nothing is more probable than the conformity and relation of the body to the soul:
"Ipsi animi magni refert, quali in corpore locati sint: multa enim e corpore existunt, quae acuant mentem: multa quae obtundant;"
["It is of great consequence in what bodies minds are placed, for many things spring from the body that may sharpen the mind, and many that may blunt it." — Cicero, Tusc. Quaes., i. 33.]

This refers to an unnatural ugliness and deformity of limbs; but we also call ugliness a certain unattractiveness at first sight, mostly lodged in the face, which puts us off on very slight grounds — by the complexion, a spot, a rough expression, for reasons often wholly inexplicable, in members otherwise of good symmetry and proportion. The deformity that clothed the very beautiful soul of La Boetie was of this kind: that superficial ugliness, which is nevertheless always the most imperious, does the least damage to the state of the mind, and carries little certainty in the opinions of men. The other kind, which is never properly called deformity, being more substantial, strikes deeper. Not every shoe of smooth shiny leather, but every shoe well made, shows the shape of the foot inside. As Socrates said of his face, it betrayed an equal ugliness in his soul, if he hadn't corrected it by education; but in saying so, I take it he was joking, as was his way; never did so excellent a soul form itself.

I can't repeat often enough what high esteem I have for beauty — that potent and advantageous quality. He (La Boetie) called it "a short tyranny," and Plato "the privilege of nature." We have nothing that excels it in reputation. It holds first place in human commerce; it presents itself in front; seduces and prepossesses our judgments with great authority and remarkable impression. Phryne would have lost her case in the hands of an excellent advocate had she not, by opening her robe, corrupted her judges with the lustre of her beauty. And I find that Cyrus, Alexander, and Caesar — the three masters of the world — never neglected beauty in their greatest affairs; nor did the first Scipio. The same word in Greek means both fair and good; and Holy Writ often says good when it means fair: I would willingly maintain the priority among good things, according to the song Plato calls trivial, taken from some ancient poet — "health, beauty, riches." Aristotle says that the right of command belongs to the beautiful, and that when there's a person whose beauty approaches the images of the gods, veneration is equally due to him. To the man who asked why people more often and more lastingly keep the company of handsome people, he said, "That question is only for the blind to ask." Most of the philosophers, and the greatest, paid for their schooling and acquired wisdom by the favour and mediation of their beauty. Not only in the men who serve me, but also in beasts, I count it within two fingers' breadth of goodness.

And yet I fancy that those features and moulds of face, and those lineaments by which men guess at our inward complexions and our fortunes to come, is a matter that doesn't very directly or simply fall under the chapter of beauty and deformity — any more than every good odour and serenity of air promises health, or every fog and stink infection in a time of plague. Those who accuse ladies of contradicting their beauty by their behaviour don't always hit the mark; in a face that isn't of the best, there may dwell some air of probity and trustworthiness — as, on the other hand, I've read, between two beautiful eyes, threats of a dangerous and malignant nature. There are favourable physiognomies: so that in a crowd of victorious enemies, you'll readily choose, among men you never saw before, one over another to whom to surrender, and to whom to entrust your life — and yet not properly because of beauty.

A person's look is only a feeble warranty, and yet it's something to be considered. If I had to lash anyone, I'd most severely scourge the wicked ones who give the lie to and betray the promises nature has planted in their foreheads; I'd punish malice with greater severity when it appears under a mild and gentle aspect. It seems that there are some lucky and some unlucky faces; and I believe there's some art in distinguishing affable from merely simple faces, severe from rugged, malicious from pensive, scornful from melancholic, and other such neighbouring qualities. There are beauties that are not only haughty but sour, and others that are not only gentle but, beyond that, insipid; to predict future events from them is a matter I'll leave undecided.

I have, as I've said elsewhere about my own case, simply and implicitly embraced this ancient rule: "That we cannot fail in following Nature," and that the sovereign precept is to conform ourselves to her. I haven't, like Socrates, corrected my natural composition by the force of reason, and haven't disturbed my inclination by art in the least. I've let myself go as I came; I don't struggle. My two principal parts live, of their own accord, in peace and good understanding — but my nurse's milk, thank God, was tolerably wholesome and good. Shall I say in passing that I see held in greater esteem than it deserves, and in use only among us, a certain image of scholastic probity — a slave to precepts, fettered with hope and fear? I'd want it to be such that laws and religions shouldn't make it, but perfect and authorise it; such that it finds it has within itself enough to support itself without help, born and rooted in us from the seed of universal reason imprinted in every man by nature. That reason which strengthens Socrates against his vicious bent renders him obedient to the gods and to men of authority in his city: courageous in the face of death, not because his soul is immortal, but because he himself is mortal. It's a doctrine ruinous to all government, and much more harmful than ingenious and subtle, that persuades the people that a religious belief alone is enough, without conduct, to satisfy divine justice. Practice shows us a vast difference between devotion and conscience.
I have a favourable face, both in form and in interpretation:
"Quid dixi, habere me? imo habui, Chreme."
["What did I say? that I have? no, Chremes, I had." — Terence, Heaut., act i., sec. 2, v. 42.]
"Heu! tantum attriti corporis ossa vides;"
Alas! of a worn body thou seest only the bones.

and one that makes quite the opposite show from that of Socrates. It has often happened that, on the mere credit of my presence and air, people who had no acquaintance with me at all have placed very great confidence in me, whether in their own affairs or mine; and I've obtained, in foreign parts, singular and rare favours because of it. But the following two examples are perhaps worth particular telling. A certain person planned to surprise my house and me in it; his scheme was to come to my gates alone and be insistent about being let in. I knew him by name, and had good reason to place confidence in him, since he was my neighbour and somehow related to me. I had the gates opened to him, as I do for everyone. There I found him, with every appearance of alarm, his horse panting and exhausted. He gave me this story: that about half a league off he had met with a certain enemy of his, whom I also knew, and had heard of their quarrel; that this enemy had given him a very brisk chase; that he had been caught in disorder, his party being too weak, and had fled to my gates for refuge; and that he was in great anxiety for his followers, whom (he said) he assumed were all either dead or taken. I innocently did my best to comfort, reassure, and refresh him. Shortly after came four or five of his soldiers, presenting themselves with the same look of alarm, asking to come in too; and then more, and still more, very well mounted and armed, to the number of twenty-five or thirty, pretending the enemy was at their heels. This mystery began to awaken my suspicion a little; I wasn't unaware of the age I was living in, of how much my house might be envied, and I had several examples among my acquaintance of mishaps of this kind. But thinking there was nothing to be gained, having begun to do them a courtesy, unless I went through with it, and that I couldn't disengage myself from them without spoiling everything, I let myself go in the most natural and simple way, as I always do, and invited them all in. And in truth I'm naturally very little inclined to suspicion and distrust; I willingly lean toward excuse and the gentlest interpretation; I take men as in the common order, and I don't more readily believe in those perverse, unnatural inclinations — unless convinced by manifest evidence — than I do in monsters and miracles. I'm also a man who willingly commits himself to Fortune and throws himself headlong into her arms; and I have so far found more reason to applaud than to blame myself for doing so, since I have always found her more discreet about, and a greater friend to, my affairs than I am myself. There are some actions in my life of which the conduct may justly be called difficult, or, if you like, prudent; of these, supposing a third had been my own, doubtless the other two-thirds were absolutely hers. We make a mistake, I think, in not trusting Heaven enough with our affairs, and in pretending to more from our own conduct than properly belongs to us; and that's why our designs so often miscarry. Heaven is jealous of the extent we attribute to the right of human prudence above its own, and cuts it back all the more sharply the more we amplify it. The latecomers remained on horseback in my courtyard, while their leader, who was with me in the parlour, wouldn't have his horse put up in the stable, saying he should be leaving immediately as soon as he had news of his men. He saw himself master of his plot; nothing remained but execution. He has since said many times — for he wasn't ashamed to tell the story himself — that my face and frankness had snatched the treachery out of his hands. He remounted, his followers — who'd had their eyes fixed on him to see when he would give the signal — being very much astonished to see him come away and leave his prey behind him.

Another time, relying on some truce just published in the army, I took a journey through a very dangerous country. I hadn't gone far before I was discovered, and two or three parties of horsemen were sent out from various places to seize me; one of them caught up with me on the third day, and I was attacked by fifteen or twenty masked gentlemen, followed at a distance by a band of foot soldiers. I was taken, drawn into the thick of a neighbouring forest, dismounted, robbed, my trunks rifled, my money-box taken, and my horses and equipment divided up among new masters. We had, in this copse, a very long argument about my ransom, which they set so high it was obvious they didn't recognise me. They were, moreover, in heated debate about my life; and, in truth, several signs made it clear I was in real danger:
"Tunc animis opus, Aenea, tunc pectore firmo."
["Then, Aeneas, there is need of courage, of a firm heart." — Aeneid, vi. 261.]

I kept insisting on the truce, and would let them keep what they'd already taken from me — which wasn't to be despised — without any promise of further ransom. After we'd been in this place two or three hours, and they had mounted me on a horse not likely to run away from them, and committed me to the guard of fifteen or twenty arquebusiers, and dispersed my servants to others, having given orders that they should carry us off as prisoners by different routes, and I being already two or three musket-shots from the place,
"Jam prece Pollucis, jam Castoris, implorata,"
["By a prayer addressed now to Pollux, now to Castor." — Catullus, lxvi. 65.]

suddenly an unexpected change occurred. I saw the chief return to me with gentler language, searching among the troopers for my scattered belongings, and causing as much as could be recovered to be given back to me, even down to my money-box. But the best present they made me was my liberty; the rest didn't much concern me at the time. I still don't really understand the true cause of so sudden a change, of this reconsideration without any apparent prompting, of so miraculous a repentance, at such a time, in a planned and deliberate enterprise, one that had become legitimate through usage (for from the first I had openly told them of what party I was, and where I was going). The most prominent man among them, who pulled off his mask and told me his name, repeatedly told me at the time, over and over, that I owed my deliverance to my face, and to the liberty and boldness of my speech, that made me unworthy of such a misadventure, and should secure me from its repetition. It's possible the Divine goodness chose to make use of this slight instrument for my preservation; and it defended me, moreover, the next day from other and worse ambushes, of which these very assailants had warned me. The last of these two gentlemen is still living to tell the story; the first was killed not long ago.

If my face didn't speak for me, if men didn't read in my eyes and in my voice the innocence of my intention, I wouldn't have lived so long without quarrels and without giving offence, given my indiscreet readiness to say whatever comes into my head, and to judge so rashly of things. This manner may, with reason, seem uncivil, and ill-suited to our way of conversation; but I've never met anyone who judged it outrageous or malicious, or who took offence at my liberty, if he had it from my own mouth: words repeated have another kind of sound and meaning. Nor do I hate anyone. And I'm so slow to give offence that I can't do it, even for reason's own sake; and when occasion has required me to sentence criminals, I've rather chosen to fail in point of justice than to do it:
"Ut magis peccari nolim, quam satis animi ad vindicanda peccata habeam."
["So that I had rather men should not commit faults than that I should have sufficient courage to condemn them." — Livy, xxxix. 21.]

Aristotle, they say, was reproached for having been too merciful to a wicked man. "I was indeed," said he, "merciful to the man, but not to his wickedness." Ordinary judgments exasperate themselves into punishment by the horror of the deed; but mine is cooled by it.
