Except for old age, which is an undoubted sign of the approach of death, I see in all other events few signs of the future on which we can ground our divination. I judge of myself only by actual sensation, not by reasoning; to what end, since I am resolved to bring nothing to it but expectation and patience? Will you know what I gain by it? Look at those who do otherwise, and who rely on so many different persuasions and counsels; how often the imagination presses on them without any bodily pain. I have many times amused myself, when I was well and out of danger and entirely free from these threatening attacks, by communicating them to physicians as if just beginning to declare themselves in me; I underwent the decree of their dreadful conclusions, being all the while quite at my ease, and so much the more grateful to the favour of God and the better satisfied of the vanity of this art.

There is nothing that ought to be so much recommended to youth as activity and watchfulness: our life is nothing but movement. I bestir myself only with great difficulty, and am slow in everything — in rising, in going to bed, in eating: seven o'clock in the morning is early for me, and where I rule, I never dine before eleven, nor sup till after six. I formerly attributed the cause of the fevers and other illnesses I fell into to the heaviness that long sleeping had brought on me, and I have always repented going back to sleep in the morning. Plato is angrier at excess of sleep than at excess of drink. I love to lie hard, and alone — even without my wife, as kings do; pretty well covered with clothes. They never warm my bed; but since I have grown old, they give me at need cloths to lay on my feet and stomach. They found fault with the great Scipio that he was a great sleeper; not, in my opinion, for any other reason than that men were displeased that he alone should have nothing in him to find fault with. If I am at all particular in my way of life, it is rather in my lying than in anything else; but in general I give way and accommodate myself to necessity as well as any one. Sleep has taken up a great part of my life, and I still continue, at the age I now am, to sleep eight or nine hours at a stretch. I wean myself usefully from this proneness to sloth, and am evidently the better for doing so. I find the change a little hard at first, but in three days it is over; and I see few people who live with less sleep when there is need, who exercise themselves more constantly, or to whom long journeys are less troublesome. My body is capable of a firm, but not of a violent or sudden, exertion. I have given up of late violent exercises and those that make me sweat: my limbs grow weary before they are warm. I can stand a whole day together, and never tire of walking; but from my youth I have preferred riding on paved roads; on foot, I get up to the haunches in dirt, and little fellows as I am are liable in the streets to be elbowed and jostled for want of presence. I have always loved to rest myself, whether sitting or lying, with my heels as high as or higher than my seat.

There is no profession as pleasant as that of arms — a profession both noble in its execution (for valour is the stoutest, proudest, and most generous of all virtues), and noble in its cause; there is no use either more universal or more just than the protection of the peace and greatness of one's country. The company of so many noble, young, and active men delights you; the ordinary sight of so many tragic spectacles, the freedom of unstudied conversation, a masculine and unceremonious way of life, please you; the variety of a thousand different actions; the rousing harmony of martial music that ravishes and inflames both your ears and your soul; the honour of this occupation, even its hardships and difficulties, which Plato holds so light that in his Republic he makes women and children share them — all this is delightful to you. You volunteer for particular exploits and dangers, as you judge of their lustre and importance; and as a volunteer, you find even life itself excusably spent:
"Pulchrumque mori succurrit in armis."
["It is fine to die sword in hand." — Aeneid, ii. 317.]

To fear common dangers that concern so great a multitude of men, not to dare what so many sorts of souls — what a whole people — dare, is for a heart that is poor and mean beyond measure: company encourages even children. If others excel you in knowledge, in gracefulness, in strength, or in fortune, you have alternative resources at your disposal; but to give place to them in steadiness of mind, you can blame no one but yourself. Death is more abject, more languishing, and more troublesome in bed than in a fight; fevers and catarrhs are as painful and mortal as a musket shot. Whoever has fortified himself bravely against the accidents of common life need not work up his courage to be a soldier:
"Vivere, mi Lucili, militare est."
["To live, my Lucilius, is to be a soldier." — Seneca, Epist., 96.]

I do not remember ever having had the itch, and yet scratching is one of nature's sweetest gratifications, and so much at hand; but repentance follows too near. I use it most in my ears, which are now and then apt to itch.

I came into the world with all my senses intact, even to perfection. My stomach is conveniently good, as also my head and my breath; and they uphold themselves for the most part even in the heat of fevers. I have passed the age that some nations, not without reason, have prescribed as so just a limit for life that they would not allow men to exceed it; and yet I have intermissions, though short and inconstant, so clean and sound as to be little inferior to the health and pleasantness of my youth. I don't speak of vigour and sprightliness; it isn't reasonable that they should follow me beyond their limits:
"Non hoc amplius est liminis, aut aquae / Coelestis, patiens latus."
["I am no longer able to stand waiting at a door in the rain." — Horace, Od., iii. 10, 9.]

My face and my eyes betray my condition at once; all my changes begin there, and seem somewhat worse than they really are. My friends often pity me before I feel the cause in myself. My looking-glass does not frighten me; for even in my youth I have more than once had a sickly complexion of ill augury, without any great consequence, so that the physicians, not finding any inward cause matching that outward alteration, attributed it to my mind and to some secret passion that was tormenting me within; but they were deceived. If my body would govern itself as well by my rule as my mind does, we would move a little more at our ease. My mind was then not only free from trouble but, moreover, full of joy and satisfaction, as it commonly is, half by its complexion, half by its design:
"Nec vitiant artus aegrae contagia mentis."
["Nor do the diseases of the body ever affect my mind." — Ovid, Trist., iii. 8, 25.]

I am of the opinion that this temper of my soul has often lifted my body from its lapses; the body is often depressed, but if the other is not brisk and gay, it is at least quiet and at rest. I had a quartan fever for four or five months that made me look miserably ill; my mind was always, if not calm, at least pleasant. If the pain be outside me, the weakness and languor do not much afflict me; I see various bodily faintings that horrify me to name, which yet I should fear less than a thousand passions and agitations of the mind I see about me. I have given up running; it is enough that I can crawl along. Nor do I complain more of the natural decay I feel in myself:
"Quis tumidum guttur miratur in Alpibus?"
["Who is surprised to see a swollen goitre in the Alps?" — Juvenal, xiii. 162.]
— than I regret that my duration shall not be as long and entire as that of an oak.

I have no reason to complain of my imagination; I have had few thoughts in my life that have so much as broken my sleep, except those of desire, which have woken me without afflicting me. I dream but rarely, and then of chimeras and fantastic things, commonly produced from pleasant thoughts, and rather ridiculous than sad; and I believe it is true that dreams are faithful interpreters of our inclinations — but it takes art to sort and understand them.
"Res, quae in vita usurpant homines, cogitant, curant, vident, / Quaeque agunt vigilantes, agitantque, ea si cui in somno accidunt, / Minus mirandum est."
["It is less a wonder if what men practise, think, care for, see, and do when waking should also affect them when asleep." — Attius, cited in Cicero, De Divinatione, i. 22.]

Plato says, moreover, that it is the office of prudence to draw lessons of divination concerning the future from dreams. I don't know about that, but there are wonderful instances of it, related by Socrates, Xenophon, and Aristotle — men of impeccable authority. Historians say that the Atlantes never dream — who also never eat any animal food, which I add because perhaps that is the reason they never dream, for Pythagoras prescribed a certain diet to produce suitable dreams. Mine are very mild, without any tossing of the body or noise of voice. I have seen several of my acquaintance wonderfully disturbed by them. Theon the philosopher walked in his sleep, and so did the servant of Pericles, and that on the tiles and top of the house.

I hardly ever choose my dish at table, but take the next at hand, and reluctantly change it for another. A confusion of meats and a clatter of dishes displease me as much as any other confusion: I am easily satisfied with a few dishes; and I am an enemy to Favorinus's opinion, that at a feast they should snatch away from you the meat you like and set a plate of another sort before you; and that it is a poor supper if you don't fill your guests with the rumps of various fowls, the beccafico being the only bird worth eating whole. I usually eat salt meats, yet I prefer bread that has no salt in it; and my baker never sends any other to my table, contrary to the custom of the country. In my infancy, what they had most to correct in me was a refusal of the things that children usually love best, like sugar, sweetmeats, and march-panes. My tutor fought against this aversion to delicate things as a kind of over-niceness; and indeed it is nothing else but a difficulty of taste, in whatever it applies itself to. Whoever cures a child of an obstinate liking for brown bread, bacon, or garlic, cures him also of pampering his palate. There are some who affect temperance and plainness by sighing for beef and ham among the partridges. It is all very fine; this is the delicacy of the delicate; it is the taste of a pampered fortune that grows tired of ordinary and accustomed things:
"Per quae luxuria divitiarum taedio ludit."
["By which the luxury of wealth makes sport of tedium." — Seneca, Epist., 18.]
Not to make good cheer with what another is enjoying, and to be particular in what one eats, is the essence of this vice:
"Si modica coenare times olus omne patella."
["If you are afraid to sup off all your greens from a small dish." — Horace, Epist., i. 5, 2.]

There is, indeed, this difference, that it is better to oblige one's appetite to things that are most easy to come by; but it is always vice to oblige oneself. I formerly said of a kinsman of mine that he was overnice, who, by having served in our galleys, had unlearned the use of beds and of undressing when he went to sleep.

If I had any sons, I would willingly wish them my fortune. The good father God gave me — who has nothing from me except an acknowledgment of his goodness, but truly a very hearty one — sent me from my cradle to be brought up in a poor village of his, and kept me there all the while I was at nurse, and longer still, raising me in the meanest and commonest way of living:
"Magna pars libertatis est bene moratus venter."
["A well-governed stomach is a great part of liberty." — Seneca, Epist., 123.]

Never take upon yourselves, and much less hand over to your wives, the care of your children's upbringing; leave their formation to fortune, under the common and natural laws; leave it to habit to train them to frugality and hardship, that they may rather descend from rigour than mount up to it. His scheme aimed at yet another end — to make me familiar with the people and with the condition of men who most need our assistance, considering that I should rather pay regard to those who hold out their arms to me than to those who turn their backs on me; and for this reason he had me held at the font by persons of the meanest fortune, so as to oblige and attach me to them.

Nor has his plan succeeded altogether badly with me; for whether on the score of the greater honour in such a condescension, or out of a natural compassion that has a very great power over me, I have an inclination toward the lower sort of people. The faction which I should condemn in our wars I should condemn more sharply when it was flourishing and successful; it would somewhat reconcile me to it to see it miserable and overwhelmed. How willingly do I admire the fine humour of Cheilonis, daughter and wife to kings of Sparta. While her husband Cleombrotus, in the commotion of her city, had the advantage over Leonidas her father, she, like a good daughter, stuck close to her father in all his misery and exile, against the conqueror. But when the chance of war turned, she changed her will with the change of fortune, and bravely turned to her husband's side, and went with him wherever his ruin carried him — admitting, it seems to me, no other choice than to cleave to the side that stood most in need of her, and where she could best show her compassion. I am naturally more inclined to follow the example of Flaminius, who rather lent his help to those who had most need of him than to those who had power to do him good, than that of Pyrrhus, who was of a humour to truckle to the great and lord it over the poor.

Long sittings at table both trouble me and do me harm; for, whether because I was used to it as a child, I eat all the time I sit. Therefore at my own house, though the meals there are of the shortest, I usually sit down a little while after the others, after the manner of Augustus; but I do not imitate him in rising before them; on the contrary, I love to sit on a long while, and to hear them talk, so long as I am not one of the talkers; for I tire and hurt myself by speaking on a full stomach, as much as I find it very wholesome and pleasant to argue and to strain my voice before dinner.

The ancient Greeks and Romans had more reason than we in setting apart for eating, which is one of the principal actions of life — if they were not prevented by other extraordinary business — many hours, and the greater part of the night; eating and drinking less hurriedly than we, who carry on all our actions in a great rush; and in extending this natural pleasure to more leisure and better use, mixing it with profitable conversation.

Those whose business it is to take care of me may easily keep me from eating anything they think will hurt me, for in such matters I never crave nor miss anything I don't see; but if it once comes within my sight, it is no use trying to talk me out of it; so that when I mean to fast I have to be kept apart from the suppers, and only have so much served me as is needed for a prescribed light collation; for if I sit down at the table, I forget my resolution. When I order my cook to change the way of dressing some dish, the whole household knows what it means — that my stomach is out of order, and that I shall not touch it.

I like to have all meats that will bear it very little boiled or roasted, and prefer them very high — even, as regards some, quite gone. Nothing but hardness generally offends me (of any other quality I am as patient and indifferent as any man I have known); so that, contrary to the common temper, even in fish it often happens that I find them both too fresh and too firm — not for want of teeth, which I have always had good, even to excellence, and which age does not now begin to threaten. I have always been used every morning to rub them with a napkin, and before and after dinner. God is favourable to those whom he makes die by degrees; it is the only benefit of old age. The last death will be that much the less painful; it will kill only a half or a quarter of a man. One tooth has lately fallen out without being drawn and without pain; it was the natural term of its duration. That part of me, and several others, are already dead — others half dead, of those that were most active and in the first rank during my vigorous years; so do I melt and steal away from myself. What folly it would be in my understanding to apprehend the height of this fall, when so much of it has already been accomplished, as if it were from the very top! I hope I shall not. In truth, I find a principal consolation in meditating my death — that it will be just and natural — and that from now on I cannot in this matter either require or hope from Destiny any but an unlawful favour. Men make themselves believe that we formerly had longer lives, and greater stature. But they deceive themselves; and Solon, who was of those elder times, limits the duration of life to seventy years. I, who have so much and so universally adored that maxim of the ancients, "The mean is best," and who have held the most moderate measures to be the most perfect — shall I claim an immoderate and extraordinary old age? Whatever happens contrary to nature's course may be troublesome; but whatever comes according to it should always be pleasant:
"Omnia, quae secundum naturam fiunt, sunt habenda in bonis."
["All things that are done according to nature are to be reckoned good." — Cicero, De Senect., c. 19.]
And so, says Plato, the death caused by wounds and diseases is violent; but the death that comes upon us as old age leads us to it is, of all, the easiest, and in some way delicious:
"Vitam adolescentibus vis aufert, senibus maturitas."
["Young men are taken off by violence, old men by maturity." — Cicero, ibid.]

Death mixes and mingles itself with life throughout; decay anticipates death's hour, and pushes itself even into the course of our advance. I have portraits of myself taken at twenty-five and at thirty-five; I compare them with the latest one: how many times it is no longer me; how much more does my present image differ from those earlier ones than it does from my dying one? It is too much to abuse nature, to make her trot so far that she has to leave us at last, and abandon our conduct, our eyes, teeth, legs, and all the rest to the mercy of a foreign and haggard face, and hand us over into the hands of art, being weary of following us herself.

I am not excessively fond either of salads or fruits, except for melons. My father hated all sorts of sauces; I love them all. Eating too much hurts me; but as to the quality of what I eat, I do not yet certainly know that any sort of meat disagrees with me; nor have I noticed that the moon — full or wane — or the season, autumn or spring, has any influence on me. We have in us movements that are inconstant and unknown; radishes, for example, I first found welcome to my stomach, then nauseous, and now welcome again. In several other things, I find my stomach and appetite vary in the same way; I have shifted again and again from white wine to claret, from claret to white wine.

I am a great lover of fish, and consequently make my fasts feasts and feasts fasts; and I believe what some people say, that it is more easily digested than flesh. As I make a conscience of eating flesh on fish days, so my taste makes a conscience of mixing fish and flesh; the difference between them seems to me too great.

From my youth I have sometimes skipped a meal: either to sharpen my appetite for the next morning (for, as Epicurus fasted and made lean meals to accustom his pleasure to make do without abundance, I, on the contrary, do it to prepare my pleasure to make better and more cheerful use of abundance); or I fasted to keep my vigour for the service of some action of body or mind, for both the one and the other are cruelly dulled in me by repletion; and, above all things, I hate that foolish coupling of so healthful and sprightly a goddess with that little belching god, bloated with the fumes of his liquor. Or I fasted to cure my queasy stomach, or for want of fit company; for I say, as that same Epicurus did, that one is not so much to consider what one eats as with whom; and I commend Chilo, who would not engage himself to attend Periander's feast until he had first heard who the other guests were to be. No dish is so agreeable to me, no sauce so appetising, as that which is got out of company. I think it more wholesome to eat more slowly and less, and to eat more often; but I would have appetite and hunger consulted; I should take no pleasure in being fed with three or four pitiful and stinted meals a day, after a medicinal manner. Who will assure me that, if I have a good appetite in the morning, I shall have one again at supper? But we old fellows especially, let us take the first convenient time of eating, and leave to the almanac-makers their hopes and prognostics. The utmost fruit of my health is pleasure: let us catch hold of the present and known. I avoid invariable laws of fasting; let the man who would have one form serve him avoid keeping at it; we harden ourselves in it; our strength is stupefied and laid asleep in it; six months later you will find your stomach so inured to it that all you will have got is the loss of your liberty to do otherwise — but to your prejudice.

I never keep my legs and thighs warmer in winter than in summer; one simple pair of silk stockings is all. I have allowed myself, for the relief of my colds, to keep my head warmer, and my belly, on account of my colic; my diseases in a few days settled in to that, and disdained my ordinary provisions: we soon move from a coif to a kerchief over it, from a simple cap to a quilted hat. The trimmings of the doublet must not merely be ornamental; there must be added a hare's skin, or a vulture's skin, and a cap under the hat; follow this gradation, and you will be off on a very fine course. I will do nothing of the kind, and would willingly leave off what I have begun. If you fall into any new inconvenience, all this is labour lost; you are accustomed to it; seek out something else. So they destroy themselves who submit to be pestered with these enforced and superstitious rules; they must add something more, and something more on top of that; there is no end of it.

As regards our business and our pleasures, it is much more convenient, as the ancients did, to lose one's dinner and defer making good cheer till the hour of retirement and repose, without breaking up the day; and so was I formerly used to do. As to health, since by experience I find the contrary — that it is better to dine, and that the digestion is better while one is awake. I am not very much given to thirst, either well or sick; my mouth, indeed, is apt to be dry, but without thirst; and ordinarily I never drink except with the thirst that is created by eating, and well into the meal. I drink pretty well for a man of my size: in summer, and at a relishing meal, I not only exceed the limits of Augustus, who drank but three times exactly, but, so as not to offend Democritus's rule, who forbade men to stop at four times as an unlucky number, I proceed at need to a fifth glass, about three half-pints. For little glasses are my favourites, and I like to drink them off — which others avoid as an unbecoming thing. I mix my wine sometimes with half water, sometimes with a third part; and when I am at home, by an ancient custom that my father's physician prescribed for him and for himself, the wine intended for me is mixed in the buttery two or three hours before it is brought in. It is said that Cranabs, king of Attica, was the inventor of this custom of diluting wine; whether useful or not, I have heard disputed. I think it more decent and wholesome for children to drink no wine till after sixteen or eighteen years of age. The most usual and common manner of living is the most fitting; all particularity, in my opinion, is to be avoided; and I should as much hate a German who mixed water with his wine as I should a Frenchman who drank it pure. Public usage gives the law in these things.

I fear a mist, and flee from smoke as from the plague: the first repairs I made in my own house were to the chimneys and the privies — the common and insupportable defects of all old buildings; and among the difficulties of war I reckon the choking dust they made us ride in a whole day together. I have a free and easy respiration, and my colds for the most part go off without trouble to the lungs and without a cough.

The heat of summer is more an enemy to me than the cold of winter; for, besides the inconvenience of heat being less easily remedied than cold, and besides the force of the sunbeams that strike on the head, all glaring light offends my eyes, so that I could not now sit at dinner facing a flaming fire.

To dull the whiteness of paper, in those times when I was more used to reading, I laid a piece of glass on my book, and found my eyes much relieved by it. I am to this hour — at the age of fifty-four — ignorant of the use of spectacles; and I can see as far as ever I did, or as anyone else. It is true that in the evening I begin to feel a little disturbance and weakness in my sight if I read — an exercise I have always found troublesome, especially at night. Here is one step back, and a very plain one; I shall retire another, from the second to the third, and so to the fourth, so gently that I shall be stark blind before I am sensible of the age and decay of my sight: so cunningly do the Fatal Sisters unravel our lives. I also doubt whether my hearing is beginning to grow thick; and you will see that I shall have half lost it before I notice, when I shall still lay the blame on the voices of those who speak to me. A man has to screw up his soul to a high pitch to make it sensible how it is ebbing away.

My walking is quick and firm; and I scarcely know which of the two, my mind or my body, I have most trouble to keep in the same state. The preacher is very much my friend who can hold my attention through a whole sermon: in places of ceremony, where everyone's face is so starched, where I have seen the ladies keep even their eyes so fixed, I could never order it so that some part or other of me did not stir; so that even when I was seated, I was never settled. As to gesticulation: I am never without a switch in my hand, walking or riding. As the philosopher Chrysippus's maid said of her master, that he was only drunk in his legs, for it was his habit to be always kicking them about wherever he sat — and she said it when, the wine having made all his companions drunk, he found no change in himself at all — so it may have been said of me from my infancy, that I had either folly or quicksilver in my feet, so much stirring and restlessness there is in them, wherever they are set.

It is unbecoming — and bad for the health, and even for the pleasure of eating — to eat greedily as I do; I often bite my tongue, and sometimes my fingers, in my haste. Diogenes, meeting a boy eating like that, boxed his tutor's ears. There were men at Rome who taught people to chew, as well as to walk, with a good grace. I lose by it the leisure of speaking, which gives great relish to the table — provided the conversation be suitable, that is, pleasant and short.

There is jealousy and envy among our pleasures; they cross and hinder one another. Alcibiades, a man who well understood how to make good cheer, banished even music from the table, that it might not disturb the entertainment of conversation — for the reason, as Plato tells us, "that it is the way of ordinary people to call in fiddlers and singers at their feasts, for want of good conversation and pleasant talk, with which men of understanding know how to entertain one another." Varro requires all this in entertainments: "persons of graceful presence and agreeable conversation, who are neither silent nor garrulous; neatness and delicacy, both of food and place; and fair weather." The art of dining well is no slight art, the pleasure no slight pleasure; neither the greatest captains nor the greatest philosophers have disdained the use or science of eating well. My imagination has delivered to my memory three meals which fortune made wonderfully sweet to me, on different occasions in my more flourishing age; my present state excludes me from such; for every one, according to the good temper of body and mind he then finds himself in, brings to it his own particular grace and savour. I, who only crawl on the earth, hate this inhuman wisdom that would have us despise and hate all care of the body; I look on it as an equal injustice to take a disgust at natural pleasures as to be too much in love with them. Xerxes was a blockhead who, surrounded by all human delights, proposed a reward to anyone who could find him out new ones; but the man who cuts off any of those pleasures that nature has provided for him is not much less of a blockhead. A man should neither pursue nor avoid them, but receive them. I receive them, I confess, a little too warmly and kindly, and easily let myself follow my natural propensions. We have no need to exaggerate their emptiness; they themselves will sufficiently make us sensible of it, thanks to our sick wet-blanket mind, which puts us out of taste with them as with itself; it treats both itself and all it receives one while better, another while worse, according to its insatiable, vagabond, and shifting essence:
"Sincerum est nisi vas, quodcunque infundis, acescit."
["Unless the vessel be clean, whatever you pour into it turns sour." — Horace, Epist., i. 2, 54.]

I, who boast that I so eagerly and particularly embrace the conveniences of life, find them, when I look at them closely, very little more than wind. But what? We are all wind throughout; and even the wind, more sensible than we, loves to bluster and shift from corner to corner, and contents itself with its proper offices, without desiring stability and solidity — qualities not its own.

The pure pleasures of the imagination, as well as the pure pains, are the greatest, say some, as was shown by the scale of Critolaus. No wonder; the imagination makes them to its own liking, and cuts them out of the whole cloth; of this I see notable examples every day, and perhaps to be wished for. But I, of a mixed and heavy condition, cannot snap so quickly at this one simple object, but lazily let myself be carried away by the present pleasures of the general human law — sensibly intellectual, intellectually sensible. The Cyrenaic philosophers hold that as bodily pains, so bodily pleasures are the more powerful, both as double and as more just. There are some, as Aristotle says, who, out of a savage kind of stupidity, dislike them; and I know others who, out of ambition, do the same. Why don't they at the same time give up breathing? Why don't they live on their own resources? Why don't they refuse the light, because it is gratuitous, and costs them neither invention nor effort? Let Mars, Pallas, or Mercury supply them with their light, instead of Venus, Ceres, and Bacchus. These boastful tempers may counterfeit some content — for what won't fancy do? But as to wisdom, there is not a touch of it. Won't they go on looking for the squaring of the circle even when on their wives? I hate that we should be required to have our minds in the clouds when our bodies are at table; I would not have the mind nailed there, nor wallow there; I would have it take its place there and sit, but not lie down. Aristippus maintained only the body, as if we had no soul; Zeno held to the soul alone, as if we had no body; both faultily. Pythagoras, they say, followed a philosophy that was all contemplation, Socrates one that was all conduct and action; Plato found a middle way between the two; but they only say so for the sake of talking. The true balance is to be found in Socrates; and Plato is much more Socratic than Pythagoric, and it becomes him better. When I dance, I dance; when I sleep, I sleep. When I walk alone in a beautiful orchard, if my thoughts have been some part of the time taken up with external occurrences, I bring them back at another time to the walk, to the orchard, to the sweetness of that solitude, and to myself.

Nature has, mother-like, seen to it that the actions she has imposed on us for our necessity should be pleasurable to us; and she invites us to them not only by reason, but also by appetite; it is unjust to break her laws. When I see both Caesar and Alexander, in the middle of their greatest business, so fully enjoying human and bodily pleasures, I do not say that they relaxed their minds; I say that they strengthened them by subjecting these violent occupations and laborious thoughts, by the vigour of their courage, to the ordinary uses of life; wisely so, had they believed that the latter was their ordinary vocation, the former their extraordinary one. We are great fools. "He has spent his life in idleness," we say. "I have done nothing today." What? have you not lived? That is not only the most fundamental of your occupations, but the most illustrious. "Had I been put to the management of great affairs, I would have made it seen what I could do." Have you known how to meditate and manage your life? You have performed the greatest work of all. To show and develop herself, nature needs only fortune; she manifests herself equally at every stage, and behind a curtain as well as without one. Have you known how to regulate your conduct? You have done a great deal more than the man who has composed books. Have you known how to take repose? You have done more than the man who has taken empires and cities.

The glorious masterpiece of man is to live to purpose; all other things — to reign, to lay up treasure, to build — are at most little appendices and props. I take pleasure in seeing the general of an army, at the foot of a breach he is presently to assault, give himself wholly and freely at dinner to talk and be merry with his friends; and in Brutus, when heaven and earth were conspired against him and the Roman liberty, stealing some hour of the night from his rounds to read and annotate Polybius with all calm. It is for little souls, buried under the weight of affairs, not to know how to disengage themselves cleanly from them, nor how to lay them aside and take them up again:
"O fortes, pejoraque passi / Mecum saepe viri! nunc vino pellite curas: / Cras ingens iterabimus aequor."
["O brave spirits, who have often suffered worse with me, drink the cares away; tomorrow we will once more embark on the vast sea." — Horace, Od., i. 7, 30.]

Whether in jest or in earnest, that theological and Sorbonnical wine, and their feasts, have become a proverb, I find it reasonable that they should dine so much the more commodiously and pleasantly, in proportion as they have profitably and seriously spent the morning at the work of their schools. The consciousness of having well spent the other hours is the just and savoury sauce of the dinner table. The sages lived so; and that inimitable striving toward virtue which astonishes us in both the Catos, that severe humour of theirs, even to the point of being importunate, gently submits and yields itself to the laws of the human condition, of Venus and of Bacchus — according to the precepts of their sect, which require the perfect sage to be as expert and intelligent in the use of natural pleasures as in all the other duties of life:
"Cui cor sapiat, ei et sapiat palatus."

Relaxation and ease, it seems to me, wonderfully honour and best become a strong and generous soul. Epaminondas did not think that to take part, and to do so heartily, in the songs and sports and dances of the young men of his city was anything that derogated from the honour of his glorious victories and the perfect purity of manners that was in him. And among the many admirable acts of the elder Scipio — a man worthy to be reputed of a heavenly extraction — there is nothing that gives him more grace than to see him carelessly and childishly amusing himself with gathering and choosing shells and playing at quoits,
[This game, as the "Dictionnaire de Trévoux" describes it, is one in which two persons compete to see which of them can soonest pick up some object.]

— amusing and tickling himself in setting down in comedies the meanest and most popular actions of men. And his head full of the wonderful enterprise of Hannibal and Africa, visiting the schools in Sicily, attending lectures on philosophy — to the point of arming the blind envy of his enemies at Rome. Nor is there anything more remarkable about Socrates than that, old as he was, he found the time to have himself taught dancing and the playing of instruments, and thought it time well spent. This same man was seen in an ecstasy, standing on his feet a whole day and a night together, in the presence of the whole Greek army, surprised and absorbed by some profound thought. He was the first of so many valiant men in the army to run to the rescue of Alcibiades, when he was hard pressed by the enemy, to shield him with his own body, and disengage him from the crowd by sheer force of arms. It was he who, in the battle of Delium, lifted up and saved Xenophon when he had fallen from his horse; and who, among all the people of Athens — enraged as they were by so unworthy a spectacle — first stepped forward to rescue Theramenes, when the Thirty Tyrants were leading him to execution by their attendants, and gave up his bold enterprise only at the request of Theramenes himself, though he had only two others following him in all. He was seen, when courted by a beauty with whom he was in love, to maintain a severe abstinence at need. He was seen ever to go to war and to walk on ice with bare feet; to wear the same robe winter and summer; to surpass all his companions in patience in bearing hardships, and to eat no more at a feast than at his own private dinner. He was seen, for twenty-seven years together, to endure hunger, poverty, the indocility of his children, and the claws of his wife with the same countenance. And, in the end, calumny, tyranny, imprisonment, fetters, and poison. But was this man obliged to drink full bumpers by any rule of civility? He was also the man in the whole army with whom the advantage in drinking remained. And he never refused to play at noisettes, or to ride the hobby-horse with children, and it became him well; for all actions, says philosophy, equally become and equally honour a wise man. We have material enough to do it, and we ought never to be weary of presenting the image of this great man in all the patterns and forms of perfection. There are very few examples of life that are full and pure; and we wrong our teaching every day in setting before ourselves those that are weak and imperfect, scarcely good for any one service, and that rather hold us back — corrupters rather than correctors of manners. The people deceive themselves; a man goes much more easily indeed by the extremes — where the extremity serves him as a boundary, a stop, and a guide — than by the middle way, broad and open; and according to art, more than according to nature; but with much less nobility and credit.

Greatness of soul consists not so much in mounting and pressing forward as in knowing how to govern and circumscribe itself; it takes everything for great that is sufficient, and shows itself by preferring moderate to eminent things. There is nothing so fine and legitimate as well and duly to play the man; nor any science so arduous as to know how to live this life well and naturally; and of all the infirmities we have, the most barbarous is to despise our being.

Whoever wants to keep his spirit apart, when the body is unwell, to protect it from the contagion, let him by all means do it if he can; but otherwise let him on the contrary favour and assist the body, and not refuse to share in its natural pleasures with a conjugal complacency, bringing to it — if it be the wiser — moderation, lest by indiscretion they should be confounded with displeasure. Intemperance is the pest of pleasure; and temperance is not its scourge, but rather its seasoning. Eudoxus, who set the sovereign good in pleasure, and his companions, who put so high a value on it, tasted it in its most charming sweetness by means of temperance, which in them was singular and exemplary.
I enjoin my soul to look on pain and pleasure with an eye equally regulated:
"Eodem enim vitio est effusio animi in laetitia quo in dolore contractio,"
["For the same imperfection produces the expansion of the mind in pleasure and its contraction in sorrow." — Cicero, Tusc. Quaes., iv. 31.]

— and equally firm; but the one gaily and the other sternly; and, so far as it is able, as careful to extinguish the one as to extend the other. Judging rightly of good brings with it the judging soundly of evil. Pain has something of the inevitable in its gentle beginnings, and pleasure something of the avoidable in its excessive end. Plato couples them together, and wills that it should equally be the office of fortitude to fight against pain, and against the immoderate and charming blandishments of pleasure. They are two fountains, from which whoever draws — when and as much as he needs — whether city, man, or beast — is very fortunate. The first is to be taken medicinally and on necessity, and more sparingly; the other for thirst, but not to drunkenness. Pain, pleasure, love, and hatred are the first things a child is sensible of; if, when reason comes, they apply it to themselves, that is virtue.

I have a special vocabulary of my own; I "pass away time" when it is bad and uneasy, but when it is good I do not pass it away: "I taste it over again, and adhere to it"; one must run over the bad and settle on the good. This ordinary phrase of pastime and passing away the time represents the practice of those wise sort of people who think they cannot do better with their lives than let them run out and slide away, pass them over and avoid them, and as much as they can ignore them and shun them as a thing of troublesome and contemptible quality. But I know it to be quite another sort of thing, and find it valuable and convenient even in its latest decay, where I now enjoy it; and nature has delivered it into our hands in such, and in so favourable, circumstances that we have only ourselves to blame if it is troublesome to us or escapes us unprofitably:
"Stulti vita ingrata est, trepida est, tota in futurum fertur."
["A fool's life is thankless, anxious, and wholly bent on the future." — Seneca, Epist., 15.]

Nevertheless I compose myself to lose mine without regret — but as a thing that is perishable by its condition, not as one that molests or annoys me. Nor does it properly become any but those pleased to live not to be displeased when they die. There is good housekeeping in enjoying life: I enjoy it double to what others do, for the measure of its enjoyment depends on our more or less application to it. Chiefly because I perceive mine to be so short in time, I want to extend it in weight; I will stop the speed of its flight by the speed of my grasp, and compensate by vigorous use for the speed of its running away. In proportion as the possession of life is shorter, I must make it deeper and fuller.

Others feel the pleasure of contentment and prosperity; I feel it too, as well as they, but not as it passes and slips by; one should study it, taste it, and ruminate over it to render due thanks to him who grants it to us. They enjoy the other pleasures as they do that of sleep, without knowing it. To the end that even sleep itself should not so stupidly escape me, I have formerly had myself disturbed in my sleep, so that I might better and more sensibly relish and taste it. I deliberate with myself over contentment; I do not skim it over but plumb it; and I bend my reason, now grown perverse and peevish, to receive it. Do I find myself in any calm composure? Is there any pleasure that tickles me? I don't let it just play with my senses; I associate my soul with it too — not to engage itself there, but to take delight in it; not to lose itself, but to be present there; and I employ it, on its part, to view itself in this prosperous state, to weigh and appreciate its happiness, and to amplify it. It reckons how much it stands indebted to God that its conscience and intestine passions are at rest; that the body is in its natural disposition, enjoying in good order and competence the soft and soothing functions by which he, of his grace, is pleased to compensate the sufferings with which his justice, at his good pleasure, chastises us. It reflects how great a benefit it is to be so protected that wherever it turns its eye the heavens are calm around it. No desire, no fear, no doubt troubles the air; no difficulty, past, present, or to come, that its imagination may not pass over without offence. This consideration takes a great lustre from the comparison of differing conditions. So it is that I present to my thought, in a thousand aspects, those whom fortune or their own error carries away and torments; and again, those who — more like me — receive their good fortune so negligently and incuriously. They are the folks who spend their time indeed; they pass over the present and what they possess, to wait on hope, and for shadows and vain images that fancy puts before them:
"Morte obita quales fama est volitare figuras, / Aut quae sopitos deludunt somnia sensus:"
["Such forms as are said to hover about after death, or such dreams as cheat the slumbering senses." — Aeneid, x. 641.]
— which hasten and lengthen their flight in proportion as they are pursued. The fruit and end of their pursuit is to pursue; as Alexander said, that the end of his labour was to labour:
"Nil actum credens, cum quid superesset agendum."
["Thinking nothing was done, if anything remained to be done." — Lucan, ii. 657.]

For my part, then, I love life and cultivate it, such as it has pleased God to bestow it on us. I do not desire that it should be without the necessity of eating and drinking; and I should think it a not less excusable failing to wish it had been twice as long;
"Sapiens divitiarum naturalium quaesitor acerrimus:"
["A wise man is the keenest seeker after natural riches." — Seneca, Epist., 119.]

Nor that we should sustain ourselves by putting only a little of that drug into our mouths by which Epimenides took away his appetite and kept himself alive; nor that we should stupidly beget children with our fingers or heels, but, with reverence be it spoken, that we might voluptuously beget them with our fingers and heels; nor that the body should be without desire, and without titillation. These are ungrateful and wicked complaints. I accept kindly, and with gratitude, what nature has done for me; I am well pleased with it, and proud of it. A man does wrong to that great and omnipotent giver to refuse, annul, or disfigure his gift; all goodness himself, he has made everything good:
"Omnia quae secundum naturam sunt, aestimatione digna sunt."
["All things that are according to nature are worthy of esteem." — Cicero, De Fin., iii. 6.]

Of the philosophical opinions, I preferably embrace those that are most solid — that is to say, the most human and most our own. My talk is, like my manners, low and humble. Philosophy plays the child, in my view, when it puts itself upon its "therefores" to preach to us that it is a barbarous alliance to marry the divine with the earthly, the reasonable with the unreasonable, the severe with the indulgent, the honest with the dishonest; that pleasure is a brutish quality, unworthy to be tasted by a wise man; that the sole pleasure he extracts from the enjoyment of a fair young wife is a pleasure of his conscience at performing an action according to order, as he might put on his boots for a profitable journey. Oh, if its followers had no more right, nor nerves, nor vigour in deflowering their wives than in its lesson!

This is not what Socrates says, who is its master and ours: he values, as he ought, bodily pleasure; but he prefers that of the mind as having more force, constancy, ease, variety, and dignity. This, according to him, by no means goes alone — he is not so extravagant — but only it goes first; temperance with him is the moderator, not the adversary, of pleasure. Nature is a gentle guide — but no more sweet and gentle than prudent and just.
"Intrandum est in rerum naturam, et penitus, quid ea postulet, pervidendum."
["A man must search into the nature of things, and thoroughly examine what she requires." — Cicero, De Fin., v. 16.]

I follow her trail throughout; we have confounded it with artificial tracks; and that academic and peripatetic good, which is "to live according to her," has on this account become hard to limit and explain — and that of the Stoics, neighbouring it, "to consent to nature." Is it not an error to esteem any actions less worthy because they are necessary? And yet they will not get it out of my head that it is a very convenient marriage of pleasure with necessity — with which, says an ancient writer, the gods always conspire. To what end do we dismember by divorce a building so closely and brotherly knit together? Let us, on the contrary, confirm it by mutual offices: let the mind rouse and quicken the heaviness of the body, and the body steady and fix the levity of the soul:

"Qui, velut summum bonum, laudat animae naturam, et, tanquam malum, naturam carnis accusat, profecto et animam carnaliter appetit, et carnem carnaliter fugit; quoniam id vanitate sentit humana, non veritate divina."

["He who commends the nature of the soul as the supreme good, and condemns the nature of the flesh as evil, at once carnally desires the soul, and carnally flies the flesh, because he feels thus from human vanity, not from divine truth." — St. Augustine, De Civitate Dei, xiv. 5.]

In this present that God has made us, there is nothing unworthy of our care; we are answerable for it to a hair; and is it not a commission to man to conduct man according to his condition? It is express, plain, and the very chief commission, and the Creator has seriously and strictly prescribed it to us. Authority has the power to move only in matters of common judgment, and weighs more in a foreign tongue; so let us return to the charge here:
"Stultitiae proprium quis non dixerit, ignave et contumaciter facere, quae facienda sunt; et alio corpus impellere, alio animum; distrahique inter diversissimos motus?"

["Who will not say that it is the mark of folly to perform slothfully and contumaciously what has to be done, and to drive the body one way and the mind another, and to be torn between wholly different motions?" — Seneca, Epist., 74.]

To make this clear, ask anyone, some day, to tell you what whimsies and imaginings he put into his head, on account of which he turned his thoughts away from a good meal and grudged the time he spends in eating; you will find there is nothing so insipid in all the dishes at your table as this wise meditation of his (for the most part we would do better to sleep than to wake to the purpose we wake), and that his discourses and notions are not worth the worst dish there. Even if they were the ecstasies of Archimedes himself, what then? I am not here speaking of, nor mixing with the common run of us ordinary men and the vanity of the thoughts and desires that distract us, those venerable souls, elevated by the ardour of devotion and religion to a constant and conscientious meditation of divine things, who, by the energy of vivid and vehement hope — anticipating the use of the eternal nourishment, the final aim and last step of Christian desires, the sole constant and incorruptible pleasure — disdain to apply themselves to our necessitous, fluid, and ambiguous conveniences, and easily resign to the body the care and use of sensual and temporal pasture. That is a privileged study. Between ourselves, I have always observed supercelestial opinions and subterranean manners to be in singular accord.

Aesop, that great man, saw his master piss as he walked. "What then," he said, "must we drop dung as we run?" Let us manage our time; there is still a great deal of it idle and ill spent. The mind has not enough other hours in which to do its business without disassociating itself from the body in the little space the body needs for its necessities. They would put themselves out of themselves, and escape from being men. It is folly: instead of transforming themselves into angels, they transform themselves into beasts; instead of raising themselves, they lay themselves lower. These transcendent humours frighten me, like high and inaccessible places; and nothing in the life of Socrates is so hard for me to digest as his ecstasies and his commerce with demons; nothing in Plato so human as that for which they say he was called divine; and of our sciences, those seem to me most terrestrial and low that are highest mounted. I find nothing so humble and mortal in the life of Alexander as his fancies about his own immortalisation. Philotas pleasantly twitted him in his reply: he congratulated him by letter on the oracle of Jupiter Ammon, which had placed him among the gods: "On your account I am glad of it, but the men are to be pitied who have to live with a man, and obey him, who exceeds and is not contented with the measure of a man."
"Diis te minorem quod geris, imperas."
["Because you carry yourself lower than the gods, you rule." — Horace, Od., iii. 6, 5.]

The pretty inscription with which the Athenians honoured the entry of Pompey into their city is in keeping with my own sense: "By so much are you a god, as you confess yourself a man." It is an absolute, and as it were divine, perfection for a man to know how to enjoy his being lawfully. We seek out other conditions because we do not understand the use of our own, and go out of ourselves because we do not know how to live within ourselves. It is to no purpose to go on stilts, for, when on stilts, we still have to walk with our legs; and when seated on the most elevated throne in the world, we are still only seated on our backside. The fairest lives, in my opinion, are those that regularly accommodate themselves to the common and human model, without miracle, without extravagance. Old age stands a little in need of a more gentle treatment. Let us recommend that to God, the protector of health and wisdom — but let it be cheerful and sociable:
"Frui paratis et valido mihi, / Latoe, dones, et precor, integra / Cum mente; nec turpem senectam / Degere, nec cithara carentem."
["Grant me, Apollo, to enjoy what I have in good health; let me be sound in mind; let me not lead a dishonourable old age, nor want the cittern." — Horace, Od., i. 31, 17.]
